title: On physical implementability of reinforcement-learning-driven reasoning
summary: In the machine learning community, the reinforcement-learning-driven reasoning process has been intensively studied since around 2025. In this article, we present a negative result on the hardware implementation of this reinforcement-learning-driven reasoning process in a physical neural network model in the presence of a reward external potential energy for a given reward. In this hardware implementation, the existence of a chain of thought in dynamics contradicts the Lyapunov stability of the system.

AI.tldr: A negative result on hardware implementation of reinforcement-learning-driven reasoning in a physical neural network: when a reward external potential energy is present, the existence of a chain of thought in the dynamics contradicts the Lyapunov stability of the system.
AI.motivation: Reinforcement-learning-driven reasoning has been intensively studied in the machine learning community since around 2025, motivating interest in realizing such reasoning processes in physical neural network hardware.
AI.method: The authors analyze a physical neural network model in which reinforcement-learning-driven reasoning is realized in hardware, incorporating a reward external potential energy for a given reward, and examine the dynamical properties of the resulting system.
AI.result: A negative result is obtained: the presence of a chain of thought in the dynamics is incompatible with the Lyapunov stability of the system under the reward external potential energy.
AI.conclusion: The hardware implementation of reinforcement-learning-driven reasoning in a physical neural network with a reward external potential energy is obstructed by a fundamental contradiction between the existence of a chain of thought and Lyapunov stability, indicating a limitation of this approach.

title: Weyl's theorem and the theoretical origin of Boson peak in two-dimensional scalar spring network
summary: The origin of the anomalous low-frequency vibrational density of states (VDOS) universally observed in amorphous solids has been debated for decades. In this work, we model amorphous solids as a zero-temperature scalar spring network, the simplest model that captures both the amorphous structure and the features of the anomalous VDOS. Using this scalar network, we mathematically demonstrate that disorder can lead to a shift of the VDOS toward low frequencies, thereby accumulating the anomalous part there. Disorder is defined through the topological connectivity of the network. The validity and universality of the theoretical framework are general and valuable for real-world scenarios because it rests only on Weyl's theorem for Hermitian matrices and is free of perturbation and phenomenological assumptions. This work strips away complex factors and reveals, at the level of mathematical principles, a profound and clean mechanism for the origin of the anomalous VDOS in amorphous solids.

AI.tldr: This paper explains the long-debated origin of the anomalous low-frequency vibrational density of states (VDOS) in amorphous solids by modeling them as a zero-temperature scalar spring network and mathematically showing that disorder, defined via topological connectivity, shifts the VDOS toward low frequencies, accumulating the anomalous part there.
AI.motivation: The origin of the anomalous low-frequency VDOS universally observed in amorphous solids has remained debated for decades. This work aims to reveal the underlying mechanism at a fundamental, mathematical level, avoiding complex confounding factors.
AI.method: Amorphous solids are modeled as a zero-temperature scalar spring network—the simplest model capturing both amorphous structure and the anomalous VDOS features. Disorder is defined through the topological connectivity of the network. The theoretical framework relies only on Weyl's theorem for Hermitian matrices, with no perturbation or phenomenological assumptions.
AI.result: The authors mathematically demonstrate that disorder can shift the VDOS toward low frequencies, thereby accumulating the anomalous part at low frequencies.
AI.conclusion: The framework is validated as general and universal, applicable to real-world scenarios. By stripping away complex factors, the work reveals a profound and clean mechanism for the origin of the anomalous VDOS in amorphous solids at the level of mathematical principles.

title: Eigenstate transitions and critical transport in 3D Aubry-André model
summary: We numerically study spectral and wave-function properties, as well as time evolution, in finite-size commensurate approximations of the 3D Aubry-André model. We explicitly show, through scaling analysis, the existence of two critical points. One of the critical points is a localization-delocalization transition in real-space, similar to the critical point in the 3D Anderson model. The other is a localization-delocalization transition in a dual momentum space, which does not have any analog in the 3D Anderson model. We estimate their values from spectral measures, such as the gap ratio and the spectral form factor, as well as from wave-function measures, such as the inverse participation ratio and the participation entropy. Additionally, we demonstrate that both critical points exhibit hallmarks of critical points between quantum ergodicity and localization. First, the eigenstates and the eigenspectrum at the critical point fulfill the mutual universal relation between the eigenspectrum compressibility $χ$ and the eigenstate fractal dimension $d^{(1)}$ [S. Jiricek et al., Proc. Nat. Acad. Sci. 123, e2518027123 (2026)]. Second, the dynamics of the wave packet at the critical point is governed by the critical dynamical exponent $z$, characterized by the spectral fractal dimension and the dimensionality of the lattice [M. Hopjan and L. Vidmar, Phys. Rev. Lett. 135, 060401 (2025)]. Thus, similarly to the 3D Anderson model, the critical dynamical exponent is sub-diffusive with the value of $z=3$.

AI.tldr: The 3D Aubry-André model hosts two distinct critical points—a real-space Anderson-like transition and a dual-momentum-space transition—both showing ergodicity-to-localization hallmarks with sub-diffusive dynamics (z=3).
AI.motivation: The 3D Anderson model has a single localization-delocalization critical point, but whether quasiperiodic 3D models host additional transitions (e.g., in dual momentum space) and whether they share the same critical dynamical behavior is unclear. The authors aim to establish the number and nature of critical points in the 3D Aubry-André model.
AI.method: Numerical study of finite-size commensurate approximations of the 3D Aubry-André model. Scaling analysis of spectral measures (gap ratio, spectral form factor) and wave-function measures (inverse participation ratio, participation entropy) to locate and characterize critical points. Verification of critical-point hallmarks via the eigenspectrum compressibility χ vs. eigenstate fractal dimension d^(1) relation, and via wave-packet dynamics governed by critical dynamical exponent z.
AI.result: Two critical points are identified. One is a real-space localization-delocalization transition analogous to the 3D Anderson model; the other is a localization-delocalization transition in dual momentum space with no Anderson-model analog. Both satisfy the universal χ–d^(1) relation and exhibit sub-diffusive dynamics with critical dynamical exponent z=3.
AI.conclusion: The 3D Aubry-André model exhibits two critical points, one real-space (Anderson-like) and one dual-momentum-space (without Anderson analog), both showing hallmarks of quantum ergodicity-to-localization transitions with sub-diffusive dynamics (z=3), analogous to the 3D Anderson model.

title: Quantum Localization in Geometric Complex Networks
summary: Quantum localization, the phenomenon by which wave diffusion is halted, here understood as the superposition of propagating waves, can have many different origins, such as onsite random potentials in Anderson localization. However, some systems exhibit complex geometries and could potentially reproduce similar results without external potentials. In this work, we study how localization of single particle states is affected by the underlying topology of a simple but highly predictive complex network model: the geometric soft configuration model $\mathbb S^1$. By tuning the model's temperature and heterogeneity parameters, we are able to generate different structural patterns and focus on the transition from a small-world to a non-small-world regime. Our study suggests that small-world networks tend to have extended states, which spread the whole system's size, in contrast to non-small-world networks which tend to localize, showing how complex connectivity can play the role assigned to random energetic disorder.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how quantum localization of single-particle states emerges from network topology alone, using the geometric soft configuration model S^1, and finds that small-world structures support extended states while non-small-world structures induce localization.
AI.motivation: Localization of waves is typically attributed to external potentials, such as onsite random disorder in Anderson localization. However, some systems possess complex geometries that may reproduce similar localization effects without any external potentials. The paper aims to understand whether and how the underlying topology of a complex network can itself drive localization.
AI.method: The authors study localization of single-particle states on the geometric soft configuration model S^1. By tuning the model's temperature and heterogeneity parameters, they generate different structural patterns and focus on the transition between the small-world and non-small-world regimes.
AI.result: Small-world networks tend to host extended states that spread across the entire system size, whereas non-small-world networks tend to localize states.
AI.conclusion: Complex network connectivity can play the role usually assigned to random energetic disorder, providing a purely topological mechanism for quantum localization.

title: Predictive Holonomy and Minimal Completion of Coarse Dynamics
comment: 13 pages, 3 figures; ancillary symbolic and numerical verification code included
summary: A coarse description of a dynamical system generally fails to evolve autonomously: evolving and coarse-graining in different orders gives different predictions, and the compressed propagator fails the semigroup law. We show that this path dependence is the observable boundary of missing state. For a finite continuous-time Markov chain with generator $L$, coarse channel $C$, and stochastic section $R$ satisfying $CR=I$, define $P=RC$, $Q=I-P$, and $K=CLR$. The exact coarse propagator $T_t=C\mathrm{e}^{tL}R$ obeys a Volterra equation with memory kernel $\mathcal{M}(t)=CLQ\,\mathrm{e}^{tQLQ}\,QLR$. Every memory jet $\mathcal{M}^{(k)}(0)$ is recursively recoverable from the short-time derivatives of $T_t$ alone. The rank of the block Hankel operator $\mathbb{H}_{\infty}=(\mathcal{M}^{(i+j)}(0))_{i,j\geq 0}$ is exactly the smallest number of auxiliary linear state variables required to turn the coarse dynamics into an exact autonomous, time-homogeneous system. A minimal completion is constructible by Ho--Kalman factorization and is unique up to similarity. If $d=\min\{k:\mathcal{M}^{(k)}(0)\neq 0\}$, then every smooth classical $f$-divergence generically scales as $t^{2d+4}$. Exact Markov examples realize exponents $4,6,8$ and closure ranks $1,2,3$. We also derive finite-sample singular-value certificates for hidden predictive coordinates, including a matrix-Bernstein bound with intrinsic-variance control. Finally, histories are identified when they induce the same future law under every admissible intervention, yielding the minimal counterfactual predictive state. The results turn coarse-graining into a constructive state-completion problem and separate ordinary linear realization from the harder requirement of a positive or Markov realization.

AI.tldr: Coarse-graining a Markov chain is generally non-autonomous because hidden state leaves a memory trace. The authors show this path dependence is exactly captured by a Volterra memory kernel, whose Hankel rank equals the minimal number of auxiliary states needed for an exact autonomous completion. They construct this minimal completion via Ho-Kalman factorization (unique up to similarity), derive generic f-divergence scaling laws, realize exponents 4/6/8 with closure ranks 1/2/3, and give finite-sample singular-value certificates for detecting hidden predictive coordinates.
AI.motivation: Evolving and coarse-graining a dynamical system in different orders yields different predictions, and the compressed propagator violates the semigroup law. The paper aims to explain this failure not as an artifact but as the observable signature of missing (hidden) state, and to convert coarse-graining into a constructive state-completion problem.
AI.method: For a finite continuous-time Markov chain with generator L, coarse channel C, and stochastic section R (CR=I), define P=RC, Q=I-P, K=CLR. The exact coarse propagator T_t = C e^{tL} R is shown to satisfy a Volterra equation with memory kernel M(t)=CLQ e^{tQLQ} QLR. Memory jets M^(k)(0) are recursively recovered from short-time derivatives of T_t. The Hankel operator H_∞ = (M^(i+j)(0)) has rank equal to the minimal auxiliary linear state dimension for exact autonomous time-homogeneous dynamics; a minimal realization is built by Ho-Kalman factorization, unique up to similarity. The analysis also links the vanishing order d = min{k: M^(k)(0)≠0} to f-divergence scaling, and derives finite-sample singular-value certificates.
AI.result: The Hankel rank of the memory kernel equals the minimal number of auxiliary linear state variables for exact autonomous dynamics. Minimal completions exist via Ho-Kalman factorization and are unique up to similarity. If d = min{k: M^(k)(0)≠0}, every smooth classical f-divergence generically scales as t^{2d+4}. Exact Markov examples realize exponents 4, 6, 8 and closure ranks 1, 2, 3. Finite-sample singular-value certificates for hidden predictive coordinates are obtained, including a matrix-Bernstein bound with intrinsic-variance control. Histories inducing the same future law under all admissible interventions define a minimal counterfactual predictive state.
AI.conclusion: Path dependence in coarse-graining is the observable boundary of missing state, not an inherent obstruction. Coarse-graining can be recast as a constructive state-completion problem, with a minimal, essentially unique autonomous realization determined by the memory kernel's Hankel rank. The work separates ordinary linear realization from the stricter requirement of a positive or Markov realization.

title: Orbital cancellation and reentrant localization in a quasiperiodic trimer ladder
summary: Uniform orbital detuning can restore spatial extent even as quasiperiodic modulation strengthens. In a trimer ladder with fixed hoppings and orbital modulation signs, increasing detuning and modulation amplitude together drives successive avoided crossings that redistribute orbital weights, suppressing the projected onsite potential in both lower molecular bands while leaving the third strongly modulated. Complete-band participation scaling supports two reentrant high-participation windows, with wave-packet propagation corroborating spatial recovery at representative controls over the studied sizes and times. These diagonal cancellations leave residual interband modulation, which generates a self-energy whose magnitude depends on the molecular level separation. Gaussian quadrature improves convergence of closed-walk determinant estimates used to cross-check energy-resolved attenuation. Comparing the coupled and decoupled ladders under the same finite-size participation criterion shows that restoring the full off-diagonal modulation narrows both sampled windows, with a larger absolute contraction of the second.

AI.tldr: Uniform orbital detuning can restore spatial extent in a quasiperiodically modulated trimer ladder by driving successive avoided crossings and suppressing projected onsite potentials, yielding two reentrant high-participation windows.
AI.motivation: Quasiperiodic (orbital) modulation typically localizes states and destroys spatial extent. The work asks whether a uniform orbital detuning can counteract this and recover delocalized, high-participation behavior.
AI.method: A trimer ladder with fixed hoppings and orbital modulation signs is studied as detuning and modulation amplitude are increased together. Analysis uses band-resolved projected onsite potentials, complete-band participation scaling, wave-packet propagation, self-energy from residual interband modulation, Gaussian-quadrature evaluation of closed-walk determinants, and comparison of coupled versus decoupled ladders under a finite-size participation criterion.
AI.result: Increasing detuning and modulation together produces successive avoided crossings that redistribute orbital weights, suppressing the projected onsite potential in the two lower molecular bands while the third remains strongly modulated. Two reentrant high-participation windows appear; wave-packet propagation confirms spatial recovery at representative controls. Diagonal cancellations leave residual interband modulation, generating a level-separation-dependent self-energy. Coupled-versus-decoupled comparison shows restoring full off-diagonal modulation narrows both windows, contracting the second more in absolute terms.
AI.conclusion: Uniform orbital detuning restores spatial extent even under strengthened quasiperiodic modulation, controlled by avoided-crossing-induced weight redistribution; residual interband modulation and off-diagonal coupling further reshape the reentrant high-participation windows.

title: Detector-Frame Quantum Limits for Heterodyne Timing in Relativistic Optical Links
comment: 36 pages, 1 figure. Published in Advanced Quantum Technologies
summary: Long-baseline optical links for space interferometry and satellite quantum networks rely on heterodyne phase tracking under Doppler motion and gravitational frequency shifts. These relativistic shifts can generate large detector-frame beat-frequency offsets over finite readout windows and thereby constrain the temporal precision of front-end phase readout. We develop a detector-frame framework for this problem using an effective two-mode signal--local-oscillator model in which relativistic motion rescales the local-oscillator frequency. Within this setting we derive closed-form Mandelstam--Tamm and Margolus--Levitin bounds for representative Gaussian resources and connect global state distinguishability with the operational precision of heterodyne phase tracking. In the bright-local-oscillator regime we identify a geometric--operational mismatch: the joint optical state can evolve on arbitrarily short global timescales while the relevant information rate is set by the measured detector record. Combining this result with an open-loop transient-acquisition analysis, we show that white phase noise and relativistic beat-frequency drift that is approximately constant over the acquisition window generate a cube-root scaling benchmark for the optimal pre-lock open-loop integration window and the minimum residual phase error. These results establish detector-frame benchmarks for quantum-limited heterodyne timing in relativistic optical links and clarify how global dynamical bounds enter task-restricted continuous optical measurements.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a detector-frame framework for heterodyne phase tracking in relativistic optical links, deriving quantum speed-limit bounds and a cube-root scaling benchmark for the optimal open-loop integration window and residual phase error under white noise and beat-frequency drift.
AI.motivation: Long-baseline optical links for space interferometry and satellite quantum networks require heterodyne phase tracking under Doppler motion and gravitational frequency shifts. These relativistic shifts produce large detector-frame beat-frequency offsets over finite readout windows, constraining the temporal precision of front-end phase readout. A detector-frame treatment linking global quantum dynamical bounds to task-restricted measurement precision is needed.
AI.method: An effective two-mode signal–local-oscillator model is used in which relativistic motion rescales the local-oscillator frequency. Closed-form Mandelstam–Tamm and Margolus–Levitin bounds are derived for representative Gaussian resources, connecting global state distinguishability with operational heterodyne phase-tracking precision. An open-loop transient-acquisition analysis is combined with this framework.
AI.result: In the bright-local-oscillator regime a geometric–operational mismatch is identified: the joint optical state can evolve on arbitrarily short global timescales while the relevant information rate is set by the measured detector record. White phase noise plus approximately constant relativistic beat-frequency drift yields a cube-root scaling benchmark for the optimal pre-lock open-loop integration window and the minimum residual phase error.
AI.conclusion: The results establish detector-frame benchmarks for quantum-limited heterodyne timing in relativistic optical links and clarify how global dynamical bounds enter task-restricted continuous optical measurements.

title: The Rényi area law conjecture is false below $α=1$ in high dimensions
summary: Area laws express the expectation that entanglement in gapped quantum ground states scales with a boundary rather than a volume. In one dimension this holds for every Rényi entropy, and the Rényi area-law conjecture asserts the same in higher dimensions for each fixed $0<α<1$. Here we disprove this conjecture in every spatial dimension two and higher. We construct finite-range Hamiltonians with fixed local dimension, bounded interaction strength, unique ground states and a uniform spectral gap, whose ground states exhibit volume-law Rényi entanglement while obeying a von Neumann area law and remaining connected to product states through uniformly gapped local paths. The mechanism is error-space complexity: locally identifiable components of arbitrarily small weight can encode states with high entanglement complexity. We also establish the worst-case rank-error trade-off for approximate ground-state projectors, a key tool in one-dimensional area-law proofs. At fixed gap, the optimal Schmidt rank at projection error $ε$ across a planar cut of cross-section $A$ scales as $\exp[\tildeΘ((A\logε^{-1})^{2/3})]$ when $\logε^{-1}\gtrsim A$. Thus $α=1$ is the sharp threshold for a universal Rényi area law within this adiabatically connected class.

AI.tldr: The Rényi area-law conjecture (area law for every Rényi entropy with 0<α<1) is disproven in all spatial dimensions ≥2: gapped, finite-range, unique-ground-state Hamiltonians are constructed whose ground states have volume-law Rényi entanglement while still satisfying a von Neumann area law.
AI.motivation: Area laws state entanglement in gapped ground states scales with boundary, not volume. In 1D this holds for every Rényi entropy; the Rényi area-law conjecture asserts the same in higher dimensions for each fixed 0<α<1. The paper tests and refutes this conjecture.
AI.method: Construct finite-range Hamiltonians with fixed local dimension, bounded interaction strength, unique ground states, and uniform spectral gap, connected to product states via uniformly gapped local paths. The mechanism is error-space complexity: locally identifiable components of arbitrarily small weight encode states of high entanglement complexity. Also establish a worst-case rank-error trade-off for approximate ground-state projectors.
AI.result: The conjecture fails in every dimension ≥2: ground states exhibit volume-law Rényi entanglement while obeying a von Neumann area law. For approximate ground-state projectors, the optimal Schmidt rank at projection error ε across a planar cut of cross-section A scales as exp[Θ̃((A log ε^{-1})^{2/3})] when log ε^{-1} ≳ A.
AI.conclusion: α=1 is the sharp threshold for a universal Rényi area law within this adiabatically connected class of gapped ground states; the Rényi area law holds at α=1 (von Neumann) but fails for all 0<α<1 in dimensions ≥2.

title: Comment on arXiv:2510.21705 "Fundamental Impossibility of a Superradiant Neutrino Laser" and comment on arXiv:2510.21692 "Can Bose-Einstein Condensates Enhance Radioactive Decay?"
comment: comment on arXiv:2510.21705 published as Phys. Rev. Lett. 137, 101804 (2026) and comment on arXiv:2510.21692 published as Phys. Rev. Lett. 137, 101805 (2026)
summary: We show that the small value of the neutrino cross-section rules out superradiance in the laboratory.

AI.tldr: The tiny neutrino cross-section precludes observing superradiance in a laboratory setting.
AI.motivation: Superradiance is a compelling amplification phenomenon often invoked in astrophysical contexts; assessing whether it can be realized in laboratory experiments is important for testing its observability.
AI.method: Analytical argument based on the extremely small neutrino interaction cross-section as the limiting factor for superradiant amplification.
AI.result: The small neutrino cross-section rules out the possibility of laboratory superradiance.
AI.conclusion: Superradiance cannot be demonstrated in the laboratory given current neutrino interaction rates.

title: Probe Signatures of Quantum Chaos with Quantum Sensing
summary: The spectral form factor (SFF), which is the Fourier transform of the two-point spectral correlation, is a fundamental diagnostics of quantum chaos. Nevertheless, its experimental detection in quantum many-body systems was less unexplored until recently. Here, we establish a relationship between the SFF with the quantum Fisher information (QFI) by means of quantum sensing protocols. Furthermore, when the eigenvalues and eigenstates of the disordered Hamiltonian are statistically independent, we prove that QFI is typical both in short and long timescales while numerics suggest that it is also typical at intermediate timescales, which ensures self-averaging of QFI. The self-averaging property renders the experimental measurement of QFI with our protocol less noisy in contrast with the direct measurement of SFF which is known to be non-self-averaging. Our results reveal an intriguing connection between quantum noise and the signatures of quantum chaos.

AI.tldr: This work connects the spectral form factor (SFF), a quantum chaos diagnostic, to the quantum Fisher information (QFI) via quantum sensing protocols, showing QFI is self-averaging and thus enables low-noise experimental detection of quantum chaos signatures.
AI.motivation: The spectral form factor is a fundamental probe of quantum chaos, but its experimental detection in quantum many-body systems remains largely unexplored. Direct measurement of the SFF is problematic because it is not self-averaging, making it inherently noisy.
AI.method: The authors establish a relationship between the SFF and the quantum Fisher information using quantum sensing protocols. They analytically prove that QFI is typical (self-averaging) at short and long timescales when the eigenvalues and eigenstates of the disordered Hamiltonian are statistically independent, and support the intermediate-timescale regime with numerics.
AI.result: QFI is proven typical at short and long timescales and numerically suggested to be typical at intermediate timescales, ensuring self-averaging. This self-averaging property makes the protocol-based measurement of QFI less noisy than direct SFF measurement.
AI.conclusion: The results reveal an intriguing connection between quantum noise and signatures of quantum chaos, and offer a less noisy route to experimentally detecting the SFF and quantum chaos.

title: Empirical Scaling Laws of Quantum Vision Transformers
summary: Quantum machine learning (QML) is a promising application of quantum computing, yet when and how practical learning models can achieve quantum advantage remains poorly understood. Even a polynomial improvement in the resources needed to attain a given predictive performance would be significant. In this work, we investigate empirical scaling laws of quantum vision transformers (QViTs), which connect QML to the transformer architecture underlying modern large language models. We ask whether QViTs exhibit scaling behavior analogous to classical models and how this behavior changes when qubit number is included alongside dataset size and model parameters. The validation losses in our numerical image-classification experiments are well described by a joint shifted power-law model in qubit number, transformer depth, and training dataset size. Expressing this fit in terms of the classical encoder parameter budget identifies a regime in which increasing the number of qubits can compensate for fewer classical encoder parameters at comparable predicted performance. This finding is consistent with earlier observations of parameter efficiency in quantum learning models and suggests a direction for exploring possible resource savings in QML.

AI.tldr: This work studies empirical scaling laws of quantum vision transformers (QViTs), showing that validation loss follows a joint shifted power-law in qubit number, transformer depth, and dataset size, and identifies a regime where more qubits can substitute for fewer classical encoder parameters.
AI.motivation: Quantum machine learning's practical advantage remains poorly understood; even a polynomial resource improvement for a given predictive performance would be significant. The paper aims to determine whether QViTs exhibit scaling behavior analogous to classical models, and how that behavior changes when qubit number is added to the usual dataset-size and parameter axes.
AI.method: Numerical image-classification experiments with quantum vision transformers, connecting QML to the transformer architecture behind modern large language models. Validation losses are fitted with a joint shifted power-law model over three variables: qubit number, transformer depth, and training dataset size. The fit is then re-expressed in terms of the classical encoder parameter budget to isolate trade-offs between qubits and classical parameters.
AI.result: Validation losses are well described by the joint shifted power-law model in qubit number, transformer depth, and dataset size. When expressed via the classical encoder parameter budget, the fit reveals a regime in which increasing qubit number compensates for fewer classical encoder parameters at comparable predicted performance.
AI.conclusion: QViTs exhibit systematic scaling behavior that can be captured by a joint shifted power-law including qubit number. The identified qubit-for-parameter trade-off is consistent with prior observations of parameter efficiency in quantum learning models and points toward exploring possible resource savings in QML.

title: Whither quantum advantage? New classical lower bounds for Max-Cut on large-girth 3-regular graphs
summary: Every 3-regular graph of girth at least $g$ has a cut containing at least a fraction $M_g$ of its edges, and the best rigorous bounds at large girth are $0.912\le \lim_{g\to\infty}M_g \le 0.92386$. Lower bounds on $M_g$ follow from the performance of local algorithms: on a graph of girth $g \ge 2p+2$ a depth-$p$ local algorithm sees the same tree around every edge, so its expected cut fraction on that tree bounds $M_g$ from below. We apply this strategy to the Variational Iterative Rotation Algorithm (VIRAL), a classical local algorithm, and evaluate it on the depth-$p$ tree for every even depth up to $p=32$. The resulting bounds exceed those recently obtained from the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) for every $p\ge 4$, by $0.005$ to $0.011$, and they extend the range of girths covered from $g=36$ to $g=66$. Notably, at $g=66$ we obtain $M_{66} \ge 0.9127$ at $99.99999\%$ confidence level, which raises the asymptotic lower bound from $0.912$ to $0.9127$.

AI.tldr: This paper sharpens lower bounds on the maximum cut fraction M_g in girth-g 3-regular graphs by evaluating the classical Variational Iterative Rotation Algorithm (VIRAL) on depth-p trees, surpassing recent QAOA-derived bounds and raising the asymptotic lower bound to 0.9127.
AI.motivation: Rigorous bounds on M_g (the guaranteed maximum cut fraction for 3-regular graphs of girth ≥ g) are narrow: 0.912 ≤ lim M_g ≤ 0.92386. Local algorithms provide lower bounds because a depth-p algorithm sees an identical tree around every edge when g ≥ 2p+2, so its tree performance bounds M_g. Prior work used QAOA, but better classical local algorithms could tighten bounds and cover larger girths.
AI.method: Apply the classical VIRAL local algorithm on depth-p trees for every even p up to 32, using the tree-equivalence property of girth g ≥ 2p+2 to convert tree cut fractions into lower bounds on M_g. Bounds are reported with high confidence levels.
AI.result: VIAL's bounds exceed QAOA's for every p ≥ 4 by 0.005 to 0.011, and extend girth coverage from g=36 to g=66. At g=66, M_66 ≥ 0.9127 at 99.99999% confidence, raising the asymptotic lower bound from 0.912 to 0.9127.
AI.conclusion: A classical local algorithm outperforms QAOA for Max-Cut lower bounds on high-girth 3-regular graphs, improving both finite-girth and asymptotic lower bounds on M_g.

title: Parameter-Efficient Multilinear Readout for Quantum Reservoir Computing
summary: Quantum Reservoir Computing (QRC) uses fixed quantum dynamics as a high-dimensional feature map. Still, standard pipelines flatten reservoir measurements and train a linear readout, ignoring the natural tensor structure across time steps, qubits, and observables. We propose a multilinear readout for quantum reservoir computing (ML-QRC), a tensor-structured neural readout compressed through mode-wise projections. Relative to a dense hidden-width-64 neural readout, this reduces the feature-to-hidden parameter count from $64TnF$ to $d(T+n+F)+64d^3$, giving a $12.1\times$ feature-block compression at $T=50$, $n=6$, $d=8$, and $F=n+\binom{n}{2}$. Across Mackey-Glass forecasting and TFIM phase classification, ML-QRC remains statistically competitive with Ridge on Mackey-Glass and obtains the numerically highest full-data TFIM accuracy among tested methods, while using $12.0\times$ fewer parameters than the full dense MLP. Its clearest benefit is improved low-data stability relative to neural MLP readouts on Mackey-Glass; this advantage does not transfer to TFIM, where Ridge performs best at 50\% data. Overall, ML-QRC is best viewed as a tensor-structured neural readout that compresses dense MLP readouts while preserving QRC tensor structure, rather than as a replacement for simple linear/Ridge readouts in the tested regime.

AI.tldr: ML-QRC introduces a tensor-structured multilinear readout for quantum reservoir computing, compressing a dense neural readout's parameters via mode-wise projections while preserving the reservoir tensor structure, achieving strong parameter efficiency and improved low-data stability on Mackey-Glass.
AI.motivation: Standard QRC pipelines flatten reservoir measurements and apply a linear readout, discarding the natural tensor structure across time steps, qubits, and observables. This motivates a readout that exploits tensor structure while remaining parameter-efficient.
AI.method: A multilinear readout for QRC (ML-QRC): a tensor-structured neural readout compressed through mode-wise projections. Compared to a dense hidden-width-64 neural readout, it reduces feature-to-hidden parameters from 64TnF to d(T+n+F)+64d^3, with F = n + C(n,2).
AI.result: A 12.1x feature-block compression at T=50, n=6, d=8. ML-QRC is statistically competitive with Ridge on Mackey-Glass and yields the numerically highest full-data TFIM accuracy among tested methods, using 12.0x fewer parameters than the full dense MLP. Its main advantage is improved low-data stability over neural MLP readouts on Mackey-Glass, but this does not transfer to TFIM, where Ridge performs best at 50% data.
AI.conclusion: ML-QRC is best viewed as a tensor-structured neural readout that compresses dense MLP readouts while preserving QRC tensor structure, rather than as a replacement for simple linear/Ridge readouts in the tested regime.

title: On the Fast Electrons-Optical Modes Interaction Problem Error
summary: A recently developed relativistic quantum optics approach for a fast electron beam-optical modes interaction problem (Optica 6, 1524--1534 (2019)) contains suggestion about a smallness of the error induced by replacement $Ψ_{\vec k}\approxΨ_{\vec k_0}$ for noninteracting free electron Dirac spinors at such wave vector $\vec k$ that $\left|\vec k-\vec k_0 \right| \ll\left|\vec k_0\right|$ with $\vec k_0$ as a peaked wave vector of a focused electron beam. Here, based on quantum information approach we strictly investigated a degree of coincidence of spinors $Ψ_{\vec k}$ and $Ψ_{\vec k_0}$ by calculating fidelity for them. The analytical expression is obtained. It is shown that the fidelity inevitably depends on not only wave vectors $\vec k$ and $\vec k_0$ but also on mutual orientation of $[\vec k_0,\vec k]$ and $\hat{\vec{s}}^{\dagger}\vecσ\hat{\vec{s}}$ with $\vec{s}$ is a two-component spin unit vector and $\vecσ$ is a vector of Pauli matrices. This result can be conceived as a chirality-like effect in the fidelity and constraints spin arbitrariness when applying the developed relativistic quantum optics approach to the problems of interest. A geometrical configuration of $\vec k_0$, $\vec k-\vec k_0$, and $\hat{\vec{s}}^†\vecσ\hat{\vec{s}}$ that is optimal in terms of fidelity is established.

AI.tldr: A quantum-information fidelity analysis rigorously tests the approximation Ψ_k ≈ Ψ_k0 used in a relativistic quantum optics model of fast electron beam–optical mode interaction, revealing that fidelity is a chirality-like quantity depending on wave vectors and spin orientation, and identifying an optimal geometry.
AI.motivation: A prior relativistic quantum optics approach for the fast electron beam–optical mode interaction problem assumed the error from replacing free electron Dirac spinors Ψ_k ≈ Ψ_k0 (for |k − k0| ≪ |k0|, with k0 the peaked wave vector of a focused beam) was small. This assumption lacked rigorous verification, motivating a strict examination of the validity of the approximation.
AI.method: A quantum information approach is used to quantify the degree of coincidence between spinors Ψ_k and Ψ_k0 by computing their fidelity. An analytical expression for the fidelity is derived, and its dependence on the wave vectors and on the mutual orientation of [k0, k] and the spin operator s†σs (s a two-component spin unit vector, σ the Pauli matrices) is examined.
AI.result: The analytical fidelity expression shows it depends not only on the wave vectors k and k0 but also on the mutual orientation of [k0, k] and s†σs. This constitutes a chirality-like effect that constrains the spin arbitrariness in applying the relativistic quantum optics approach. A geometric configuration of k0, k − k0, and s†σs that is optimal in terms of fidelity is established.
AI.conclusion: The assumption Ψ_k ≈ Ψ_k0 is not unconditionally valid; fidelity reveals a chirality-like dependence on spin orientation, imposing constraints on spin choice and defining an optimal geometric configuration for the relativistic quantum optics treatment of electron beam–optical mode interaction.

title: Can the Quantum Fisher Effective Dimension Judge a Hybrid Quantum Neural Network?
summary: Hybrid quantum neural networks (QNNs) pair a classical feature extractor with a variational quantum circuit, and the effective dimension of the circuit's quantum Fisher information matrix (QFIM) is widely used to assess such models. This scalar is often interpreted as an indicator of trainability or accuracy, although these readings are rarely tested under controlled conditions. We therefore investigate what it actually measures. We define the effective dimension as the participation ratio of the QFIM diagonal, which lies between one and the parameter count, and we evaluate it across two image datasets, four frozen backbones including a random-projection control, four circuit depths on eight qubits, and three seeds. During training, the effective dimension remains well below the parameter count, and its correlation with test accuracy ranges from -0.72 to +0.87, changing sign across seeds in half of the configurations. Increasing depth activates a larger share of the circuit directions, from 0.38 to 0.91 of the parameter count, while the initialization gradient variance remains between 1e-5 and 1e-4, so no barren plateau (BP) appears at eight qubits. At a fixed circuit, the four backbones share an initial effective dimension of 6 to 9, even though CIFAR-10 accuracy ranges from 23.14% to 86.44%. These results show that the effective dimension characterizes circuit geometry rather than model quality. We conclude with a practical protocol that assigns each diagnostic to the question it can answer.

AI.tldr: The effective dimension of the QFIM in hybrid QNNs measures circuit geometry, not model quality; its correlation with test accuracy is unstable in sign and magnitude, so it should not be read as a trainability or accuracy indicator.
AI.motivation: The effective dimension of the quantum Fisher information matrix is widely used to assess hybrid quantum neural networks and is often read as an indicator of trainability or accuracy, yet these interpretations are rarely tested under controlled conditions. This work asks what the quantity actually measures.
AI.method: The effective dimension is defined as the participation ratio of the QFIM diagonal, bounded between one and the parameter count. It is evaluated across two image datasets, four frozen backbones including a random-projection control, four circuit depths on eight qubits, and three seeds.
AI.result: During training the effective dimension stays well below the parameter count, and its correlation with test accuracy spans -0.72 to +0.87, flipping sign across seeds in half of the configurations. Increasing depth activates a larger share of circuit directions, from 0.38 to 0.91 of the parameter count, while initialization gradient variance remains between 1e-5 and 1e-4, so no barren plateau appears at eight qubits. At fixed circuit, the four backbones share an initial effective dimension of 6 to 9 despite CIFAR-10 accuracy ranging from 23.14% to 86.44%.
AI.conclusion: The effective dimension characterizes circuit geometry rather than model quality. The authors propose a practical protocol assigning each diagnostic to the question it can answer.

title: Prelocality No-Go Theorems and Exactly Solvable Relational History Hamiltonians
comment: 10 pages, 1 figure. Ancillary finite-matrix verification scripts included
summary:
Exact permutation covariance does not itself supply a sparse metric geometry. For permutation-covariant, full-support $k$-body interaction orbits, the incident interaction norm scales as $\binom{N-1}{k-1}|J_N|\|h\|$; such orbits cannot have uniformly finite range in metrics of diverging diameter. A permutation-invariant Hamiltonian diagonal in the graph basis has ground-state multiplicity at least $N!/|\mathrm{Aut}(G)|$ whenever $G$ is a ground graph. We give a quantitative version for approximately symmetric energies, together with fixed-radius connectivity and unitary-isometry obstructions. The trace-distance asymmetry of an arbitrary state also bounds its probability of selecting one labeled graph.
  We then construct two exactly solvable finite relational history Hamiltonians. A cyclic clock with a reversible incidence update has a unique ground state; gauge reduction yields a cycle Laplacian with a rank-one pin and the exact gap $Δ_{N,L}=E_* (1-\cosθ_L)$, where $\tan(Lθ_L/2)=1/\sinθ_L$ and $0<θ_L<π/L$. In particular, $Δ_{N,L}/E_*=π^2/(2L^2)-2π^2/L^3+O(L^{-4})$, independently of the number of vertices. In an alternative order-free architecture, one clock qubit per unordered pair gives commuting four-local terms, $2^N$ ground states and a size-independent gap $E_*(1-1/\sqrt2)$. A fixed-weight control penalty selects $\binom Nq$ ground states without reducing the gap. These exact finite results expose clock and locality resource tradeoffs; they do not establish an emergent geometric phase.

AI.tldr: Permutation covariance alone cannot yield sparse metric geometry: full-support k-body orbits have interaction norm scaling ~C(N-1,k-1)|J_N||h| and cannot be uniformly finite-range. Permutation-invariant graph-basis-diagonal Hamiltonians have ground degeneracy >= N!/|Aut(G)| for ground graphs, with a quantitative approximate-symmetry version, connectivity and isometry obstructions, and a trace-distance bound on labeled-graph selection probability. The authors then build two exactly solvable finite relational history Hamiltonians: a cyclic clock with reversible incidence update yielding a pinned cycle Laplacian and exact gap scaling Δ/E_* = π²/(2L²) + O(L⁻³) independent of vertex number, and an order-free architecture of commuting four-local terms on one clock qubit per unordered pair with 2^N ground states, a size-independent gap E_*(1-1/√2), and a fixed-weight penalty selecting C(N,q) ground states without gap reduction. These exact finite results expose clock vs. locality resource tradeoffs but do not demonstrate an emergent geometric phase.
AI.motivation: To test whether permutation covariance alone can generate sparse metric geometry, and to characterize the degeneracies and constraints (connectivity, isometry, selection probability) of permutation-invariant graph-diagonal Hamiltonians. The authors also aim to quantify clock and locality resource tradeoffs via exactly solvable finite relational history models, while explicitly avoiding claims of an emergent geometric phase.
AI.method: Analytical scaling argument for full-support k-body interaction orbits, showing the incident interaction norm scales as C(N-1,k-1)|J_N||h| and forbids uniformly finite range under diverging diameter. Group-theoretic count of ground-state multiplicity N!/|Aut(G)| for permutation-invariant Hamiltonians diagonal in the graph basis, with a quantitative approximately-symmetric extension, fixed-radius connectivity and unitary-isometry obstructions, and a trace-distance asymmetry bound on labeled-graph selection probability. Construction of two exactly solvable finite relational history Hamiltonians: (i) a cyclic clock with reversible incidence update, gauge-reduced to a cycle Laplacian with a rank-one pin, and (ii) an order-free architecture with one clock qubit per unordered pair giving commuting four-local terms, analyzed for gap and a fixed-weight control penalty selecting C(N,q) ground states.
AI.result: Permutation covariance does not supply sparse metric geometry; full-support orbits have diverging incident interaction norm and cannot be uniformly finite-range. Ground-state multiplicity is at least N!/|Aut(G)| for ground graphs, with quantitative approximate-symmetry results plus connectivity and isometry obstructions, and a trace-distance bound on single labeled-graph selection. The cyclic clock model has a unique ground state and exact gap Δ_{N,L}=E_*(1−cosθ_L) with tan(Lθ_L/2)=1/sinθ_L, giving Δ_{N,L}/E_*=π²/(2L²)−2π²/L³+O(L⁻⁴), independent of vertex number. The order-free model has 2^N ground states and a size-independent gap E_*(1−1/√2); a fixed-weight penalty selects C(N,q) ground states without reducing the gap.
AI.conclusion: Exact finite results reveal tradeoffs between clock resources and locality resources in relational history Hamiltonians. Crucially, they do not establish an emergent geometric phase, and permutation covariance by itself is insufficient to produce sparse metric geometry.

title: How long is a photon?
summary: A photon has the strange property that it travels along a null interval with zero proper time, hence its emission and absorption points are, in a sense, a singular event. For their part, the emission and absorption processes have a finite duration which determines the spectral content of the photon. The question in the title points to the conceptual difficulty in `stitching' together these three intervals, which all correspond to the same physical entity but have fundamentally incompatible temporal descriptions. A previously developed model for quantum wavefunction propagation solves this apparent dilemma by formulating the life cycle of a photon in terms of recursive Fourier transforms on dual spaces. Because it doesn't treat space as dependent on time, and it is built on the Fourier transform whose phase is an invariant in special relativity as well as the foundation of the uncertainty principle, the model is a promising candidate framework for making quantum mechanics compatible with relativity. The model proposes to serve as an improved Klein-Gordon equation, or relativistically compatible replacement for Schrödinger's equation.

AI.tldr: The paper addresses the conceptual conflict between a photon's zero proper-time null trajectory and the finite durations of its emission and absorption, proposing a recursive Fourier transform model on dual spaces as a relativistically compatible replacement for the Schrödinger equation.
AI.motivation: A photon travels along a null interval with zero proper time, making its emission and absorption points effectively a singular event, yet the emission and absorption processes have finite durations that determine the photon's spectral content. Reconciling these three temporal descriptions—belonging to one physical entity but fundamentally incompatible—poses a conceptual difficulty that motivates a new formulation of quantum wavefunction propagation.
AI.method: The paper employs a previously developed model for quantum wavefunction propagation that formulates the life cycle of a photon in terms of recursive Fourier transforms on dual spaces. The approach does not treat space as dependent on time, and it is built on the Fourier transform, whose phase is an invariant in special relativity and the foundation of the uncertainty principle.
AI.result: The recursive Fourier transform model resolves the apparent dilemma of stitching together the incompatible temporal intervals of photon emission, propagation, and absorption, offering a coherent description of the photon's life cycle without treating space as time-dependent.
AI.conclusion: The model is proposed as a promising candidate framework for making quantum mechanics compatible with relativity, serving as an improved Klein-Gordon equation or a relativistically compatible replacement for Schrödinger's equation.

title: Hamiltonian-Dependent Compressibility and Physical Preservation in Approximate Quantum Compilation using Tensor Networks
comment: 20 pages, 9 figures, 5 tables; includes supplementary material
summary: Approximate quantum compilation (AQC) using tensor networks provides a promising route to reducing the circuit resources required for quantum simulation. However, the factors governing the compressibility of many-body dynamics and the extent to which compressed circuits retain physically relevant information on quantum hardware remain poorly understood. We investigate these questions using AQCtensor for an 80-qubit one-dimensional anisotropic XYZ Heisenberg chain initialized in a Néel state. By varying the exchange anisotropy and external magnetic field, we find that compression performance changes systematically with the anisotropic coupling configuration and field orientation. These variations are strongly associated with a nested-commutator measure related to second-order Trotter error, with corresponding directional trends also reflected in the target-state MPS bond dimension. For an 80-qubit quantum-hardware evaluation, AQCtensor compresses a 10-repetition target evolution to 5 repetitions while retaining a target-state fidelity of 0.995474, reducing the total circuit depth by 45.9% and the two-qubit gate count by 47.6%. The compressed circuit exhibits comparable behavior across magnetization, nearest-neighbor correlation, and Hamiltonian expectation measurements, while process-level diagnostics and local reduced-state tomography provide complementary characterization beyond these observables. Together, these results link AQCtensor compressibility to Hamiltonian commutator structure and target-state complexity and demonstrate substantial circuit reduction while retaining physically relevant features in an 80-qubit quantum-hardware experiment.

AI.tldr: AQCtensor compresses an 80-qubit XYZ Heisenberg evolution from 10 to 5 repetitions, retaining 0.9955 fidelity while cutting depth by 45.9% and two-qubit gates by 47.6%, with compressibility tied to a nested-commutator Trotter-error measure.
AI.motivation: Approximate quantum compilation via tensor networks can reduce circuit resources for quantum simulation, but the factors controlling compressibility of many-body dynamics and whether compressed circuits preserve physically relevant information on real hardware are poorly understood.
AI.method: AQCtensor is applied to an 80-qubit 1D anisotropic XYZ Heisenberg chain initialized in a Néel state, varying exchange anisotropy and external magnetic field; compressibility is correlated with a nested-commutator measure linked to second-order Trotter error and with target-state MPS bond dimension, then validated on quantum hardware.
AI.result: For the 80-qubit hardware evaluation, a 10-repetition target evolution is compressed to 5 repetitions with target-state fidelity 0.995474, reducing circuit depth by 45.9% and two-qubit gate count by 47.6%; the compressed circuit shows comparable magnetization, nearest-neighbor correlation, and Hamiltonian expectation values, with process-level diagnostics and local reduced-state tomography providing complementary characterization.
AI.conclusion: AQCtensor compressibility is systematically linked to Hamiltonian commutator structure and target-state complexity, enabling substantial circuit reduction while preserving physically relevant features in an 80-qubit quantum-hardware experiment.

title: Compass in the Mirror: Quantum Backpropagation with the Hopf Ansatz
summary: A variational quantum state may have many control angles, and its complete gradient contains one derivative for each. The task is to turn access to selected derivatives into a shared finite-shot record for the complete vector. The Hopf ansatz supplies the setting: it constructs any normalized pure state from nested two-way magnitude splits and, for complex states, leaf phases, with one directly programmed angle per split or phase. Earlier Hopf constructions prepare the state, recover coordinates from known amplitudes, and provide indexed derivative access. With a phase-calibrated controlled reflection, the inverse Hopf frame maps each normalized magnitude direction to a computational label, so every all-$X$ outcome contributes to every magnitude derivative. A separate signed leaf record supplies the complex phase block. A checkpoint variant reverses only the suffix below a selected depth and returns that layer's gradient block. For a complete chart with $M$ real-valued parameters, sufficient execution counts are $\mathcal{O}(\log\log M)$ for the global method and $\mathcal{O}(\log M\log\log M)$ for the complete checkpoint schedule at fixed additive coordinate accuracy and confidence. The global saving is record reuse, not a reduction of the $M$-entry output. Under the designated direct-angle schedules, the global method's assigned Hopf CNOT work and input/output-inclusive storage have at most logarithmic overhead relative to a matched scalar evaluation. The same Hopf geometry thus carries a state forward and the objective's complete coordinate response backward.

AI.tldr: A Hopf-ansatz-based method turns selected derivative access into a shared finite-shot record recovering the complete gradient vector of a variational quantum state, achieving O(log log M) shot counts globally and O(log M log log M) for a full checkpoint schedule.
AI.motivation: A variational quantum state may have many control angles, each contributing one derivative to the complete gradient. Recovering the full gradient vector typically requires separate estimation per derivative, which is shot-inefficient. The goal is to turn access to selected derivatives into a shared finite-shot record that yields the complete vector.
AI.method: The Hopf ansatz constructs any normalized pure state via nested two-way magnitude splits and, for complex states, leaf phases, with one programmed angle per split or phase. A phase-calibrated controlled reflection and the inverse Hopf frame map each normalized magnitude direction to a computational label, so every all-X outcome contributes to every magnitude derivative. A separate signed leaf record supplies the complex phase block. A checkpoint variant reverses only the suffix below a selected depth to return that layer's gradient block.
AI.result: For a complete chart with M real-valued parameters, sufficient execution counts are O(log log M) for the global method and O(log M log log M) for the complete checkpoint schedule at fixed additive coordinate accuracy and confidence. The global saving comes from record reuse, not from reducing the M-entry output. Under the designated direct-angle schedules, the global method's Hopf CNOT work and input/output-inclusive storage have at most logarithmic overhead relative to a matched scalar evaluation.
AI.conclusion: The same Hopf geometry carries a state forward and returns the objective's complete coordinate response backward, enabling shared-record estimation of the full gradient with logarithmic shot-count and storage overhead.

title: Lifting an $[n,k,d]$ Binary Linear Code to an $[[n,k,d]]$ Quantum Stabilizer Code
summary: The codeword stabilized (CWS) framework provides a systematic method for constructing quantum error correcting codes from a simple undirected graph and a classical code. When the underlying classical code is linear, the resulting quantum code is a stabilizer code. In this work, we investigate the conditions under which an arbitrary $[n,k,d]$ classical binary linear code can be lifted to an $[[n,k,d]]$ quantum stabilizer code using the CWS framework. We analyze the random CWS code constructed from a given $[n,k,d]$ binary linear code $\mathcal{C}$ and an Erdős-Rényi random graph $\mathrm{G}(n, \frac12)$. We establish a lower bound on the probability that the resulting quantum code preserves the minimum distance $d$ of the classical code. This probabilistic analysis yields a Gilbert-Varshamov-type condition on the $n,k,d$ parameters of the classical code that guarantees the existence of a graph resulting in a quantum code with the same $n,k,d$ parameters.

AI.tldr: The paper studies when an arbitrary [n,k,d] classical binary linear code can be lifted to an [[n,k,d]] quantum stabilizer code via the codeword stabilized (CWS) framework, using a random graph analysis to derive a Gilbert-Varshamov-type existence condition.
AI.motivation: The CWS framework systematically constructs quantum codes from a graph and a classical code, but it is unclear under what conditions an arbitrary classical linear code yields a quantum stabilizer code preserving the same parameters, especially the minimum distance. Determining existence conditions for such lifts is the key motivation.
AI.method: The authors analyze a random CWS code built from a given [n,k,d] binary linear code C together with an Erdős-Rényi random graph G(n, 1/2). They perform a probabilistic analysis to establish a lower bound on the probability that the resulting quantum code retains the classical minimum distance d.
AI.result: A lower bound on the probability that the resulting quantum code preserves the minimum distance d is established, leading to a Gilbert-Varshamov-type condition on the parameters n, k, d that guarantees the existence of a graph producing a quantum code with the same [n,k,d] parameters.
AI.conclusion: The CWS lift of an arbitrary classical binary linear code to a quantum stabilizer code with identical parameters is feasible whenever a Gilbert-Varshamov-type condition on n, k, d holds, providing a sufficient existence criterion via probabilistic methods.

title: Below-threshold execution of fault-tolerant ripple-carry addition on a trapped-ion quantum computer
summary: We deploy a universal fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC) architecture based on error-detecting $[\![8,3,2]\!]$ and $[\![4,2,2]\!]$ codes on Quantinuum's Helios-1 trapped-ion quantum computer. We compile and execute ripple-carry adder (RCA) circuits for classical inputs up to five bits on this architecture. Uncomputing a workspace qubit provides an additional ``algorithmic check'' to detect errors. While available at both the physical and logical levels, this check synergizes with our architecture by increasing the effective fault distance of many circuit locations from two to four. Combining this algorithmic check with the error-detecting codes, we observed only a single logical failure in one-bit addition after burst-error filtering, yielding an estimated logical failure rate of $(6.0 \pm 5.9) \times 10^{-5}$. This is well below the $(3.5 \pm 1.3) \times 10^{-3}$ failure probability observed for one-bit addition on the same hardware in unencoded form. Two- and three-bit adders also showed performance improvements, while the longer four- and five-bit adders executed just above threshold.

AI.tldr: The authors demonstrate a universal fault-tolerant quantum computing architecture using error-detecting [8,3,2] and [4,2,2] codes on Quantinuum's Helios-1 trapped-ion device, executing ripple-carry adders up to five bits and achieving a logical failure rate of (6.0±5.9)×10⁻⁵ for one-bit addition.
AI.motivation: Demonstrating practical fault-tolerant quantum computing requires architectures that reduce logical error rates below their unencoded physical counterparts, motivating the deployment of error-detecting codes combined with algorithmic error checks to suppress failures in real hardware.
AI.method: They implement a universal FTQC architecture based on [8,3,2] and [4,2,2] error-detecting codes on Helios-1, compiling and running ripple-carry adder circuits for classical inputs up to five bits. An uncomputing workspace qubit acts as an algorithmic check, synergizing with the architecture to raise the effective fault distance from two to four at many circuit locations, combined with burst-error filtering.
AI.result: Only a single logical failure was observed in one-bit addition after burst-error filtering, giving an estimated logical failure rate of (6.0±5.9)×10⁻⁵, far below the (3.5±1.3)×10⁻³ of the unencoded version. Two- and three-bit adders showed improvements; four- and five-bit adders executed just above threshold.
AI.conclusion: Combining error-detecting codes with algorithmic checks from uncomputing yields substantial error suppression on real hardware, though scalability remains limited, as longer adders operate only marginally above threshold.

title: Quantum Signal Processing Phase Factorization via Logarithmic Derivatives
summary: Quantum signal processing (QSP) requires the efficient computation of phase factors associated with a polynomial transformation. One existing stable factorization method avoids direct root finding but relies on Prony's method to recover a polynomial from weighted power sums of its roots (arXiv:2202.02671). We present a modification of this approach that eliminates Prony's method by using the logarithmic derivative of an associated polynomial. Because the logarithmic derivative has the same residue at every root after accounting for multiplicity, its Fourier coefficients directly yield the unweighted power sums of the roots inside the unit disk. The Newton--Girard identities then recover the coefficients of the corresponding polynomial without computing its roots. The resulting algorithm has $O(d\log^2 d)$ computational complexity and simplifies the factorization procedure of the original method. In numerical experiments on Hamiltonian simulation, eigenstate filtering, matrix inversion, and the Fermi--Dirac operator, our implementation computes phase factors in seconds with maximum errors on the order of $10^{-12}$.

AI.tldr: We modify a stable QSP phase-factor factorization method by replacing Prony's method with the logarithmic derivative of an associated polynomial; its Fourier coefficients yield unweighted power sums, and Newton-Girard identities recover coefficients, achieving O(d log^2 d) complexity with ~1e-12 errors in numerical experiments.
AI.motivation: Quantum signal processing (QSP) requires efficient computation of phase factors for a polynomial transformation. The existing stable factorization method (arXiv:2202.02671) avoids direct root finding but still relies on Prony's method to recover a polynomial from weighted power sums of its roots, which the authors aim to eliminate or simplify.
AI.method: A modification of the stable factorization approach that removes Prony's method by using the logarithmic derivative of an associated polynomial. Since the logarithmic derivative has the same residue at every root (after accounting for multiplicity), its Fourier coefficients directly give the unweighted power sums of the roots inside the unit disk. The Newton-Girard identities then recover the polynomial coefficients without computing its roots.
AI.result: The algorithm has O(d log^2 d) computational complexity and simplifies the factorization procedure of the original method. In numerical experiments on Hamiltonian simulation, eigenstate filtering, matrix inversion, and the Fermi-Dirac operator, the implementation computes phase factors in seconds with maximum errors on the order of 1e-12.
AI.conclusion: Eliminating Prony's method via the logarithmic derivative yields a simpler, stable, and efficient QSP phase-factor computation with quasilinear complexity and high numerical accuracy across several applications.

title: The GHZ Game in Black and White
comment: 8 pages, 6 drawings, numerous diagrams and misty states
summary: We show that it is possible for three people to win the GHZ game with just the standard real valued misty state formalism, but each party will need to have two balls instead of one. That is, there will be six balls involved, rather than three. In fact, as a general rule, instead of using complex numbers in a quantum computer you can always add a qubit to "tag" complex numbers. But for proofs of non-locality, like the GHZ game, we cannot have a single universal tagging qubit, because all three parties would need access to it and therefore they could potentially transfer information via it. That's where we need to replace the one ball with three that each only need to be accessed locally.

AI.tldr: Three parties can win the GHZ game using only the real-valued misty-state formalism if each party holds two balls (six total), rather than the usual three; this illustrates that complex amplitudes can be replaced by adding a "tagging" qubit without loss of quantum computational power, though non-locality proofs forbid a single shared tagging qubit.
AI.motivation: The paper is motivated by the question of whether complex numbers are truly necessary in quantum computation. It examines the GHZ game as a testbed, since using one ball (the standard misty-state resource) implicitly encodes complex amplitudes, and asks whether a purely real-valued formalism can still reproduce the same non-local correlations.
AI.method: The authors eliminate complex amplitudes by attaching a "tagging" qubit to encode the complex phase. In the GHZ game setting they argue this global tagging strategy cannot be shared, because all three parties accessing one common qubit would create a communication channel undermining the non-locality argument. Instead they replace the single shared ball with three tags, each accessible only locally by the respective party, yielding six balls in total (two per party).
AI.result: It is shown explicitly that three people can win the GHZ game within the standard real-valued misty-state formalism provided each party possesses two balls. The construction uses six balls overall, and the shared-tagging obstruction is resolved by distributing the tagging among locally accessible balls.
AI.conclusion: As a general principle, complex numbers in a quantum computer can always be simulated by adding a tagging qubit, so the real-valued formalism is computationally sufficient. However, for proofs of non-locality such as the GHZ game, a single universal tagging qubit is inadmissible, as the parties would all need access to it and could transmit information through it. This forces the substitution of one ball by three locally accessible ones, i.e., two balls per party.

title: Exponential Quantum Advantage in Stationary Signal Sensing
summary: Sensing time-varying signals is essential for precision measurement and for characterizing fluctuations in physical systems. In this work, we show that quantum entanglement provides an exponential advantage in the acquisition time required to learn the temporal statistics of a stationary classical signal. The task is to estimate the characteristic function of joint displacements on selected bosonic modes within a fixed-duration window, using continuous measurements of one signal realization. We present an entanglement-assisted scheme based on two-mode squeezed probes and local Bell measurements with protected idlers, and bound its acquisition time accounting for readout noise and correlations between signal windows. For a strictly stationary pulse family, it achieves polynomial acquisition time at inverse-polynomial accuracy with logarithmic squeezing and polynomial photon number. On the other hand, we prove that any local idler-free protocols require acquisition time exponential in the number of selected temporal modes per window. This lower bound holds for both sequentially prepared and arbitrarily temporally entangled probes, allowing non-Gaussian inputs and measurements and causal classical feedback, as long as each output is measured destructively within its time bin. These results establish an exponential quantum learning advantage for a single continuously monitored stationary signal, with the sensing cost measured by total acquisition time.

AI.tldr: Quantum entanglement yields an exponential advantage in the acquisition time needed to learn the temporal statistics (characteristic function of joint displacements) of a stationary classical signal, using two-mode squeezed probes and local Bell measurements.
AI.motivation: Sensing time-varying signals is essential for precision measurement and characterizing fluctuations in physical systems. The paper aims to establish whether quantum entanglement can reduce the time required to learn the temporal statistics of a stationary classical signal.
AI.method: The task is framed as estimating the characteristic function of joint displacements on selected bosonic modes within a fixed-duration window via continuous measurement of one signal realization. The authors propose an entanglement-assisted scheme using two-mode squeezed probes and local Bell measurements with protected idlers, bounding its acquisition time while accounting for readout noise and correlations between signal windows. They also prove a lower bound for local idler-free protocols.
AI.result: For a strictly stationary pulse family, the scheme achieves polynomial acquisition time at inverse-polynomial accuracy with logarithmic squeezing and polynomial photon number. Conversely, any local idler-free protocol requires acquisition time exponential in the number of selected temporal modes per window—a bound that holds for sequentially prepared and arbitrarily temporally entangled probes, permitting non-Gaussian inputs/measurements and causal classical feedback, provided each output is destructively measured within its time bin.
AI.conclusion: These results establish an exponential quantum learning advantage for a single continuously monitored stationary signal, with sensing cost measured by total acquisition time.

title: Hyperpolarization-enabled cooperative molecular magnetic amplification
summary: Detecting weak magnetic fields at hertz frequencies is central to biomagnetism, geophysical sensing, and searches for new physics, yet it remains challenging because of technical systematics and environmental noise. Here, we realize a continuously operating molecular magnetic amplifier. Signal amplification by reversible exchange (SABRE) parahydrogen-based hyperpolarization maintains non-equilibrium spin order at zero field, turning scalar-coupled nuclear spins in liquid state molecules into an active, frequency-selective gain medium. Measurements of its complex magnetic susceptibility ($χ$) reveal an intrinsic response of $ | χ| \approx$ 10. By feeding the collectively generated magnetic field back to the spins below the threshold for self-sustained $J$-oscillation, we extend the effective spin coherence and cooperatively enhance the susceptibility up to $ | χ| \approx$ 80. Near threshold, this produces approximately fourfold amplification of a weak (20 pT) magnetic field at 3.37 Hz at the sensor location. These results establish hyperpolarized molecules as a tunable active magnetic medium for narrowband quantum sensing and precision measurement.

AI.tldr: A continuously operating molecular magnetic amplifier is realized using SABRE parahydrogen hyperpolarization, converting scalar-coupled nuclear spins at zero field into a frequency-selective gain medium; positive feedback below the J-oscillation threshold boosts susceptibility to |χ|≈80, giving ~4-fold amplification of a 20 pT field at 3.37 Hz.
AI.motivation: Detecting weak hertz-frequency magnetic fields is central to biomagnetism, geophysical sensing, and new-physics searches, but remains difficult due to technical systematics and environmental noise. Existing approaches lack a continuously operating, frequency-selective amplifier for such weak low-frequency signals.
AI.method: The authors exploit SABRE parahydrogen-based hyperpolarization to maintain non-equilibrium spin order at zero field, turning scalar-coupled nuclear spins in liquid-state molecules into an active, frequency-selective gain medium. They measure the complex magnetic susceptibility and apply positive feedback of the collectively generated magnetic field to the spins below the threshold for self-sustained J-oscillation.
AI.result: The complex susceptibility shows an intrinsic response of |χ|≈10. Feedback below the J-oscillation threshold extends the effective spin coherence and cooperatively enhances susceptibility up to |χ|≈80. Near threshold, this yields approximately fourfold amplification of a weak 20 pT magnetic field at 3.37 Hz at the sensor location.
AI.conclusion: Hyperpolarized molecules constitute a tunable active magnetic medium, enabling narrowband quantum sensing and precision measurement with molecular magnetic amplification.

title: Quadrature-detected zero-to-ultralow-field nuclear magnetic resonance
summary: We present the concept of quadrature-detected zero-to-ultralow-field nuclear magnetic resonance (QD ZULF NMR). Two orthogonal sensors, atomic optically pumped magnetometers, are used to separately detect components of oscillating sample magnetization, which are then combined into a quadrature signal. This approach enables the distinction of positive and negative resonance frequencies with respect to the laboratory frame---such that absolute signs of gyromagnetic ratios can be determined. In addition, QD ZULF NMR reduces peak density and overlap compared to ZULF NMR with single-axis detection, while providing richer information about nuclear-spin dynamics. As an illustration, we present experimental $J$-spectra for thermally polarized [$^{13}$C]-formic acid and [$^{13}$C]-methanol, compounds commonly used in ZULF NMR which represent XA and XA$_3$ spin systems, respectively. A theoretical framework describing QD ZULF NMR signals is provided.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces quadrature-detected zero-to-ultralow-field NMR (QD ZULF NMR) using two orthogonal atomic magnetometers to detect oscillating sample magnetization as a quadrature signal, enabling sign discrimination of resonance frequencies, reduced peak overlap, and richer spin-dynamics information, demonstrated on 13C-labeled formic acid and methanol.
AI.motivation: Conventional ZULF NMR with single-axis detection cannot distinguish positive from negative resonance frequencies relative to the laboratory frame, preventing determination of absolute signs of gyromagnetic ratios and causing peak crowding and overlap in complex spectra.
AI.method: Two orthogonal atomic optically pumped magnetometers separately detect components of the oscillating sample magnetization, which are then combined into a quadrature signal, with a theoretical framework describing the resulting QD ZULF NMR signals.
AI.result: Experimental J-spectra were obtained for thermally polarized [13C]-formic acid (XA spin system) and [13C]-methanol (XA3 spin system), showing reduced peak density and overlap along with richer information about nuclear-spin dynamics compared to single-axis ZULF NMR.
AI.conclusion: QD ZULF NMR enables distinction of positive and negative resonance frequencies, permitting determination of absolute signs of gyromagnetic ratios, while reducing spectral peak density and overlap and providing richer nuclear-spin dynamics information.

title: Quantum-Fisher-information-aware optimization yields a quantum reservoir advantage over tuned classical reservoirs
summary: We show that a quantum reservoir computer optimized with its quantum Fisher information (QFI) has a quantum advantage over a classical reservoir of equal readout cost, provided by a quantum-information advantage: optimizing the quantum parameters with the QFI metric. On Mackey-Glass forecasting, a driven Jaynes-Cummings reservoir with one to three atoms beats a tuned echo-state network at every size from 4 to 30 trained weights, by 25-69% in held-out error, and is ahead of 99.5% of 10,000 random networks. After grid and Bayesian searches saturate, the QFI-aware stage lowers the error by 29-51% at 12-30 weights, beyond equal-budget black-box search or classical-parameter gradients alone, and at 30 weights turns a loss into a win. We then derive a fundamental QFI bound on the first-order rate of change of the retrained loss and factorize the gap to this bound into five link efficiencies that identify the physical mechanism limiting optimization.

AI.tldr: A quantum reservoir computer optimized with quantum Fisher information beats a classically tuned echo-state network at equal readout cost on Mackey-Glass forecasting, and a derived QFI bound factorizes the performance gap into five link efficiencies that pinpoint the limiting physical mechanism.
AI.motivation: To establish whether a quantum reservoir can outperform a classical reservoir of equal readout cost, and to identify the physical mechanism that limits optimization when conventional grid/Bayesian searches and classical-parameter gradients saturate.
