AI.method: Optimize a quantum reservoir's quantum parameters using the quantum Fisher information (QFI) metric. Benchmark a driven Jaynes-Cummings reservoir (one to three atoms) against a tuned echo-state network at 4-30 trained weights on Mackey-Glass forecasting, comparing against grid and Bayesian searches and classical-parameter gradients. Derive a fundamental QFI bound on the first-order rate of change of the retrained loss and factorize the gap to this bound into five link efficiencies.
AI.result: The Jaynes-Cummings reservoir beats the tuned echo-state network at every size from 4 to 30 weights by 25-69% in held-out error and outperforms 99.5% of 10,000 random networks. The QFI-aware stage lowers error by 29-51% at 12-30 weights beyond equal-budget black-box search or classical-parameter gradients alone, turning a loss into a win at 30 weights.
AI.conclusion: Optimizing with the QFI metric confers a quantum-information advantage over classical reservoirs of equal readout cost, and the derived QFI bound with its five link efficiencies identifies the physical mechanism limiting optimization.

title: Harmonic Reduction of Spin-Coupled Grover Walks on Hypercubes via Quantum Bernoulli Noises
summary: We consider spin-coupled Grover walks on hypercubes within the framework of quantum Bernoulli noises (QBN). We identify parity-dependent harmonic subspaces generated by the central Hamming layers: in even dimension they give a fixed-point subspace, whereas in odd dimension the walk reduces on the harmonic subspace to an explicit eight-dimensional reduced dynamics. Using symmetric-group representation theory, we characterize the corresponding isotypic structure and determine the reduced spectrum. The harmonic reduction also yields explicit long-time probability behavior and shows that the resulting states may occupy an asymptotically vanishing fraction of the hypercube while still spanning its full Hamming diameter.

AI.tldr: The paper studies spin-coupled Grover walks on hypercubes using quantum Bernoulli noises, identifies parity-dependent harmonic subspaces from central Hamming layers, characterizes their isotypic structure via symmetric-group representation theory, computes the reduced spectrum, and derives long-time probability behavior showing asymptotically vanishing occupation yet full Hamming-diameter support.
AI.motivation: Understanding the long-time dynamics of spin-coupled quantum walks is difficult due to large state spaces and complex symmetry structure. The paper is motivated by the need for a reduced, symmetry-informed description of such walks on hypercubes within the quantum Bernoulli noise framework.
AI.method: Spin-coupled Grover walks on hypercubes are formulated under quantum Bernoulli noises. Central Hamming layers generate parity-dependent harmonic subspaces. Even dimensions yield a fixed-point subspace, while odd dimensions give an explicit eight-dimensional reduced dynamics. Symmetric-group representation theory is used to characterize the isotypic decomposition and determine the reduced spectrum.
AI.result: A parity-dependent harmonic reduction is obtained. In even dimension the harmonic subspace is a fixed-point set; in odd dimension the walk reduces to an explicit 8-dimensional dynamics. The isotypic structure and reduced spectrum are determined. Explicit long-time probability behavior is derived, indicating states that occupy an asymptotically vanishing fraction of the hypercube while still spanning its full Hamming diameter.
AI.conclusion: The harmonic reduction provides a tractable, symmetry-based framework for spin-coupled Grover walks on hypercubes under quantum Bernoulli noises, yielding explicit spectral and long-time probabilistic information and revealing states with vanishing occupancy but full Hamming-diameter span.

title: Fast continuous ion transport through X-junctions with low motional excitation for QCCD architectures
summary: Trapped ion quantum computing based on the quantum charge coupled device (QCCD) architecture uses functional zoning and ion transport to enable high fidelity computation and all to all qubit connectivity. As trapped ion quantum processing units (QPU) scale, 90° X-junction turns account for an increasing fraction of total transport time. Frequent junction crossings, therefore, make transport speed and final phonon excitation direct determinants of quantum algorithm execution efficiency. However, complex electric fields in X-junctions complicate waveform design, making it difficult to achieve high speed and low final phonon excitation simultaneously. Here, we develop a waveform design method for low-phonon-excitation high-speed X-junction(LHX-T) transport. It integrates low barrier pseudopotential channel design using multiple radio frequency (Multi-RF), multidimensional shortcut to adiabaticity dynamics, and constrained DC voltage optimization over the entire transport sequence. This framework connects waveform design, control, and computational validation, with smooth multichannel waveforms computed rapidly through a Karush-Kuhn-Tucker(KKT) linear system. The resulting waveform transports a single $^{171}Yb^+$ ion through a 90° turn in $5μs$ at an average speed of 14.6 m/s. Over 50 consecutive round trips, the final equivalent coherent phonon number consistently stays below 0.001, with no noticeable accumulation over time. System level evaluations at the QCCD scale show that the median duration of a single execution cycle is reduced by about $30\%$ across various circuit types. The fraction of execution time spent on transport decreases from approximately $70\%$ to $55\%$. This approach offers a means of designing fast ion transport waveforms with low phonon excitation for scalable QCCD based QPUs and provides a technical basis for efficient execution of quantum algorithms.

AI.tldr: This paper develops LHX-T, a waveform design method that transports a single trapped ion through a 90° X-junction in 5 μs at 14.6 m/s with final coherent phonon number below 0.001, reducing QCCD cycle duration by ~30%.
AI.motivation: In QCCD trapped-ion QPUs, 90° X-junction turns dominate transport time as systems scale. Frequent junction crossings make transport speed and final phonon excitation key determinants of algorithm efficiency, but complex X-junction electric fields make it hard to simultaneously achieve high speed and low final phonon excitation.
AI.method: LHX-T integrates low-barrier pseudopotential channel design using Multi-RF, multidimensional shortcut-to-adiabaticity dynamics, and constrained DC voltage optimization over the whole transport sequence. It connects waveform design, control, and computational validation, computing smooth multichannel waveforms rapidly via a Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) linear system.
AI.result: A single ¹⁷¹Yb⁺ ion traverses a 90° turn in 5 μs at an average speed of 14.6 m/s. Over 50 consecutive round trips, final equivalent coherent phonon number stays below 0.001 with no noticeable accumulation. System-level QCCD evaluations show median single execution cycle duration reduced by ~30% across circuit types, with transport time fraction dropping from ~70% to ~55%.
AI.conclusion: This approach enables designing fast ion transport waveforms with low phonon excitation for scalable QCCD-based QPUs, providing a technical basis for efficient quantum algorithm execution.

title: Sample-Size Scalability and Representation Sensitivity of Quantum Machine Learning Models for Higgs Boson Event Classification
summary: Quantum machine learning offers new approaches to multivariate event classification in high-energy physics, but its performance relative to optimized classical methods remains uncertain under limited training data and restricted quantum resources. We investigate the sample-size scalability and representation sensitivity of a quantum support vector machine and a variational quantum classifier for Higgs-boson signal--background discrimination using simulated events from the ATLAS Higgs Machine Learning Challenge. The models are trained on balanced subsets ranging from 250 to 4000 events and evaluated on held-out samples preserving the original class distribution. Principal component analysis (PCA) and autoencoder (AE) representations are examined to reduce the input dimensionality and quantum-resource requirements. Four optimized classical classifiers are used as benchmarks under a common preprocessing, validation, and evaluation protocol. We assess training-sample scalability in classical and quantum classifiers using a four-component PCA representation and examine representation sensitivity through a secondary matched-event comparison of four- and eight-component PCA representations. Within the evaluated Higgs-boson classification setting, the QSVM showed stronger performance than the VQC at larger training sample sizes, while remaining below the best-performing classical classifiers.

AI.tldr: This study compares quantum (QSVM, VQC) and four optimized classical classifiers for Higgs-boson signal-background discrimination using simulated ATLAS Higgs ML Challenge events, examining sample-size scalability (250-4000 events) and representation sensitivity (PCA/AE).
AI.motivation: Quantum machine learning offers new approaches to multivariate event classification in high-energy physics, but its performance relative to optimized classical methods remains uncertain under limited training data and restricted quantum resources.
AI.method: Models (QSVM and VQC) trained on balanced subsets of 250-4000 events, evaluated on held-out samples preserving original class distribution; PCA and autoencoder representations used for dimensionality and quantum-resource reduction; four optimized classical classifiers as benchmarks under a common preprocessing, validation, and evaluation protocol; sample-size scalability assessed using a four-component PCA representation, and representation sensitivity via matched-event comparison of four- and eight-component PCA representations.
AI.result: QSVM showed stronger performance than the VQC at larger training sample sizes, while remaining below the best-performing classical classifiers within the evaluated Higgs-boson classification setting.
AI.conclusion: In this Higgs-boson classification setting, quantum classifiers did not surpass optimized classical methods; QSVM scaled better than VQC with training size but stayed below the best classical benchmark.

title: Entanglement-Capability-Aware Finite-Bond Circuit Cutting for Distributed Quantum Computing
summary: Distributed quantum computing distributes workloads that exceed a single processor's capacity across resource-constrained components. Circuit cutting enables this decomposition, but its effectiveness depends on partition choice. We present SACE, a Simulation-Aware Circuit Partitioning framework with Entanglement-Capability-Aware Screening. EP-Cost screens partitions using a parameter-dependent entanglement-capability proxy and native implementation cost. Under reconstruction constraints, finite-bond refinement selects the candidate that minimizes the worst-subcircuit discrepancy between normalized MPS simulations at bond dimensions $χ$ and $2χ$. Across 14 exhaustively enumerated small-scale candidate spaces, EP-Cost-guided genetic algorithm selections attain co-optimal native quasiprobability decomposition (QPD) overhead, with a median within-circuit Spearman correlation of 0.9965 between EP-Cost and QPD overhead. At matched cut counts, EP-Cost reduces QPD overhead by $25.20\times$ and $16.89\times$ for 8- and 9-qubit QFT circuits, respectively, and improves sampled reconstruction. On 12-qubit approximate QFT, deterministic reconstruction reduces Pauli-observable mean absolute error in all six low-bond conditions and total-variation distance in five. With five cuts and 7,776 QPD terms, SACE is best on all four reconstruction metrics in four of six conditions. At 24 qubits, SACE improves exact-local QFT accuracy in all 30 instance-bond-dimension conditions against each EP-Cost-only, Kernighan-Lin, and spectral baseline. The 50-qubit QFT comparisons remain favorable as reference convergence improves. Weighted QAOA circuits provide complementary, more bond-sensitive evidence. Refinement benefits persist across three search methods; larger candidate panels improve the optimized proxy without guaranteeing lower exact-local error.

AI.tldr: SACE is a simulation-aware circuit-partitioning framework for distributed quantum computing that uses an entanglement-capability-aware proxy (EP-Cost) plus finite-bond refinement to pick cut locations minimizing reconstruction error and QPD overhead.
AI.motivation: Circuit cutting lets workloads exceeding one processor be split across resource-constrained components, but performance hinges on the partition choice; better, simulation-aware selection is needed.
AI.method: EP-Cost screens partitions via a parameter-dependent entanglement-capability proxy and native implementation cost; under reconstruction constraints, finite-bond refinement selects the candidate minimizing worst-subcircuit discrepancy between normalized MPS simulations at bond dimensions χ and 2χ. Evaluated with genetic-algorithm search, Kernighan-Lin, and spectral baselines on QFT and weighted QAOA circuits.
AI.result: Across 14 enumerated small-scale spaces, EP-Cost-guided GA selections are co-optimal in native QPD overhead (median in-circuit Spearman 0.9965). At matched cut counts, EP-Cost cuts QPD overhead 25.20×/16.89× for 8-/9-qubit QFT and improves sampled reconstruction. On 12-qubit approximate QFT, refinement lowers Pauli-observable MAE in all six low-bond conditions and TVD in five; with five cuts and 7,776 QPD terms SACE is best on all four metrics in four of six conditions. At 24 qubits, SACE improves exact-local QFT accuracy in all 30 instance-bond conditions versus EP-Cost-only, Kernighan-Lin, and spectral baselines; 50-qubit QFT comparisons stay favorable as reference convergence improves.
AI.conclusion: SACE yields co-optimal, cheap-to-screen partitions and bond-refined choices that consistently lower reconstruction error and QPD overhead; refinement gains hold across search methods, and larger candidate panels improve the proxy without guaranteeing lower exact-local error.

title: Exploring Dynamical Quantum Phase Transitions via the Dynamical Phase Accumulated at an Equilibrium Critical Point
summary: We investigate dynamical quantum phase transitions (DQPTs) generated by a two-step linear quench with a finite waiting time at the equilibrium critical point. The waiting stage leads to the accumulation of a dynamical phase that depends on the waiting time and directly reflects the critical spectral structure. In the transverse Ising chain, this accumulated phase modifies the critical structure of DQPTs from a single-critical-mode (SCM) regime to a multiple-critical-mode (MCM) regime. We analytically and numerically determine the boundary between the two regimes. Along this boundary, the waiting time approaches a constant in the sudden-quench limit, whereas in the slow-quench limit it follows Kibble--Zurek (KZ) scaling with the quench time. In the SCM regime, the rate function exhibits a conventional linear singularity, $r(t)-r(t^{*})\propto |t-t^{*}|^α$, with the critical exponent $α=1$ near the critical time. At the SCM--MCM boundary, this exponent changes to $α=1/2$, leading to a divergent first derivative of the rate function. Additional discrete parameter lines with $α=1/2$ also appear within the MCM regime in the parameter plane spanned by the waiting and quench times. Our findings establish a direct connection between the accumulated dynamical phase and the critical structure of DQPTs, further supported by an extended Su--Schrieffer--Heeger (SSH) model.

AI.tldr: A finite waiting stage at the equilibrium critical point in a two-step linear quench accumulates a dynamical phase that reshapes dynamical quantum phase transitions, switching criticality from a single-critical-mode regime to a multiple-critical-mode regime and changing the rate-function critical exponent from alpha=1 to alpha=1/2 at the boundary.
AI.motivation: The paper seeks to understand how a finite waiting time at the equilibrium critical point, inserted into a two-step linear quench protocol, affects dynamical quantum phase transitions, since such a waiting stage accumulates a dynamical phase that should encode the critical spectral structure.
AI.method: The authors study two-step linear quenches with a finite waiting time at the equilibrium critical point, deriving the accumulated dynamical phase and analyzing its effect on the critical structure of DQPTs. They combine analytical treatment and numerics for the transverse Ising chain, determine the SCM-MCM boundary and its scaling limits, and corroborate the results with an extended Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (SSH) model.
AI.result: The waiting-induced dynamical phase modifies DQPT criticality from a single-critical-mode (SCM) regime to a multiple-critical-mode (MCM) regime. The SCM-MCM boundary is determined analytically and numerically; along it the waiting time approaches a constant in the sudden-quench limit and follows Kibble-Zurek scaling with quench time in the slow-quench limit. In the SCM regime the rate function shows a linear singularity with critical exponent alpha=1, which becomes alpha=1/2 at the boundary (divergent first derivative). Additional discrete parameter lines with alpha=1/2 also appear within the MCM regime.
AI.conclusion: The accumulated dynamical phase directly controls the critical structure of DQPTs, mapping the transition between SCM and MCM regimes and tuning the rate-function critical exponent, a finding supported by the extended SSH model.

title: Scalability and performance metrics for boson sampling devices
summary: Linear-optical platforms provide a promising route to demonstrate quantum computational advantage, particularly through the boson sampling problem. While a boson sampling system should be large enough to show the quantum advantage, the size of the boson sampling problem is often restricted by experimental constraints. In particular, as a boson sampling system is scaled up, experimental constraints can limit its effective problem size to permit efficient classical simulation. In this paper, we investigate the theoretical scalability bounds for boson sampling systems under practical experimental conditions, including photon loss, mode mismatch, and input state error. We employ non-negativity conditions for phase-space quasiprobability distribution functions to analyze these effects. In addition, we introduce two device-level metrics, the boson sampling score which measures the usable capacity of a given device and the boson sampling volume which provides a common hardware-level benchmark for comparing different platforms and assessing their access to an advantage-relevant problem size regime. Our results provide fundamental insights into the performance of boson sampling systems under realistic experimental conditions and offer practical guidelines for scaling up boson sampling systems.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes theoretical scalability bounds for boson sampling under practical experimental conditions (photon loss, mode mismatch, input state errors) using phase-space quasiprobability non-negativity conditions, and introduces two device-level metrics: the boson sampling score and the boson sampling volume.
AI.motivation: Boson sampling is a promising route to quantum computational advantage, but its problem size is constrained by experimental limitations. As systems scale up, these constraints can cap the effective problem size to within the regime that remains efficiently classically simulable, undermining any claimed advantage. There is a need to understand fundamental scalability bounds under realistic conditions.
AI.method: The authors employ non-negativity conditions for phase-space quasiprobability distribution functions to analyze the effects of photon loss, mode mismatch, and input state error on boson sampling systems. They also define two device-level metrics: the boson sampling score (usable device capacity) and the boson sampling volume (a hardware-level benchmark for comparing platforms and assessing whether a system reaches an advantage-relevant problem-size regime).
AI.result: Theoretical scalability bounds for boson sampling systems are established under practical experimental conditions, and the two proposed metrics quantify usable capacity and enable cross-platform comparison of access to advantage-relevant problem sizes.
AI.conclusion: The findings provide fundamental insights into boson sampling performance under realistic experimental conditions and offer practical guidelines for scaling up boson sampling systems.

title: Reducing Trust Cost in Quantum Application Development Using AI
summary: Generative AI can be a powerful tool for supporting the design and implementation of quantum applications, whereas the burden of checking whether generated circuits realize the intended computation increases. In this study, we regard this burden of human understanding, checking, and judgment as ``trust cost,'' and propose a development methodology that integrates AI and formal verification to reduce it. In the proposed development methodology, the implementation is divided into three components: a target mathematical specification, a quantum circuit, and a correspondence theorem and its proof that prove the agreement between the two. This division separates the specifications and theorem statements checked by humans from the theorem proofs entrusted to mechanical checking. As a concrete development example of this proposal, we describe an implementation for the time evolution of a stochastic particle system and its results.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces "trust cost" as the human burden of understanding, checking, and judging AI-generated quantum circuits, and proposes a development methodology that integrates generative AI with formal verification to reduce this cost.
AI.motivation: Generative AI can support the design and implementation of quantum applications, but it shifts a heavy burden onto humans to verify whether generated circuits correctly realize the intended computation. This human understanding, checking, and judgment burden is framed as "trust cost," which the proposed methodology aims to reduce.
AI.method: The proposed methodology divides the implementation into three components: (1) a target mathematical specification, (2) a quantum circuit, and (3) a correspondence theorem with its proof establishing agreement between the specification and the circuit. This division separates the specifications and theorem statements to be checked by humans from the theorem proofs delegated to mechanical checking.
AI.result: The paper presents a concrete development example: an implementation for the time evolution of a stochastic particle system, along with its results, demonstrating the proposed methodology.
AI.conclusion: By integrating generative AI with formal verification and structuring implementations into specification, circuit, and correspondence theorem, the methodology reduces the human trust cost of validating AI-generated quantum circuits.

title: Clifford Invariants and Three-Copy Quantum Tests
comment: GAP code is available in the GitHub repository: https://github.com/luanyongzhi/qutrit-character-table
summary: We give an explicit treatment of the third tensor power of the Clifford representation on $n$ qutrits, for $n\geq2$. This representation has five pairwise inequivalent irreducible constituents, with multiplicities $1,1,1,1,2$. The decomposition reduces the Clifford twirl of a tensor cube to four real parameters. Two of them are spectral moments of the input. The other two are cubic invariants expressed as sums of cubes of the Weyl characteristic function and the discrete Wigner function. On trace-one Hermitian matrices, the invariant polynomials of degree at most three are spanned by the constant function and four algebraically independent functions. These functions do not separate Clifford orbits. For pure inputs a single parameter suffices. We recover its range and the characterization of its maximum by stabilizer states. We bound the stabilizer fidelity, determine full separability across the three copies in the symmetric family, and recover the criterion for a complex projective $3$-design. We classify the jointly invariant quantum Boolean functions. For stabilizer testing and for testing unknown observables we give explicit bounds on copies and queries. We also give character formulas for the finite projective Clifford groups and record the complete character table for two qutrits.

AI.tldr: The paper explicitly decomposes the third tensor power of the Clifford representation on n qutrits (n≥2) into five inequivalent irreducible constituents with multiplicities 1,1,1,1,2, reducing the Clifford twirl of a tensor cube to four real parameters, and derives various bounds, classifications, and character formulas.
AI.motivation: Understanding the invariants and decomposition of tensor powers of the Clifford representation is important for quantum information tasks such as stabilizer testing, quantum Boolean function classification, and design theory. The third tensor power is the first nontrivial case where multiplicities exceed one, making an explicit treatment valuable.
AI.method: The authors compute the explicit decomposition of the third tensor power of the Clifford representation on n qutrits into five pairwise inequivalent irreducible constituents. They express the Clifford twirl of a tensor cube via four real parameters: two spectral moments of the input and two cubic invariants (sums of cubes of the Weyl characteristic function and the discrete Wigner function). They analyze invariant polynomials of degree at most three on trace-one Hermitian matrices, bound stabilizer fidelity, determine full separability across three copies in the symmetric family, and derive character formulas and tables for finite projective Clifford groups.
AI.result: The representation has five inequivalent irreducible constituents with multiplicities 1,1,1,1,2. Invariant polynomials of degree ≤3 are spanned by the constant function and four algebraically independent functions, which do not separate Clifford orbits. For pure inputs a single parameter suffices; its range and maximum (characterized by stabilizer states) are recovered. The paper bounds stabilizer fidelity, determines full separability across the three copies in the symmetric family, recovers the criterion for a complex projective 3-design, classifies jointly invariant quantum Boolean functions, gives explicit bounds on copies and queries for stabilizer testing and testing unknown observables, and records the complete character table for two qutrits.
AI.conclusion: The explicit treatment of the third tensor power of the Clifford representation yields a complete invariant-theoretic and representation-theoretic description, with applications to stabilizer testing, separability, design criteria, and quantum Boolean function classification, along with character formulas for finite projective Clifford groups.

title: Avoiding Defects within Heavy-Hexagon Architecture
summary: When implementing scalable fault-tolerant quantum computing using superconducting quantum processors, one of the critical challenges to overcome is the presence of defective qubits arising from fabrication and calibration imperfections. A defect on a specific qubit severely restricts the connectivity between adjacent qubits, disrupts stabilizer measurements, induces frequent detection events, and consequently inflates the logical error rate. To mitigate this issue, various strategies have been proposed, such as syndrome extraction circuits based on stabilizer folding and the construction of super-stabilizers via gauge operators. However, these methods have primarily been developed for architectures with relatively high connectivity of 3 to 4. Furthermore, experimental demonstrations showing an actual reduction in logical error rates in the presence of physical hardware defects have been lacking. In this work, we propose a defect-avoidance scheme tailored for the heavy-hexagon architecture, which features a lower connectivity of 2 to 3. While previous approaches required four measurement cycles to measure all gauge operators comprising a super-stabilizer, our proposed scheme completes all gauge measurements within only two cycles. We experimentally validate this approach on IBM quantum hardware by identifying physical defects and implementing the defect-avoidance circuits. As a result, avoiding the defect yields an approximately 10\% reduction in the logical error rate per cycle for both logical $X$ and $Z$ errors. These findings demonstrate that defects in superconducting hardware can be successfully handled even under the constrained connectivity of heavy-hexagon lattices, and that defect avoidance substantially reduces logical errors on real quantum hardware.

AI.tldr: This work proposes a defect-avoidance scheme for heavy-hexagon superconducting architectures (connectivity 2–3) that measures all gauge operators of a super-stabilizer in only two cycles, and experimentally demonstrates ~10% reduction in logical error rate per cycle on IBM quantum hardware.
AI.motivation: Defective qubits from fabrication and calibration imperfections disrupt connectivity, stabilizer measurements, and induce frequent detection events, inflating logical error rates. Existing mitigation strategies (stabilizer folding, super-stabilizers via gauge operators) target higher-connectivity architectures (3–4) and lack experimental validation showing actual logical error reduction on real defective hardware.
AI.method: The authors design a defect-avoidance scheme specifically for the heavy-hexagon lattice (connectivity 2–3). Unlike prior approaches requiring four measurement cycles to measure all gauge operators comprising a super-stabilizer, their scheme completes all gauge measurements within two cycles. They then identify physical defects on IBM quantum hardware and implement the corresponding defect-avoidance circuits for experimental validation.
AI.result: Avoiding the defect yields approximately 10% reduction in logical error rate per cycle for both logical X and Z errors, validated experimentally on IBM quantum hardware.
AI.conclusion: Defects in superconducting hardware can be successfully handled even under the constrained connectivity of heavy-hexagon lattices, and defect avoidance substantially reduces logical errors on real quantum hardware.

title: Classical Communication Helps Single-Shot Quantum Compression
comment: 23 pages, no figures, comments are welcome
summary: Free classical communication can yield an unbounded single-shot saving in quantum compression, even though it leaves the asymptotic rate of an i.i.d. source unchanged. At every fixed error in $(0,1)$, we exhibit sources whose unassisted compression cost is arbitrarily large, yet a single qubit suffices with classical communication and no preshared entanglement. We establish this separation by determining the exact optimal source fidelity for compression through an $m$-dimensional noiseless quantum channel, with and without free classical communication, while preserving correlations with an inaccessible reference. Without classical assistance, the optimal fidelity is exactly the Ky Fan norm $\|ρ\|_{(m)}$, the sum of the $m$ largest eigenvalues of the source state. With classical assistance, we obtain an explicit spectral threshold formula and a protocol attaining it. Classical communication strictly improves fidelity whenever $m$ is smaller than the source rank. The corresponding compression costs are two smoothed versions of the log-rank entropy, also called max-entropy: trace-distance smoothing under local operations and quadratic smoothing under LOCC. For i.i.d. copies of a fixed source with positive entropy variance, however, the two costs have identical first-, second-, and third-order asymptotic terms. For nonlattice spectra, we determine the constant-order advantage: classical communication saves $\log_2(e)-1$ bits per block asymptotically, and the ratio of assisted to unassisted minimum communication dimensions converges to $2/e$.

AI.tldr: Free classical communication can save an unbounded number of qubits in single-shot quantum compression while leaving the asymptotic i.i.d. rate unchanged; the paper pins down the exact optimal fidelity and cost functions with and without classical assistance.
AI.motivation: Quantum compression typically allows a small error and asks for the minimum dimension of a noiseless channel preserving correlations with an inaccessible reference. It is known that free classical communication does not change the asymptotic i.i.d. rate. The paper asks whether it can nonetheless help dramatically in the single-shot (finite-blocklength) regime, and if so, by how much.
AI.method: The authors characterize the exact optimal source fidelity for compression through an $m$-dimensional noiseless quantum channel, both with and without free classical communication, while preserving correlations with a reference. They derive closed-form expressions: without assistance the fidelity equals the Ky Fan norm $\|\rho\|_{(m)}$; with classical assistance they obtain an explicit spectral threshold formula together with an achieving protocol. They also connect the resulting compression costs to smoothed versions of the log-rank (max-) entropy and analyze higher-order asymptotics via entropy variance.
AI.result: At every fixed error in $(0,1)$, there exist sources whose unassisted compression cost is arbitrarily large while a single qubit plus classical communication suffices (no preshared entanglement). Classical communication strictly improves fidelity whenever $m$ is below the source rank. The two compression costs correspond to two smoothings of the log-rank entropy: trace-distance smoothing under local operations and quadratic smoothing under LOCC. For i.i.d. copies of a fixed source with positive entropy variance, both costs share identical first-, second-, and third-order asymptotic terms. For nonlattice spectra, classical communication saves $\log_2(e)-1$ bits per block asymptotically, and the ratio of assisted to unassisted minimum communication dimensions converges to $2/e$.
AI.conclusion: Free classical communication provides an unbounded single-shot advantage in quantum compression—reducing arbitrarily large costs to one qubit—even though it does not improve the asymptotic i.i.d. rate. The exact trade-offs are captured by a spectral threshold formula and two smoothings of the max-entropy, with a constant-order asymptotic saving of $\log_2(e)-1$ bits per block for nonlattice spectra.

title: Entanglement generation from degeneracy breaking of superradiant Liouvillian steady states by local operations
summary: Superradiance is a collective optical effect where emitters cooperatively radiate with a maximal intensity scaling proportional to the square of the number of emitters. Despite the superradiant cascade transitioning through highly entangled states, it has been shown that, for dynamics along the Dicke ladder, superradiance need not generate entanglement between the emitters. By contrast, we show how introducing incoherent local processes -- normally considered detrimental to both entanglement and superradiance -- can generate high levels of inter-emitter entanglement. We develop a general framework, using degenerate non-Hermitian perturbation theory, for the study of superradiant Liouvillian steady-state degeneracy breaking by these local operations from a few emitters up into the thermodynamic limit. From this, we are able to show that entanglement becomes ubiquitous in this regime and demonstrate its robustness against other forms of symmetric environmental noise. In the regime where pumping dominates, we find that population accumulates towards the maximally entangled minimal pseudo-spin states, corresponding to multi-emitter singlet states. This provides a deeper insight into many-body entanglement and the curious connection between local operations and entanglement generation.

AI.tldr: Introducing incoherent local processes (usually seen as detrimental) into superradiant dynamics can break Liouvillian steady-state degeneracy and generate high, robust inter-emitter entanglement, culminating in maximally entangled multi-emitter singlet states.
AI.motivation: Superradiance is a collective effect where emitters radiate cooperatively with intensity scaling as the square of emitter number. Although the superradiant cascade passes through highly entangled states, for dynamics along the Dicke ladder superradiance need not generate inter-emitter entanglement. The authors aim to show that local incoherent processes, normally considered harmful to entanglement and superradiance, can in fact create strong inter-emitter entanglement.
AI.method: The authors develop a general theoretical framework based on degenerate non-Hermitian perturbation theory to study how local incoherent operations break the degeneracy of superradiant Liouvillian steady states, spanning from a few emitters to the thermodynamic limit.
AI.result: Entanglement becomes ubiquitous in this regime and is robust against other forms of symmetric environmental noise. In the pumping-dominated regime, population accumulates toward the maximally entangled minimal pseudo-spin states, corresponding to multi-emitter singlet states.
AI.conclusion: Local incoherent processes can generate high levels of inter-emitter entanglement, providing deeper insight into many-body entanglement and the connection between local operations and entanglement generation.

title: A complete classification of operator controllability for closed three-level quantum systems driven by a single control
summary: In this work, we study operator controllability of finite-dimensional closed quantum systems driven by a single coherent control. Two general Lie-algebraic results on controllability of such systems are proved. The first gives sufficient conditions under which controllability of the system is preserved when controlled energy-level shifts are added. The second gives a sufficient basis-element condition under which the dynamical Lie algebra contains $\mathfrak{su}(N)$ and the system is therefore operator controllable. These results, together with known controllability conditions, are applied to obtain a complete classification of operator controllability of all three-level quantum systems in terms of their free and interaction Hamiltonian matrix elements. This classification covers all combinations of energy-level and level-spacing degeneracies, two or three allowed transitions, as well as the presence or absence of controlled energy-level shifts, and gives necessary and sufficient conditions for operator controllability in each case.

AI.tldr: This paper establishes two general Lie-algebraic results on operator controllability of finite-dimensional closed quantum systems driven by a single coherent control, and applies them to fully classify controllability of all three-level quantum systems.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to understand when a closed quantum system driven by a single coherent control is operator controllable, and specifically to comprehensively classify controllability for three-level systems under various degeneracy and transition configurations.
AI.method: Two general Lie-algebraic results are proved: (1) sufficient conditions for controllability preserved when controlled energy-level shifts are added, and (2) a sufficient basis-element condition under which the dynamical Lie algebra contains su(N), implying operator controllability. These are combined with known controllability conditions and applied to three-level systems.
AI.result: A complete classification of operator controllability for all three-level quantum systems in terms of free and interaction Hamiltonian matrix elements is obtained, covering all combinations of energy-level and level-spacing degeneracies, two or three allowed transitions, and presence or absence of controlled energy-level shifts, with necessary and sufficient conditions in each case.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides a rigorous Lie-algebraic framework and a full controllability classification for three-level quantum systems, offering necessary and sufficient conditions for operator controllability across all relevant configurations.

title: Partial-coherence weak measurement of polarization qubits with a temporal pointer: theory and experiment
summary: Weak measurement has proven useful for metrology, for probing quantum paradoxes, and for the direct measurement of quantum states. Weak measurements of polarization qubits with temporal pointers provide a direct route to weak-value characterization, including in regimes where the pointer is only partially coherent. We derive a closed-form expression for the post-selected temporal shift that interpolates between the incoherent and coherent (ideal) weak-measurement limits through a single parameter $ν$, the pointer visibility. The expression is experimentally tested for a range of polarization states spanning three trajectories corresponding to rotations about the principal axes of the Poincaré sphere. Two of the trajectories provide parameter-free benchmarks, with the real part of the weak value following $\cos^2θ$ and $1/2$. In contrast, the weak value along the third trajectory is sensitive to incoherence and is well described by the single-parameter partial-coherence model, from which a reduced pointer visibility is obtained. Time shifts are extracted from the smoothed derivative of the pulse leading edge with internal calibration, reaching few-picosecond precision on 10 ns optical pulses using commercial components. The same apparatus also gives qualitative access to the imaginary quadrature through the frequency centroid, showing that temporal weak measurements remain accessible and quantitative in partially coherent pulsed systems.

AI.tldr: The paper derives and experimentally validates a closed-form model for the post-selected temporal shift in weak measurements of polarization qubits, parameterized solely by pointer visibility ν, that interpolates between the incoherent and coherent weak-measurement limits.
AI.motivation: Weak measurement is valuable for metrology, probing quantum paradoxes, and direct state measurement. However, weak-value characterization is typically treated in the ideal coherent limit, whereas realistic temporal pointers are often only partially coherent. A quantitative description bridging the incoherent and coherent regimes is needed.
AI.method: The authors derive a closed-form expression for the post-selected temporal shift governed by a single parameter, the pointer visibility ν. They test it on polarization states spanning three trajectories corresponding to rotations about the principal axes of the Poincaré sphere, extracting time shifts from the smoothed derivative of the pulse leading edge with internal calibration, achieving few-picosecond precision on 10 ns optical pulses using commercial components. The imaginary quadrature is accessed qualitatively via the frequency centroid.
AI.result: Two trajectories yield parameter-free benchmarks, with the real part of the weak value following cos²θ and 1/2. The third trajectory is sensitive to incoherence and is well described by the single-parameter partial-coherence model, yielding a reduced pointer visibility.
AI.conclusion: Temporal weak measurements remain accessible and quantitative in partially coherent pulsed systems, with the single-parameter visibility model capturing the interpolation between incoherent and coherent limits.

title: Entanglement detection in dynamical quantum systems
summary: Quantum science and engineering increasingly target the exploitation and control of large-scale dynamical systems. As system size grows, novel phenomena and quantum advantages emerge, but the resulting many-body dynamics become correspondingly harder to monitor and characterize. In particular, the underlying Hamiltonian often lacks symmetries, and the induced many-body dynamics quickly become hard to track. Focusing on one of the most important quantum features---entanglement---we demonstrate that, for a broad class of common Hamiltonian models, one can design effective witnesses that detect both the presence and structure of entanglement over relatively long evolution times. Inspired by stabilizer-based simulation, we track the evolution of generalized stabilizers of the underlying state and use them to construct linear entanglement witnesses. Through numerical experiments on Heisenberg-type Hamiltonians with up to twelve qubits, we show that the required number of measurement settings can be kept at a modest scale as the system size increases, and entanglement detection remains effective over evolution times that significantly exceed those accessible to naive approaches. The corresponding calculations can be carried out largely symbolically. Furthermore, unlike accurate state simulation, the stabilizer-based design of entanglement witnesses can be performed in a much more coarse-grained, digitized manner. We hope these results will stimulate further exploration of the quantum control of large systems.

AI.tldr: This paper designs linear entanglement witnesses for large many-body quantum systems by tracking the evolution of generalized stabilizers, enabling entanglement detection over long timescales with a modest number of measurement settings.
AI.motivation: As quantum systems grow in size, novel phenomena and quantum advantages emerge, but the resulting many-body dynamics become increasingly hard to monitor and characterize. The underlying Hamiltonian often lacks symmetries, and the induced dynamics quickly become difficult to track, making entanglement detection a key challenge.
AI.method: Inspired by stabilizer-based simulation, the authors track the evolution of generalized stabilizers of the underlying state and use them to construct linear entanglement witnesses. The approach exploits symbolic computation and a coarse-grained, digitized design rather than accurate state simulation.
AI.result: Numerical experiments on Heisenberg-type Hamiltonians with up to twelve qubits show that the required number of measurement settings stays modest as system size increases, and entanglement detection remains effective over evolution times significantly exceeding those accessible to naive approaches.
AI.conclusion: Stabilizer-based entanglement witnesses can detect both the presence and structure of entanglement over relatively long evolution times and can be designed in a coarse-grained, digitized manner, which may stimulate further exploration of quantum control of large systems.

title: Generative learning of time series with holographic quantum circuit sampling
summary: Quantum generative models face growing qubit requirements and concentrated loss landscapes when learning long time series. Here we introduce holographic quantum circuit sampling (HQCS), which combines mid-circuit measurements, qubit reuse and independently parameterized temporal blocks to generate trajectories with a fixed number of qubits. For Haar-random HQCS and a normalized exponential kernel, we prove inverse-polynomial bounds on maximum mean discrepancy loss variance, contrasting with exponential concentration in global Haar-random generators. For generic members of a family of nonstationary Markov processes, temporal parameterization reduces exact-generation gate counts from quadratic to linear in sequence length relative to a specified class of repeated shared-block generators. Simulations demonstrate learning of Gaussian autoregressive processes and historical Volatility Index (VIX) trajectories, with the latter achieving over tenfold lower maximum mean discrepancy than the tested classical benchmarks. These results establish a framework for quantum time-series generation with fixed qubit requirements and provable avoidance of exponential loss concentration as sequence length grows.

AI.tldr: HQCS uses mid-circuit measurements, qubit reuse, and independently parameterized temporal blocks to generate long time series with a fixed qubit count, with provable inverse-polynomial loss variance and linear gate scaling.
AI.motivation: Quantum generative models struggle with long time series due to growing qubit requirements and concentrated (exponentially vanishing) loss landscapes as sequence length increases.
AI.method: Holographic quantum circuit sampling (HQCS) combines mid-circuit measurements, qubit reuse, and independently parameterized temporal blocks. The authors analyze Haar-random HQCS with a normalized exponential kernel, proving inverse-polynomial bounds on maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) loss variance, and study exact-generation gate counts for a family of nonstationary Markov processes versus repeated shared-block generators.
AI.result: Proved inverse-polynomial MMD loss variance bounds versus exponential concentration in global Haar-random generators. Temporal parameterization reduces exact-generation gate counts from quadratic to linear in sequence length. Simulations learned Gaussian autoregressive processes and historical VIX trajectories, the latter achieving over tenfold lower MMD than tested classical benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: HQCS provides a framework for quantum time-series generation with fixed qubit requirements and provable avoidance of exponential loss concentration as sequence length grows.

title: Signal-to-noise problems in fault-tolerant quantum computation
summary: Quantum computation offers a promising alternative to classical Monte Carlo methods by naturally avoiding sign problems through unitary evolution. A common misconception follows from this: because quantum simulation sidesteps the sign problem, it is often assumed to be an essentially perfect substitute for classical sampling. This is false---quantum measurements are intrinsically stochastic, and estimating observables often requires a number of samples that grows exponentially with system size, time separation, or inverse temperature, exactly as in the classical signal-to-noise problem. In this work, we analyze the origin and structure of signal-to-noise problems in quantum computation, drawing parallels with classical Monte Carlo, and demonstrate that such noise persists even in sign-problem-free regimes. We discuss strategies to mitigate it, in particular a quantum generalization of Stein control variates construction, in which unbiased estimators are built from operator commutators $[X,A]$ and their discrete diagonal counterparts, and validate the approach with exactly solvable numerical examples that quantify the achievable variance reduction. Our results underscore that variance reduction, not merely sign-problem avoidance, is required to make quantum algorithms practically viable for many-body physics.

AI.tldr: Quantum computation avoids the sign problem but still suffers from intrinsic measurement noise; the authors analyze these signal-to-noise problems and propose a quantum generalization of Stein control variates using operator commutators to reduce variance.
AI.motivation: There is a common misconception that because quantum simulation sidesteps the classical sign problem, it is an essentially perfect substitute for classical sampling. The paper argues this is false: quantum measurements are intrinsically stochastic, and estimating observables can require exponentially many samples—mirroring the classical signal-to-noise problem—even in sign-problem-free regimes.
AI.method: The authors analyze the origin and structure of signal-to-noise problems in quantum computation, drawing parallels with classical Monte Carlo. To mitigate the noise, they introduce a quantum generalization of Stein control variates, constructing unbiased estimators from operator commutators $[X,A]$ and their discrete diagonal counterparts.
AI.result: The approach is validated with exactly solvable numerical examples that quantify the achievable variance reduction.
AI.conclusion: The results underscore that variance reduction, not merely sign-problem avoidance, is required to make quantum algorithms practically viable for many-body physics.

title: Monogamy of quantum steering in exciton--cavity optomechanical system
summary: In this work, we study a theoretical scheme to investigate the monogamy of quantum steering in a hybrid exciton--cavity optomechanical (EOM) system. Within the Gaussian-state formalism, we quantify the steerability among the exciton, photon, and mechanical modes in both the steady-state and dynamical regimes. We establish and verify CKW-type monogamy inequalities for Gaussian steering and demonstrate that the distribution of bipartite steering among the three modes can be controlled through the system parameters. We further examine the influence of thermal noise and temporal evolution on the steering properties and the corresponding monogamy relations. Our results show that increasing the temperature generally suppresses the strength of Gaussian steering and modifies the degree of steering sharing imposed by the CKW-type monogamy relations. In contrast, in the dynamical regime, the steerability can increase with evolution time over suitable temporal windows, indicating that the transient dynamics can be exploited to enhance quantum correlations. These results highlight the potential of hybrid exciton--optomechanical platforms for controllable quantum correlations and provide a promising route toward the generation and manipulation of multipartite quantum resources.

AI.tldr: This work theoretically investigates monogamy of Gaussian quantum steering among exciton, photon, and mechanical modes in a hybrid exciton–cavity optomechanical system, showing parameter-controllable steering distribution and verifying CKW-type monogamy inequalities in steady-state and dynamical regimes.
AI.motivation: Understanding how bipartite quantum steering is distributed and shared among multiple modes is fundamental for multipartite quantum resources. Hybrid exciton–optomechanical platforms offer a promising but underexplored setting for controllable quantum correlations, motivating a systematic study of steering monogamy under realistic conditions such as thermal noise and dynamics.
AI.method: The authors adopt a Gaussian-state formalism to quantify steerability among exciton, photon, and mechanical modes. They establish and verify CKW-type monogamy inequalities for Gaussian steering, analyze the bipartite steering distribution as a function of system parameters, and examine the effects of thermal noise (temperature) and temporal evolution in both steady-state and dynamical regimes.
AI.result: CKW-type monogamy inequalities for Gaussian steering are established and verified, and the distribution of bipartite steering among the three modes is shown to be controllable via system parameters. Increasing temperature generally suppresses Gaussian steering strength and modifies the degree of steering sharing dictated by the monogamy relations, whereas in the dynamical regime steerability can increase with evolution time within suitable temporal windows, indicating transient dynamics can enhance quantum correlations.
AI.conclusion: Hybrid exciton–optomechanical platforms are promising for controllable quantum correlations, offering a viable route toward the generation and manipulation of multipartite quantum resources via parameter tuning and transient dynamics.

title: Photonic realization of an electromagnetic cavity field with uniform mirror motion
summary: We perform a detailed mathematical study of the effective Hamiltonian describing a non-stationary electromagnetic cavity field, introduced by C.~K.~Law, in the presence of uniform linear motion. We find that the corresponding dynamical equations admit a unitary diagonalization and that the normalized velocity of motion satisfies the two-sided bound $\lvert v/c \rvert \lesssim 10.1716$. Although this result is mathematically consistent, the interval obtained is an order of magnitude larger than the physically admissible range $\lvert v/c \rvert < 1$. To address this limitation, we propose a reinterpretation of bosonic coupling terms as generators of the symplectic algebra $\mathrm{Sp}(4,\mathbb{R})$, identifying them with transformations that can be implemented through linear optical elements. Within this photonic approach, the coupling parameters are not restricted to small values, allowing us to explore regimes of strong effective interactions. In this case, we demonstrate the generation of two-mode squeezed states and derive analytical expressions for the average photon number in each mode. Furthermore, we analyze statistical properties that characterize mixedness and entanglement, including intermode correlations, the Mandel parameter, and the linear entropy. The corresponding Wigner function provides a phase-space visualization of the system's behavior, illustrating the connection between cavity motion, mode coupling, and nonclassical field correlations via the underlying symplectic algebra.

AI.tldr: A non-stationary cavity field under uniform linear motion is studied; the effective Hamiltonian admits unitary diagonalization with a mathematically consistent but physically loose velocity bound, and recasting the bosonic couplings as Sp(4,R) generators yields a photonic scheme for strong-coupling two-mode squeezing.
AI.motivation: The effective Hamiltonian of a non-stationary electromagnetic cavity field under uniform linear motion (introduced by C. K. Law) is examined rigorously. The derived dynamical equations give a velocity bound that, while mathematically consistent, is an order of magnitude larger than the physical bound |v/c| < 1, motivating an alternative framework that avoids small-coupling restrictions.
AI.method: Detailed mathematical analysis of the effective Hamiltonian; unitary diagonalization of the dynamical equations. Reinterpretation of bosonic coupling terms as generators of the symplectic algebra Sp(4,R), identified with transformations implementable via linear optical elements, allowing non-perturbative coupling regimes. Derivation of two-mode squeezed states and analytical expressions for the average photon number per mode; computation of statistical quantifiers (intermode correlations, Mandel parameter, linear entropy) and the Wigner function.
AI.result: The diagonalization yields a two-sided bound on the normalized velocity, |v/c| ≲ 10.1716, which exceeds the physical range |v/c| < 1 by roughly an order of magnitude. Within the photonic approach, strong effective interactions are accessible; two-mode squeezed states are generated, analytical average photon numbers per mode are obtained, and mixedness/entanglement statistics (correlations, Mandel parameter, linear entropy) plus the Wigner function are characterized.
AI.conclusion: The symplectic Sp(4,R) reformulation connects cavity motion, mode coupling, and nonclassical field correlations, providing an experimentally feasible linear-optics route to strong-coupling two-mode squeezing and a phase-space visualization of the resulting nonclassical states.

title: Receiver-Constrained Recovery Placement for Encoded-Qutrit Teleportation under Monitored Decay
summary: Using established probabilistic measurement-reversal theory, we study recovery placement in encoded-qutrit teleportation under monitored decay. We characterize the success advantage of reversing a no-jump map only on the encoded support and compare two receiver capabilities. The restricted-map construction applies to general finite-dimensional supports; explicit timing results are obtained for a coherent V-type sender, a $Λ$-type receiver, and $S=\{0,2\}$, within a prescribed family of maximal exact sender reversals. With one outcome-independent full-space receiver filter, we maximize success probability at fixed total time subject to a minimum success-weighted conditional fidelity. A single preassigned recovery time yields up to three duration-dependent regimes: no sender reversal, the earliest feasible intermediate reversal, and final-time reversal. If recovery times may be randomized independently of the input and only the pooled successful ensemble must meet the fidelity requirement, the optimum over all such timing distributions mixes the two endpoints for $ΓT \ge (\ln 3)/2$. With Bell-outcome-dependent nonunitary receiver recovery, each accepted full-column-rank transfer branch can instead be reversed exactly. For the same model and sender-operation family, omitting sender reversal uniquely maximizes the exact-teleportation success probability for every finite $T>0$ at positive decay rate. Partial pathway coherence further distinguishes relative support gain from absolute recovery success: the long-time dark-state plateau survives only for fully coherent decay. These results show how receiver control capabilities and the meaning of the fidelity constraint determine whether intermediate sender recovery is useful.

AI.tldr: This work applies probabilistic measurement-reversal theory to recovery placement in encoded-qutrit teleportation under monitored decay, showing that whether intermediate sender recovery helps depends on receiver control capabilities and the interpretation of the fidelity constraint.
AI.motivation: Teleportation under monitored decay suffers fidelity loss, and recovery operations (sender reversal and receiver filtering) must be placed and timed well. It is unclear when an intermediate sender reversal is beneficial versus omitting it, and how this depends on the receiver's control capabilities and on how the fidelity constraint is defined.
AI.method: Probabilistic measurement-reversal theory is used to characterize the success advantage of reversing a no-jump map restricted to the encoded support. A restricted-map construction for general finite-dimensional supports is developed, with explicit timing results for a coherent V-type sender, a Λ-type receiver, and S={0,2} within a prescribed family of maximal exact sender reversals. Two receiver capabilities are compared: an outcome-independent full-space filter maximizing success at fixed total time under a minimum success-weighted conditional fidelity, and Bell-outcome-dependent nonunitary recovery that exactly reverses each accepted full-column-rank transfer branch. Timing is analyzed for a single preassigned recovery time and for randomized recovery times independent of the input with only the pooled successful ensemble meeting the fidelity constraint; partial pathway coherence is also examined.
AI.result: A single preassigned recovery time yields up to three duration-dependent regimes: no sender reversal, the earliest feasible intermediate reversal, and final-time reversal. For randomized recovery times, the optimum mixes the two endpoints when ΓT ≥ (ln 3)/2. With Bell-outcome-dependent nonunitary receiver recovery, each accepted full-column-rank transfer branch can be reversed exactly, and omitting sender reversal uniquely maximizes exact-teleportation success probability for every finite T>0 at positive decay rate. Partial pathway coherence separates relative support gain from absolute recovery success: the long-time dark-state plateau survives only for fully coherent decay.
AI.conclusion: Receiver control capabilities and the meaning of the fidelity constraint jointly determine whether intermediate sender recovery is useful, with exact branch reversal eliminating the benefit of sender reversal and partial coherence erasing the long-time dark-state plateau.

title: Criticality Concentrates Extensive Sensing Information into a Local Readout
summary: We show that criticality concentrates extensive sensing information into a local trajectory. In the rapid-readout limit of an all-to-all dissipative feedback network, a single binary trajectory has a Fisher-information rate linear in $N$ for a common weak field, as does the full record. Critical slowing does not remove this gain because the local weight of the slow mode decreases with $N$. An analytic bound guarantees that the local record retains more than half of the full information across the entire channel-parameter range. We also identify how parameter drives and observation dynamics determine local access to collective information beyond permutation symmetry. Furthermore, our sparse-readout theorem establishes a $k^{-1}$ decay of fractional information loss: only $Θ(\varepsilon^{-1})$ trajectories are needed to retain a fraction $1-\varepsilon$ of the full information rate. Any growing readout set, even of vanishing density, asymptotically recovers the full common-field Fisher-information rate.

AI.tldr: Criticality concentrates extensive collective sensing information into a locally observed binary trajectory; a single trajectory retains over half the full Fisher information, and only Θ(ε⁻¹) trajectories are needed to preserve a fraction 1−ε of it.
AI.motivation: Collective sensing typically assumes access to the full network record, but realistic readout is local and sparse. The paper asks whether the extensive (linear-in-N) Fisher information about a common weak field survives when only local trajectories are observed, especially in the critical, rapid-readout regime where critical slowing might be expected to destroy the gain.
AI.method: Analysis of an all-to-all dissipative feedback network in the rapid-readout limit, treating a single binary trajectory as the local record. Fisher-information rate of the local trajectory versus the full record; analytic bound on retained information across the channel-parameter range; identification of the roles of parameter drives and observation dynamics beyond permutation symmetry; a sparse-readout theorem for fractional information loss.
AI.result: A single binary trajectory has a Fisher-information rate linear in N, matching the full record's scaling. Critical slowing does not eliminate this gain because the slow mode's local weight decreases with N. An analytic bound guarantees the local record retains more than half of the full information across the entire channel-parameter range. Fractional information loss decays as k⁻¹, so only Θ(ε⁻¹) trajectories retain a fraction 1−ε of the full rate; any growing readout set, even of vanishing density, asymptotically recovers the full common-field Fisher-information rate.
AI.conclusion: Criticality enables local—not merely global—access to extensive collective sensing information, making sparse, low-density readout asymptotically sufficient and providing a quantitative trade-off between readout sparsity and information retained.

title: Genuine Information Backflow Requires Noncommuting Initial System States
comment: 21 pages, 4 figures. Submitted to Open Systems & Information Dynamics
summary: The Gorini-Kossakowski-Lindblad-Sudarshan (GKLS) equation, a cornerstone of open-system theory, describes Markovian semigroup dynamics in which information about the initial preparation cannot revive. Beyond this regime, information revivals are widely interpreted as backflow from a non-Markovian environment. However, a decrease followed by an increase in information retrievable from the system need not imply that information has returned from the environment [PRX Quantum 6, 020316 (2025)]. It may instead arise from noise correlations unrelated to the system's initial preparation, carried by inert degrees of freedom that never interact with the system and therefore cannot mediate backflow. Such revivals are called extrinsic; genuine backflow is reserved for revivals that cannot be explained this way. The framework developed in that work, however, assumes access to arbitrary initial system states, an assumption often incompatible with physical constraints or limited experimental control. This leaves open which properties of the available preparations are necessary for an information revival to certify genuine backflow. Here we extend the framework to allow the description of restricted families of initial states and show that genuine backflow is possible only if the family contains noncommuting states. If all available states commute, as in a classical stochastic process, every revival can be explained by a suitable inert extension and is therefore extrinsic. Noncommutativity of the available system states is thus necessary for information revivals to provide an operational signature of environmental memory.

AI.tldr: The paper extends a framework for distinguishing genuine information backflow from extrinsic revivals (caused by inert noise correlations) to settings with restricted initial-state families, proving that noncommutativity of the available preparations is necessary for revivals to certify genuine environmental memory.
AI.motivation: Information revivals in open-system dynamics are commonly taken as signatures of non-Markovian backflow from the environment. A recent result (PRX Quantum 6, 020316 (2025)) showed this interpretation fails: revivals can be extrinsic, arising from noise correlations carried by inert degrees of freedom that never interact with the system. That framework, however, presupposes access to arbitrary initial system states, which is often unattainable under physical constraints or limited experimental control. It thus remained unclear which properties of the actually available preparations are required for a revival to certify genuine backflow.
AI.method: The authors generalize the existing framework to describe restricted families of initial states rather than arbitrary preparations, and analyze under what conditions an information revival can be attributed to genuine backflow rather than to an inert extension.
AI.result: Genuine backflow is possible only if the family of available initial states contains noncommuting states. If all available states commute—as in a classical stochastic process—every revival can be explained by a suitable inert extension and is therefore extrinsic.
AI.conclusion: Noncommutativity of the accessible system states is a necessary condition for information revivals to serve as an operational signature of environmental memory, refining the criteria for genuine non-Markovianity under realistic constraints on state preparation.

title: Breakdown of thermalization in quantum spin systems with long-range interactions
summary: Quantum thermalization of closed systems -- i.e. the relaxation of local properties to their thermodynamic value along the Hamiltonian evolution -- is generically expected in non-integrable systems at finite energy density. In this work we show that quantum spin systems with at least one spin component coupled through long-range ferromagnetic interactions, and a second spin component coupled to a field, cannot in general thermalize to a paramagnetic state whenever they have a finite, negative energy per spin. The long-range interactions we consider decay as a power law of the distance, $\sim r^{-α}$ with $α< d$, where $d$ is the number of spatial dimensions of the system. The lack of thermalization is generic to an infinite family of Hamiltonians, and it is not associated to any form of integrability. It can instead be understood by the anomalous features of the thermodynamics of the system in the paramagnetic phase, which cannot be reflected in the properties of the eigenstates. This leads to a breakdown of eigenstate typicality and of the eigenstate thermalization hypothesis. Interestingly, the non-thermal states emerging at long times in the dynamics display long-range multipartite entanglement, elevating the breakdown of thermalization to a resource.

AI.tldr: Long-range ferromagnetic spin systems with a transverse field fail to thermalize to a paramagnetic state at finite negative energy density, breaking eigenstate thermalization. The resulting non-thermal states exhibit long-range multipartite entanglement.
AI.motivation: Quantum thermalization—relaxation of local observables to thermodynamic values—is expected in generic non-integrable systems. The authors question whether this holds for long-range interacting spin systems, since long-range interactions can alter thermodynamics and elicit anomalous behavior not captured by standard eigenstate-based arguments.
AI.method: They study quantum spin systems with one spin component coupled via long-range ferromagnetic interactions decaying as a power law ∼r^{-α} (α < d, with d the spatial dimension) and a second spin component coupled to a field. They analyze the thermodynamics of the paramagnetic phase versus the properties of individual eigenstates, and examine long-time dynamics.
AI.result: For finite negative energy per spin, the systems cannot generically thermalize to a paramagnetic state. The failure is generic across an infinite family of Hamiltonians and is not tied to integrability. It stems from anomalous thermodynamic features of the paramagnetic phase that cannot be reflected in eigenstate properties, causing breakdown of eigenstate typicality and of the eigenstate thermalization hypothesis. Long-time states show long-range multipartite entanglement.
AI.conclusion: Thermalization can break down in generic, non-integrable long-range ferromagnetic spin systems due to a mismatch between thermodynamics and eigenstate structure. The emergent non-thermal states carry long-range multipartite entanglement, turning the breakdown of thermalization into a usable resource.

title: Riemannian Formulation of Sample-Based Quantum Krylov Solvers for Elliptic Problems: Energy-Norm Guarantees and Duct-Flow Applications
summary: Sample-based quantum linear solvers measure quantum Krylov states $e^{-iAT}|b\rangle$ and reconstruct the solution of $Ax=b$ classically on the observed basis states. We develop this approach for positive-definite systems that arise from elliptic partial differential equations. We show that the sampling guarantees hold in any fixed basis with an efficient transform. We then replace the variational reconstruction by a Galerkin solve on the sampled set. For this reconstruction we derive expected and high-probability energy-norm error bounds, a sample complexity in terms of the smallest sampling probability on an essential set, a computable residual certificate, and a support-completeness theorem for the dephased outcome law. We formulate the method for elliptic problems on Riemannian cross sections. In two dimensions the stiffness matrix is metric-independent in conformal coordinates, and curved vessels lead to the same matrix class. Killing symmetries of the cross section give selection rules for the measurement outcomes, and the Lie derivative of the metric gives first-order bounds for geometric perturbations. We separate operator approximations, whose effect we bound, from sampler approximations, which affect coverage but not the target. As examples we treat the implicit step of pulsatile flow in elliptic, lens-shaped, and curved ducts. In simulations of up to 12 qubits, the number of Fourier modes required for 1% error grows from 14 to 60 while the number of unknowns grows from 64 to 4096. A classical residual-greedy selection is nevertheless more efficient than quantum sampling in all cases studied, consistent with the low measured sampling efficiency. On a six-qubit trapped-ion processor, the measured outcome laws follow a replacement-noise model whose strength grows by about 0.6% per two-qubit gate, and a parity selection rule rejects shots at the predicted rate.

AI.tldr: The paper extends sample-based quantum linear solvers (QBK) to positive-definite systems from elliptic PDEs by replacing variational reconstruction with a Galerkin solve on sampled basis states, providing error bounds, sample complexity, and a residual certificate, while noting that classical residual-greedy selection still outperforms quantum sampling in tested regimes.
AI.motivation: Sample-based quantum linear solvers (e.g., QBK) reconstruct solutions to Ax=b from measured quantum Krylov states, but existing formulations lack rigorous guarantees for PDE-derived positive-definite systems and rely on variational reconstruction. The authors aim to place this approach on firmer theoretical footing for elliptic PDE problems and to characterize when the quantum sampling advantage actually materializes relative to classical methods.
AI.method: The authors replace variational reconstruction with a Galerkin solve on the sampled set. They derive expected and high-probability energy-norm error bounds, sample complexity in terms of the smallest sampling probability on an essential set, a computable residual certificate, and a support-completeness theorem for the dephased outcome law. The method is formulated for elliptic problems on Riemannian cross sections, using conformal coordinates in 2D where the stiffness matrix is metric-independent. Symmetry selection rules from Killing fields and first-order geometric perturbation bounds from the Lie derivative of the metric are used. Operator approximations and sampler approximations are separated and analyzed.
AI.result: In simulations up to 12 qubits, the number of Fourier modes needed for 1% error grows from 14 to 60 as unknowns grow from 64 to 4096. Classical residual-greedy selection is more efficient than quantum sampling in all studied cases, consistent with low measured sampling efficiency. On a six-qubit trapped-ion processor, measured outcome laws follow a replacement-noise model with strength growing ~0.6% per two-qubit gate, and a parity selection rule rejects shots at the predicted rate.
AI.conclusion: The Galerkin-based sample reconstruction yields rigorous energy-norm error bounds and sample complexity for elliptic systems, and the formulation transfers to Riemannian cross sections with symmetry-derived selection rules. However, quantum sampling efficiency was too low for the method to surpass classical residual-greedy selection in the tested regimes, indicating that practical quantum advantage requires substantially better sampling efficiency and/or lower gate noise.

title: A Quantum Analogue of the Covering Lemma: Limits of Exact Anonymous Computation
summary: Can quantum communication determine the size of an anonymous network when no size bound is known? Classical impossibility proofs rely on the covering lemma: an execution can be reproduced on a larger network with the same local structure. Quantum interference invalidates this argument - a measurement record possible on a network can become impossible on a cover. We show that the impossibility of exact counting nevertheless survives. Our main result is a quantum analogue of the covering lemma that preserves local possibilities rather than complete executions. Within a cyclic covering family, every local measurement outcome possible at a node remains possible at a corresponding node in every sufficiently large network. This holds even after information has travelled around the smaller network, beyond the reach of a simple locality argument. We extend the principle to the universal covering tree and finite covers with sufficiently long cycles. The proof combines tensor-network methods with graph coverings: a common representation across network sizes turns normalization into a constraint on which local outcomes can occur.
