For uniform synchronous protocols with independently prepared nodes, this support-lifting principle rules out zero-error counting and even the production of a guaranteed finite size bound on anonymous rings and the other cyclic covering families considered here. It also rules out exact leader election with termination in finite time with probability one on these families. Measurements, classical control, and local memory growing with time are allowed; no predetermined running-time bound is assumed. Quantum interference thus defeats execution lifting without enabling infallible certification of network size.

AI.tldr: A quantum analogue of the classical covering lemma is established, showing that quantum interference does not enable exact counting of anonymous networks when no size bound is known.
AI.motivation: Classical impossibility proofs for determining the size of an anonymous network rely on the covering lemma: an execution on a small network can be simulated on a larger one with identical local structure. Quantum interference seems to break this argument, since a measurement record possible on a network may become impossible on a cover, potentially allowing nodes to certify network size.
AI.method: The authors prove a quantum covering lemma that preserves local measurement possibilities rather than complete executions. Using tensor-network methods combined with graph coverings, they represent protocols uniformly across network sizes, turning normalization into a constraint on which local outcomes can occur. The principle is extended to universal covering trees and finite covers with sufficiently long cycles.
AI.result: Within any cyclic covering family, every local measurement outcome possible at a node remains possible at the corresponding node in every sufficiently large network, even after information has propagated around the smaller network beyond the reach of naive locality reasoning. This rules out zero-error size counting and the production of a guaranteed finite size bound for uniform synchronous protocols with independently prepared nodes on anonymous rings and related cyclic covering families.
AI.conclusion: Quantum interference defeats execution lifting but does not enable infallible certification of network size. It also rules out exact leader election with termination in finite time with probability one on these families, even allowing measurements, classical control, and unbounded local memory, with no predetermined running-time bound.

title: Non-Stationary Quantum Systems Associated with Stationary Scattering in One Dimension
summary: Stationary scattering admits a dynamical formulation in which the scattering data are extracted from the evolution operator for an effective non-stationary and non-unitary quantum system. This provides a mathematical method of solving scattering problems. We consider the possibility of realizing such a quantum system and relating the scattering information to outcomes of quantum measurements performed on it. To this end, we examine stationary scattering problems in one dimension where the scattering data consist of reflection and transmission amplitudes and the corresponding effective quantum system is a non-unitary two-level system. The states of this system identify points in a Bloch sphere $S^2$ and their evolution yields trajectories in $S^2$. Quantum measurements turn out to be capable of providing information about the reflection amplitudes. We identify configurations displaying reflectionlessness with situations where one or both of the poles of $S^2$ undergo cyclic evolutions. Spectral singularities and coherent perfect absorption correspond to dynamical spin flips which map one of the poles of $S^2$ to the other.

AI.tldr: The paper examines a non-unitary two-level quantum system realization of 1D stationary scattering, mapping reflection/transmission data onto Bloch-sphere trajectories, and shows quantum measurements can extract reflection amplitudes, with reflectionless, spectral-singularity, and coherent-perfect-absorption conditions interpreted as cyclic evolutions and spin flips on S².
AI.motivation: Stationary scattering admits a dynamical reformulation where scattering data come from the evolution operator of an effective non-stationary, non-unitary quantum system, providing a mathematical method for solving scattering problems. The authors aim to explore whether such a system can be physically realized and whether quantum measurements on it can yield scattering information.
AI.method: They study one-dimensional stationary scattering problems in which the data are reflection and transmission amplitudes and the effective quantum system is a non-unitary two-level system. Its states are mapped to points on a Bloch sphere S², and the evolution traces trajectories on S²; they then relate quantum measurements to the reflection amplitudes and classify special configurations via the resulting dynamics.
AI.result: Quantum measurements can supply information about the reflection amplitudes. Reflectionless configurations correspond to situations where one or both poles of S² execute cyclic evolutions. Spectral singularities and coherent perfect absorption correspond to dynamical spin flips that map one pole of S² to the other.
AI.conclusion: The dynamical, non-unitary two-level formulation offers a Bloch-sphere geometric picture of 1D stationary scattering, linking measurable reflection amplitudes to quantum-measurement outcomes and giving dynamical interpretations of reflectionlessness, spectral singularities, and coherent perfect absorption.

title: Separability criteria and lower bounds of entanglement via realignment
summary: The detection and quantification of quantum entanglement are central problems in quantum information science. Based on the realignment of density matrices and the vectorization of reduced density matrices, we construct a family of enhanced separability criteria for bipartite and multipartite quantum systems. Our criteria recover the previously proposed realignment-based criteria as special cases and detect more entanglement than the earlier ones. Moreover, we derive tighter lower bounds for the concurrence and the convex-roof extended negativity, criteria for detecting the genuine tripartite entanglement, and lower bounds on genuine-multipartite-entanglement concurrence. The advantages of our results are demonstrated with detailed examples.

AI.tldr: The paper constructs enhanced separability criteria for bipartite and multipartite quantum systems using realignment of density matrices and vectorization of reduced density matrices, yielding stronger entanglement detection and tighter entanglement measure bounds than prior realignment-based approaches.
AI.motivation: Detection and quantification of quantum entanglement are central problems in quantum information science. Existing realignment-based separability criteria are limited in detection capability, motivating the need for enhanced criteria that detect more entanglement and provide tighter quantified bounds.
AI.method: The authors build a family of enhanced separability criteria based on the realignment of density matrices and the vectorization of reduced density matrices, applicable to bipartite and multipartite quantum systems. They further derive lower bounds for concurrence and convex-roof extended negativity, criteria for genuine tripartite entanglement, and lower bounds on genuine-multipartite-entanglement concurrence.
AI.result: The proposed criteria recover previously proposed realignment-based criteria as special cases while detecting more entanglement than earlier ones. Tighter lower bounds for concurrence and convex-roof extended negativity are obtained, along with genuine tripartite entanglement detection criteria and lower bounds on genuine-multipartite-entanglement concurrence, with advantages demonstrated through detailed examples.
AI.conclusion: The realignment- and vectorization-based framework generalizes and strengthens existing realignment-based separability criteria, offering improved entanglement detection and quantification for bipartite and multipartite systems.

title: Molecular Vibronic Complexity as a Quantum Resource for Optimal Control: Nonadiabatic Mixing Creates Protected Coherence Subspaces in Dissipative Environments
comment: 37 pages main file; 4 pages SI; 10 figures
summary: In molecules, electronic coherence typically decays within a few hundred femtoseconds, a timescale usually attributed to the environment. We show that it is set to a large extent by which coherences are excited: the molecule can host coherences that the bath barely sees, and optimal control can find and exploit them. Using gradient-based optimal control (GRAPE) with Redfield dynamics, we maximize the total vibronic coherence between the electronic ground and an optically bright electronic excited state in a three-state model with nonadiabatic features, in two regimes of low and high nonadiabatic mixing and for different system-bath coupling strengths. The Liouvillian spectrum reveals, in both regimes, a well-separated coherence mode with substantial ground-bright character that decays on a picosecond timescale. This mode is protected by mixing with the dark state, which brings the geometry of the optically accessible excited state close to that of the ground state and thus weakens its coupling to the bath. Without prior information, GRAPE finds this mode and keeps the photoexcited wave packet near the Franck-Condon region. At equal fluence, it increases the coherence at 800 fs by more than two orders of magnitude over a Gaussian pulse at the weakest coupling, and by many more at stronger coupling. The Liouvillian predicts the bath dependence of the long-lived coherence to within 1\%, and a Gaussian pulse tuned to the mode frequency comes within 10\% of the best pulse found. Beyond two-level and spin systems, our study puts forward the vibronic structure of molecules as a route to protected coherence subspaces, identifying a dark-state protection mechanism and a design criterion based on molecular parameters. These results lay the groundwork for our goal of using vibronic molecular systems as a resource for long-lived, controllable coherences in molecular quantum information science.

AI.tldr: Electronic coherence lifetimes in molecules are largely determined by which coherences are excited, not just the environment. Using gradient-based optimal control (GRAPE) with Redfield dynamics, the authors identify a long-lived "coherence mode" that is protected by mixing with a dark state, extending coherence beyond two orders of magnitude at 800 fs.
AI.motivation: Electronic coherence in molecules typically decays within a few hundred femtoseconds, a timescale usually attributed to the environment. This work challenges that assumption by asking whether the coherence lifetime is instead determined mainly by which coherences are excited, and whether optimal control can find and exploit molecule-hosted coherences that the bath barely sees.
AI.method: A three-state model with nonadiabatic features is studied in two regimes (low and high nonadiabatic mixing) and for different system-bath coupling strengths. Gradient-based optimal control (GRAPE) combined with Redfield dynamics maximizes total vibronic coherence between the electronic ground and an optically bright electronic excited state. The Liouvillian spectrum is analyzed to characterize the coherence modes, and optimally shaped pulses are compared with Gaussian pulses.
AI.result: In both regimes, the Liouvillian spectrum reveals a well-separated coherence mode with substantial ground-bright character decaying on a picosecond timescale. This mode is protected by mixing with the dark state, which brings the optically accessible excited state geometry close to that of the ground state and weakens bath coupling. Without prior information, GRAPE finds this mode and keeps the photoexcited wave packet near the Franck-Condon region. At equal fluence, it increases coherence at 800 fs by more than two orders of magnitude over a Gaussian pulse at the weakest coupling, and by more at stronger coupling. The Liouvillian predicts the bath dependence of the long-lived coherence to within 1%, and a Gaussian pulse tuned to the mode frequency comes within 10% of the best pulse found.
AI.conclusion: Beyond two-level and spin systems, this study puts forward molecular vibronic structure as a route to protected coherence subspaces, identifying a dark-state protection mechanism and a design criterion based on molecular parameters. These results lay the groundwork for using vibronic molecular systems as a resource for long-lived, controllable coherences in molecular quantum information science.

title: Two-axis twisting by two-photon exchange: rate, depth, and the self-Kerr constraint
summary: The coherent exchange of pairs of quanta between two bosonic modes is equivalent, up to a numerical factor, to the generator of two-axis twisting, which attains Heisenberg scaling of the squeezing; we determine how much of that equivalence survives in a realistic nonlinear medium. In any such medium the exchange term is accompanied by a local Kerr nonlinearity, and within a sector of fixed particle number the Hamiltonian depends on a single dimensionless ratio of the effective Kerr strength to the exchange strength. We derive two criteria governing this ratio and show that they are independent. The first is the rate at which squeezing is generated: the exponential rate follows in closed form, vanishes exactly when the two strengths are equal in magnitude, and recovers as the square root of the detuning from that point. The second is the depth to which squeezing can be driven: at fixed particle number the attainable depth is a function of the anisotropy of the mean-field saddle alone, reaches the full two-axis-twisting value only for the isotropic saddle, and is independent of the rate, parameter sets sharing the same anisotropy but differing in rate by a sizeable factor giving depths that agree to every printed digit. The closed-form Gaussian dynamics reveals a pitfall: extracting rates from short-time data overestimates them by more than a factor of two unless the saddle is isotropic. An isotropic cubic nonlinearity imposes the value of the ratio where the rate vanishes, so realizing two-axis twisting by pair exchange requires detuning it; a moderate mismatch already recovers almost all of the optimal depth. We also explain why the constraint has not surfaced before: at two quanta the self-Kerr shifts the two coupled states equally, so the two twisting Hamiltonians are rigorously indistinguishable, the degeneracy being lifted only from four quanta.

AI.tldr: The paper examines how the equivalence between coherent pair exchange in bosonic modes and two-axis twisting (TAT) survives in realistic nonlinear media, deriving two independent criteria—squeezing rate and attainable squeezing depth—and revealing that a Kerr nonlinearity requires detuning to realize optimal TAT squeezing.
AI.motivation: Coherent exchange of quantum pairs between two bosonic modes is theoretically equivalent to the two-axis twisting generator, which achieves Heisenberg-limited squeezing. However, realistic nonlinear media inevitably introduce a local Kerr nonlinearity alongside the exchange term. The authors aim to determine how much of this ideal equivalence survives under such realistic conditions.
AI.method: Within a fixed-particle-number sector, the Hamiltonian depends on a single dimensionless ratio of effective Kerr strength to exchange strength. The authors derive two independent criteria governing this ratio: (1) the exponential rate at which squeezing is generated, obtained in closed form, and (2) the attainable squeezing depth, analyzed via the anisotropy of the mean-field saddle. They employ closed-form Gaussian dynamics to characterize these criteria and examine the role of isotropic cubic nonlinearity.
AI.result: The exponential squeezing rate vanishes exactly when Kerr and exchange strengths are equal in magnitude and recovers as the square root of the detuning from that point. The attainable depth depends solely on the anisotropy of the mean-field saddle, reaching the full TAT value only for the isotropic saddle, and is independent of the rate—parameter sets with identical anisotropy but rate differing by a sizable factor yield depths agreeing to every printed digit. Extracting rates from short-time data overestimates them by more than a factor of two unless the saddle is isotropic. An isotropic cubic nonlinearity forces the ratio to the rate-vanishing value, so realizing TAT by pair exchange requires detuning; a moderate mismatch recovers almost all optimal depth.
AI.conclusion: The equivalence between pair exchange and two-axis twisting only partially survives in realistic nonlinear media, governed by two independent criteria (rate and depth). A Kerr nonlinearity imposes a constraint requiring detuning to realize TAT. Notably, at two quanta the self-Kerr shifts the two coupled states equally, rendering the two twisting Hamiltonians rigorously indistinguishable—the degeneracy is lifted only from four quanta onward, explaining why this constraint had not surfaced previously.

title: Violation of Bell-type Inequality in the Hanbury Brown-Twiss (HBT) Toy-Model: Quantum Correlations beyond Local-Realism
summary: The Hanbury Brown-Twiss (HBT) effect marked a significant milestone in quantum optics by illustrating that intensity correlations can reveal inherently quantum features of light. Motivated by the structure of the original 8-mode HBT interferometer, we develop a simplified 4-mode toy-model that captures its essential physical ingredients while significantly reducing analytical complexity. Our toy-model provides an intuitive and well-structured framework for examining the desired correlation functions. We investigate whether our toy-model can exhibit genuinely non-classical behaviour by formulating and applying a Bell-type inequality tailored to its specific measurement configuration. Our analysis shows that the correlations generated by the toy-model violate the inequality, indicating the presence of non-local features that are incompatible with any classical hidden-variable description. The results highlight the power of simplified models in uncovering fundamental aspects of non-classicality in optical systems.

AI.tldr: A simplified 4-mode toy-model of the Hanbury Brown-Twiss interferometer is developed and shown to violate a tailored Bell-type inequality, revealing non-classical, non-local correlations.
AI.motivation: The original 8-mode HBT interferometer captures key quantum-optical features but is analytically complex. The authors seek a simpler framework that preserves the essential physics while reducing analytical difficulty, and they aim to test whether such a reduced model can still display genuinely non-classical behaviour.
AI.method: Motivated by the structure of the original 8-mode HBT setup, the authors construct a 4-mode toy-model that retains the essential physical ingredients. They then formulate a Bell-type inequality adapted to the toy-model's specific measurement configuration and evaluate the correlation functions it generates.
AI.result: The correlations produced by the toy-model violate the tailored Bell-type inequality, indicating non-local features incompatible with any classical hidden-variable description.
AI.conclusion: Simplified models can effectively uncover fundamental aspects of non-classicality in optical systems, demonstrating the utility of reduced toy-models for studying quantum correlations.

title: Quantum ordinal optimization under a fixed comparison budget
summary: Ordinal optimization selects designs that are good enough rather than optimal when evaluation is expensive and the budget is small. The alignment probability measures the chance that the selected set contains at least a prescribed number of truly good designs. We formulate quantum ordinal optimization as a class of problems that maximize this probability under a fixed oracle budget. We study exact, coherent pairwise comparisons with one selected design as a first instance, with the budget counted in comparison queries. For every classical comparison budget smaller than the number of designs, we prove that a knockout among uniformly sampled designs attains the optimum. The sample is drawn without replacement and contains one more design than the number of comparisons. For a uniformly random order, the selected design's rank has a polynomial probability law. At the same comparison budget, the maximum quantum degree is at most twice the classical maximum, a factor attained whenever there are more than twice as many designs as comparisons, so a quantum algorithm can realize rank laws that no classical algorithm with the same budget can. We determine the exact quantum optimum with one comparison for every number of designs and every good-enough set. For selecting the best of n designs, the optimal success probability with one quantum comparison is approximately 3.30/n for large n, compared with 2/n for one classical comparison. When the best design is sought, one quantum comparison gives a higher alignment probability than two classical comparisons whenever there are more than nine designs.

AI.tldr: This paper formulates quantum ordinal optimization as maximizing alignment probability under a fixed comparison-query budget, proves a classical knockout optimum, and shows quantum comparisons can achieve strictly higher alignment probability.
AI.motivation: Ordinal optimization seeks good-enough designs when evaluation is expensive and budgets are small, and alignment probability quantifies how likely the selected set contains enough truly good designs. The paper studies how quantum pairwise comparisons with a fixed oracle budget can improve this probability.
AI.method: The authors formulate quantum ordinal optimization as a class of problems maximizing alignment probability under a fixed oracle budget, focusing on exact coherent pairwise comparisons with one selected design and budget counted in comparison queries. They analyze classical knockout among uniformly sampled designs (sampled without replacement, one more design than comparisons) and derive its rank law, then compare with quantum limits via maximum quantum degree and exact quantum optima.
AI.result: For every classical comparison budget smaller than the number of designs, knockout among uniformly sampled designs attains the classical optimum. The selected design's rank under a uniformly random order follows a polynomial probability law. The maximum quantum degree is at most twice the classical maximum, and this factor is attained when designs exceed twice the comparisons, so quantum algorithms can realize rank laws impossible classically at the same budget. Exact quantum optima are determined for one comparison for every number of designs and good-enough set. For selecting the best of n designs, optimal success with one quantum comparison is about 3.30/n for large n versus 2/n classically; one quantum comparison beats two classical comparisons for n > 9.
AI.conclusion: Quantum pairwise comparisons can yield strictly higher alignment probability than classical comparisons under the same query budget, with the advantage quantified and exactly characterized for the one-comparison case.

title: End-to-End Fidelity and Rate Analysis for Zero-Added-Loss Multiplexing
summary: Zero-added-loss multiplexing (ZALM)~[Phys. Rev. Appl. {\bf 19}, 054029 (2023)] is a midpoint-source scheme for entanglement distribution. Its quantum transmitter (QTX) employs two Sagnac sources of polarization-entangled pairs plus partial Bell-state measurements (BSMs) on their idler outputs to herald entanglement in their signal outputs, thus avoiding the switching losses suffered by other multiplexing approaches. When its Sagnac sources' spontaneous parametric downconverters (SPDCs) utilize $χ^{(2)}$ crystals with phase-matched spectral islands, ZALM avoids the tradeoff between heralding efficiency and output-state fidelity incurred when conventional-crystal SPDCs' outputs are channelized by dense wavelength-division multiplexing filters. This paper reports an end-to-end fidelity and rate analysis for islands-based ZALM that includes: SPDC multipair emissions of all orders and partial-BSM losses in the ZALM QTX; loss in propagation from the ZALM QTX to Alice and Bob's quantum receivers (QRXs); loss and mode mismatch in the mode converters employed at Alice and Bob's QRXs; and loss in the partial-BSM loading of Alice and Bob's emissive quantum memories.

AI.tldr: An end-to-end fidelity and rate analysis of islands-based zero-added-loss multiplexing (ZALM) for entanglement distribution, accounting for SPDC multipair emissions, partial-BSM and propagation losses, mode-converter mode mismatch, and quantum-memory loading loss.
AI.motivation: ZALM is a midpoint-source entanglement-distribution scheme whose quantum transmitter uses two Sagnac sources of polarization-entangled pairs and partial Bell-state measurements on idler outputs to herald entanglement in signal outputs, thereby avoiding the switching losses of other multiplexing approaches. When χ(2) crystals with phase-matched spectral islands are used, ZALM avoids the heralding-efficiency versus output-state-fidelity tradeoff incurred by conventional-crystal SPDCs channelized with dense wavelength-division multiplexing filters. However, an end-to-end fidelity and rate assessment under realistic loss and imperfection mechanisms was needed.
AI.method: An end-to-end fidelity and rate analysis for islands-based ZALM that includes: SPDC multipair emissions of all orders and partial-BSM losses in the ZALM quantum transmitter; propagation loss from the transmitter to Alice's and Bob's quantum receivers; loss and mode mismatch in the mode converters at the receivers; and loss in the partial-BSM loading of Alice's and Bob's emissive quantum memories.
AI.result: The analysis quantifies end-to-end fidelity and rate for islands-based ZALM under the combined effects of multipair SPDC emission, partial-BSM loss, propagation loss, mode-converter loss and mode mismatch, and quantum-memory loading loss.
AI.conclusion: Islands-based ZALM is characterized end-to-end in terms of fidelity and rate, providing a realistic assessment of its performance as a midpoint-source entanglement-distribution scheme subject to the enumerated loss and imperfection mechanisms.

title: Local-dimension-invariant low-density parity-check stabilizer codes
summary: The protection of quantum information in systems leveraging more than two basis states (qudits) is an ongoing challenge. A tool for transforming the plethora of qubit stabilizer codes into qudit stabilizer codes is the local-dimension-invariant (LDI) extension to the stabilizer formalism. A drawback of the LDI method is that generally in order to ensure the distance of the resultant code is at least preserved the newly selected local-dimension will need to be any prime bigger than a large cutoff value. In this work we consider the repercussions of this large cutoff value, then by focusing on quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes we are able to bring down this cutoff value. Notably, we are able to reduce it in some cases to the initial local-dimension and for arbitrary CSS qubit-derived codes to singly exponential in $d$ with no dependence on the number of logicals $k$. This reduces the size of the caveat in LDI forms in their distance preservation condition.

AI.tldr: The paper reduces the large local-dimension cutoff required by the local-dimension-invariant (LDI) extension to preserve the distance of qudit stabilizer codes, achieving reductions down to the original local-dimension in some cases and to singly exponential in d (independent of k) for CSS qubit-derived codes, especially for quantum LDPC codes.
AI.motivation: Protecting quantum information in qudit systems (more than two basis states) remains challenging. The LDI extension can convert qubit stabilizer codes into qudit stabilizer codes, but it has a significant drawback: to guarantee the resultant code preserves distance, the newly chosen local dimension generally must be a prime larger than a large cutoff value, limiting practicality.
AI.method: The authors analyze the repercussions of the large cutoff value in the LDI distance-preservation condition. Focusing on quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes, they derive improved bounds that lower this cutoff value.
AI.result: The cutoff value can be reduced in some cases to the initial local-dimension, and for arbitrary CSS qubit-derived codes to singly exponential in d with no dependence on the number of logicals k.
AI.conclusion: The work mitigates the caveat in LDI distance-preservation conditions, making the LDI extension more practical for constructing distance-preserving qudit stabilizer codes, particularly qLDPC and CSS codes.

title: Quantum limit cycles from phase coupling: A framework for NISQ thermodynamic devices
summary: Quantum decoherence does not permit the operation of (new) miniaturised devices or protocols that can otherwise run unassisted in classical settings, without explicit user agent intervention in the quantum realm. Classical driving signals are inadequate to model a truly quantum device built entirely in the quantum realm. Synchronisation endures miniaturisation without sacrificing quantum coherence, unlike thermalisation. We quantise the Kuramoto model and the Van der Pol oscillator and couple it with qubit(s) to show a robust limit cycle even in typical quantum thermodynamical settings. Novel effects such as Entanglement State Revivals, Zeno locking and thermal current interference are observed. We propose toy model devices that can be implemented harnessing the Synchronisation of a qubit (or an arbitrary collection of qubits) with a nonlinear phase oscillator. The framework theory used here, Spectral Mechanics, is a fresh look at the foundations of conventional quantum mechanics and is extensible to completely new forms of interactions and models in experimental settings.

AI.tldr: Quantum decoherence hinders miniaturized quantum devices; synchronization, unlike thermalization, survives miniaturization while preserving coherence. By quantizing the Kuramoto model and Van der Pol oscillator coupled to qubits, the authors demonstrate a robust limit cycle even in typical quantum thermodynamic settings, revealing novel effects and proposing toy-model devices.
AI.motivation: Miniaturized devices and protocols that work unassisted in classical settings fail in the quantum realm due to decoherence, and classical driving signals cannot adequately model a genuinely quantum device. A framework is needed that preserves quantum coherence under miniaturization, motivating the exploration of synchronization as a decoherence-resilient mechanism.
AI.method: The authors quantize the Kuramoto model and the Van der Pol oscillator and couple them with qubit(s). They employ a framework termed Spectral Mechanics, presented as a fresh foundation for conventional quantum mechanics, to analyze the coupled dynamics in typical quantum thermodynamical settings.
AI.result: A robust limit cycle emerges even in typical quantum thermodynamical settings. Novel effects are observed, including Entanglement State Revivals, Zeno locking, and thermal current interference.
AI.conclusion: Synchronization endures miniaturization without sacrificing quantum coherence, unlike thermalization. The authors propose toy-model devices that harness the synchronization of a qubit (or an arbitrary collection of qubits) with a nonlinear phase oscillator. Spectral Mechanics is extensible to entirely new forms of interactions and models in experimental settings.

title: Quantum simultaneous decoding via pretty-good measurements of tilted states
summary: A multiple-access channel transmits messages from several senders to one receiver. For quantum outputs, the receiver must distinguish states depending on all messages, while tests for different decoding errors may not commute. In this paper, we give a self-contained account of simultaneous decoding, in which one joint measurement recovers the messages at the established achievable rates using independent codebooks. The proof combines Sen's tilted-subspace method with Cheng's analysis of the pretty-good measurement, a standard measurement for distinguishing quantum states. Auxiliary labels close to a common reference state separate the geometric directions associated with different errors. A Gram-matrix bound then allows separately chosen binary tests to certify the performance of one measurement. The labels are removed from the completed decoder, leading to a deterministic packing theorem that applies to finite state ensembles, including unequal priors. We develop the two-sender case first, with worked examples and figures, before treating any fixed number of senders. Sharper finite-error guarantees for the same decoder are developed separately, with sharp bounds for two specified steps of the analysis rather than a claim of globally optimal decoding. Applications recover known achievable rates for unassisted and entanglement-assisted classical communication, distributed classical compression with quantum side information, and coherent-state communication through a beamsplitter or passive multiport device. The common proof makes the geometric mechanism and its quantitative consequences available without repeating the construction for each application.

AI.tldr: A self-contained account of simultaneous decoding for quantum multiple-access channels, where a single joint measurement recovers all senders' messages at achievable rates with independent codebooks.
AI.motivation: In a quantum multiple-access channel, the receiver must distinguish output states that depend on all messages jointly, and the tests for different decoding errors may not commute. Existing achievable-rate results are typically proved separately for each application, obscuring the shared geometric mechanism.
AI.method: The proof combines Sen's tilted-subspace method with Cheng's analysis of the pretty-good measurement. Auxiliary labels close to a common reference state separate the geometric directions associated with different errors, and a Gram-matrix bound lets separately chosen binary tests certify the performance of a single joint measurement. The labels are then removed, yielding a deterministic packing theorem valid for finite state ensembles including unequal priors. The two-sender case is treated first, then any fixed number of senders.
AI.result: A deterministic packing theorem for finite state ensembles with unequal priors; sharper, separate finite-error guarantees for the same decoder with sharp bounds at two specified steps rather than a global optimality claim; recovery of known achievable rates for unassisted and entanglement-assisted classical communication, distributed classical compression with quantum side information, and coherent-state communication through a beamsplitter or passive multiport device.
AI.conclusion: A unified simultaneous-decoding framework makes the geometric mechanism and its quantitative consequences available across applications without repeating the construction, while providing a single joint decoder valid for any fixed number of senders.

title: Scalable Exact Non-Pauli Noise Simulation for Fault-Tolerant Quantum Circuits
summary:
Fault-tolerant quantum design relies on simulating noisy quantum error correction (QEC) circuits with hundreds to thousands of physical qubits and large circuit depths. High-throughput stabilizer simulators, such as Stim, are the de facto tools for this regime. However, these simulators typically support only Clifford gates and stochastic Pauli noise. As a result, more realistic device noise models-such as coherent control errors and thermal relaxation-are often approximated using Pauli Twirling. This replacement offers speed but can introduce inaccuracies.
  To address this, we propose QuasiStim for scalable exact QEC simulation of realistic noise, with QuasiFold as a compiler frontend and DeltaFrame as a sampling backend. QuasiFold lowers sampling overhead by merging equivalent non-Pauli sites in the quantum circuit. DeltaFrame samples the resulting stabilizer trajectories by reusing precomputed predicted references instead of resimulating the full tableau for each shot.
  QuasiFold can reduce the number of shots by over $100\times$ on bivariate-bicycle (BB) codes. Compared to a per-shot tableau simulator, DeltaFrame is $166\times$--$1331\times$ faster on rotated surface-code memory under coherent $R_Z$ noise as $d$ grows from 5 to 35. QuasiStim also makes the PTA bias measurable: the gap is non-negligible and varies with noise strength, decoder, and circuit schedule.
  QuasiStim will be open-sourced upon publication at https://github.com/isaachyw/QuasiStim

AI.tldr: QuasiStim enables scalable exact QEC simulation of realistic non-Pauli noise via two components: QuasiFold (a compiler frontend that merges equivalent non-Pauli sites to cut sampling overhead) and DeltaFrame (a sampling backend that reuses precomputed predicted references instead of resimulating full tableaus per shot).
AI.motivation: Fault-tolerant quantum design requires simulating noisy QEC circuits with hundreds to thousands of physical qubits and large depths. High-throughput stabilizer simulators (e.g., Stim) handle this regime but support only Clifford gates and stochastic Pauli noise. Realistic device noise models—coherent control errors and thermal relaxation—are therefore approximated via Pauli Twirling, which is fast but introduces inaccuracies.
AI.method: QuasiStim comprises QuasiFold, a compiler frontend that merges equivalent non-Pauli sites in the circuit to lower sampling overhead, and DeltaFrame, a sampling backend that samples resulting stabilizer trajectories by reusing precomputed predicted references rather than resimulating the full tableau per shot.
AI.result: QuasiFold reduces shot counts by over 100x on bivariate-bicycle (BB) codes. DeltaFrame is 166x–1331x faster than a per-shot tableau simulator on rotated surface-code memory under coherent R_Z noise as distance d grows from 5 to 35. QuasiStim also renders the Pauli Twirling Approximation (PTA) bias measurable, showing a non-negligible gap that varies with noise strength, decoder, and circuit schedule.
AI.conclusion: QuasiStim delivers scalable exact QEC simulation of realistic non-Pauli noise, offering substantial speedups and shot reductions while exposing previously unmeasurable PTA bias. It will be open-sourced upon publication at https://github.com/isaachyw/QuasiStim.

title: Adaptive Entanglement Witnessing for Two-Qubit Systems
summary: Entanglement witnesses are a key instrument in determining the entanglement of unknown bipartite qubit systems without requiring a full tomography. Riccardi et al. (2020) proposed a set of two-qubit witnesses, denoted $\{W^3\}$, which require a set of local measurements in three bases. In this work we propose an additional set of witnesses, denoted $\{W^5\}$, that build on $\{W^3\}$ and require measurements in two additional bases. We present an adaptive two-step method that uses the measurement results obtained for $\{W^3\}$ to select which $W^5$ to evaluate. We computationally demonstrate that our adaptive two-step protocol can identify 72% of entangled states generated according to the methods of Roik et al. (2021) while requiring measurements in only five of the nine bases needed for full quantum tomography. Additionally, we experimentally verify the behavior of both sets of witnesses using polarization-entangled photon pairs.

AI.tldr: A new set of two-qubit entanglement witnesses {W^5}, extending {W^3}, is proposed with an adaptive two-step measurement protocol that detects 72% of entangled states using only five of nine bases needed for full tomography.
AI.motivation: Entanglement witnesses are key for determining entanglement of unknown bipartite qubit systems without full tomography. Riccardi et al. (2020) proposed {W^3} witnesses requiring local measurements in three bases, but these may not cover all entangled states efficiently. This work aims to extend the witness set to improve detection coverage while keeping measurement cost low.
AI.method: The authors propose an additional set of witnesses {W^5} that build on {W^3} and require measurements in two additional bases. They design an adaptive two-step method: first, measurement results obtained for {W^3} are used to select which W^5 witness to evaluate. They computationally demonstrate the protocol on entangled states generated according to Roik et al. (2021), and experimentally verify both witness sets using polarization-entangled photon pairs.
AI.result: The adaptive two-step protocol identifies 72% of entangled states generated according to Roik et al. (2021) while requiring measurements in only five of the nine bases needed for full quantum tomography. Both sets of witnesses are experimentally verified using polarization-entangled photon pairs.
AI.conclusion: The proposed adaptive protocol significantly improves entanglement detection coverage compared to {W^3} alone, detecting 72% of entangled states with only five measurement bases, and is experimentally validated with polarization-entangled photons. This offers a practical, resource-efficient approach to entanglement detection.

title: Sequential optimization for orbital-optimized variational quantum eigensolvers
summary: Orbital optimization within the variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) framework is useful for improving active-space quality and accurately capturing electron correlation with shallow quantum circuits. The orbital-optimized unitary coupled cluster (OO-UCC) method [W. Mizukami et al., Phys. Rev. Res. 2, 033421 (2020)], in its original formulation, employs the orbital gradient and Hessian in a Newton--Laphson procedure. In this study, we propose sequential orbital-optimized unitary coupled cluster doubles (SOO-UCCD), extending the gradient-free sequential minimal optimization approach [K. M. Nakanishi et al., Phys. Rev. Res. 2, 043158 (2020)] to orbital rotation parameters. Based on the frequency structure implied by the algebraic properties of the orbital rotation generators, our method determines each orbital rotation angle from a nine-point energy profile. The energy landscape is evaluated by classically transforming the Hamiltonian integrals and contracting them with the reduced density matrices already measured for the VQE energy evaluation. This allows for orbital optimization without evaluating the orbital gradient or Hessian. By building on the core benefits of the OO-UCC framework, our method provides a gradient-free and hyperparameter-free orbital-optimization procedure. State-vector simulations for LiH in the STO-3G basis show that SOO-UCCD reproduces UCCSD-level accuracy along the bond-stretching curve and exhibits macro-iteration convergence comparable to that of L-BFGS-based orbital optimization.

AI.tldr: SOO-UCCD extends gradient-free sequential optimization to orbital rotation parameters in VQE, determining each orbital rotation angle via a nine-point energy profile to achieve UCCSD-level accuracy without gradient or Hessian evaluation.
AI.motivation: Orbital optimization in VQE improves active-space quality and captures electron correlation with shallow circuits, but the original OO-UCC uses a Newton-Raphson procedure requiring orbital gradient and Hessian, which is computationally demanding and not hyperparameter-free.
AI.method: The authors propose sequential orbital-optimized unitary coupled cluster doubles (SOO-UCCD), extending gradient-free sequential minimal optimization to orbital rotation parameters. Exploiting the frequency structure from algebraic properties of orbital rotation generators, each orbital rotation angle is determined from a nine-point energy profile. The energy landscape is computed by classically transforming Hamiltonian integrals and contracting them with reduced density matrices already measured for VQE energy evaluation.
AI.result: State-vector simulations for LiH in STO-3G basis show that SOO-UCCD reproduces UCCSD-level accuracy along the bond-stretching curve and exhibits macro-iteration convergence comparable to L-BFGS-based orbital optimization.
AI.conclusion: SOO-UCCD provides a gradient-free and hyperparameter-free orbital-optimization procedure building on the benefits of the OO-UCC framework.

title: Measuring higher-order bulk topology in a programmable quantum simulator
summary: Topological insulators lie outside the standard Landau paradigm: Instead of being characterized by local order parameters and spontaneous symmetry breaking, their defining properties are encoded in the global structure of their quantum states and manifested as robust boundary states. Crystalline higher-order topological insulators can extend this principle by hosting localized corner modes in two and higher dimensions. Although these boundary modes can be detected spectroscopically through the local density of states, determining the underlying bulk topology, for example through nested Wilson loops, remains an outstanding experimental challenge. Here we use up to 728 qubits in a superconducting analogue-digital quantum simulator to realize and probe a hierarchy of one-, two-, and three-dimensional topological insulators governed by effective tight-binding Hamiltonians. By reconstructing complex propagators from real-space measurements, we obtain complementary boundary and bulk characterizations: local densities of states reveal localized boundary modes, whereas experimentally reconstructed band projectors yield bulk topological invariants, culminating in a three-dimensional octupole moment extracted through third nested Wilson loops. These results establish a route to realizing, characterizing, and manipulating topologically protected states in programmable three-dimensional quantum matter.

AI.tldr: Using up to 728 qubits in a superconducting analogue-digital quantum simulator, the authors realize 1D, 2D, and 3D higher-order topological insulators and experimentally extract bulk topological invariants, including a 3D octupole moment via third-order nested Wilson loops.
AI.motivation: Topological insulators fall outside the standard Landau paradigm, with properties encoded in global quantum-state structure and robust boundary states rather than local order parameters. Higher-order crystalline topological insulators host localized corner modes, but while boundary modes are spectroscopically detectable via the local density of states, experimentally determining the bulk topology (e.g., via nested Wilson loops) remains an outstanding challenge.
AI.method: The authors used up to 728 qubits in a superconducting analogue-digital quantum simulator to realize a hierarchy of 1D, 2D, and 3D topological insulators governed by effective tight-binding Hamiltonians. By reconstructing complex propagators from real-space measurements, they obtained complementary boundary and bulk characterizations.
AI.result: Local densities of states revealed localized boundary modes, while experimentally reconstructed band projectors yielded bulk topological invariants, culminating in a 3D octupole moment extracted through third nested Wilson loops.
AI.conclusion: These results establish a route to realizing, characterizing, and manipulating topologically protected states in programmable three-dimensional quantum matter.

title: Multipolar Nanophotonics with Quantum Computers
summary: Small particles respond to light through electric and magnetic patterns called multipoles. Their interference determines the direction of scattered light and affects the decay of nearby emitters. Larger nanoantenna arrays, metasurfaces, and other nanophotonic systems demand increasingly costly simulations to meet strict performance and reliability requirements. We show how to represent these responses with quantum bits (qubits) and use quantum circuits to calculate scattering and the Purcell effect, the change in an emitter's decay rate caused by its surroundings. The circuits can encode known multipoles or estimate unknown ones from Maxwell's equations at the particle surface. We test the method against classical theory using an ideal quantum simulator and real IBM and IonQ quantum computers. For a silicon nanoparticle of radius 78 nm illuminated at 679 nm, IonQ gives a forward directivity of 2.984, close to the ideal dipolar value 3, quantifying the concentration of scattered light in the forward direction. For an emitter 10 nm from a gold nanoparticle and emitting at 510 nm, IBM measurements yield a calculated total decay rate 20.48 times its vacuum value versus 20.47 from theory, with correction for errors in reading the qubit states. We also establish how the number of multipoles and the required accuracy set the demands on qubits and measurements. These results motivate quantum-assisted design studies of directional radiation and emitter decay in nanophotonic systems.

AI.tldr: The paper represents optical multipole responses of nanoparticles with qubits and computes scattering (directivity) and the Purcell effect via quantum circuits, validating results against classical theory on ideal simulators and real IBM and IonQ hardware.
AI.motivation: Simulating large nanoantenna arrays, metasurfaces, and other nanophotonic systems to meet strict performance and reliability requirements is increasingly costly, motivating a more efficient computational approach.
AI.method: Encode known or Maxwell-equation-estimated multipoles into qubit representations and use quantum circuits to calculate scattering and the Purcell effect (modified emitter decay rate). Test against classical theory on an ideal quantum simulator and real IBM and IonQ quantum computers, with error correction for qubit state readout, and establish how multipole number and target accuracy determine qubit and measurement demands.
AI.result: For a 78 nm silicon nanoparticle illuminated at 679 nm, IonQ yields a forward directivity of 2.984, near the ideal dipolar value 3. For an emitter 10 nm from a gold nanoparticle at 510 nm, IBM gives a total decay rate 20.48× vacuum versus 20.47 from theory.
AI.conclusion: The method reproduces classical predictions for directional radiation and emitter decay, motivating quantum-assisted design of nanophotonic systems.

title: Permanent Thermodynamic Mpemba Inversion from Quantum-Jump Feedback
summary: We show that a common quantum-jump feedback protocol can permanently reverse the nonequilibrium free-energy ordering of two prescribed initial states while preserving their Gibbs equilibrium. The construction exploits collective compensation between monitored channels: their feedback corrections cancel at equilibrium but remain active during relaxation. This balance preserves free-energy monotonicity while allowing the relaxation modes to be reshaped. We prove that eliminating the complete slow-sector contribution of the initially higher-free-energy state, while retaining it for the comparison state, produces distinct asymptotic decay exponents. Their free-energy ratio then vanishes at long times, guaranteeing a permanent thermodynamic quantum Mpemba inversion under the same controlled dynamics. A thermal qutrit realizes the mechanism through coherence interference and exhibits distinct detection thresholds for spectral selection and exact slow-sector cancellation under feedback retuning.

AI.tldr: A quantum-jump feedback protocol reshapes relaxation modes so that an initially higher-free-energy state decays faster than a comparison state, permanently inverting the nonequilibrium free-energy ordering while preserving the Gibbs equilibrium.
AI.motivation: Nonequilibrium free-energy ordering between states typically relaxes back to the equilibrium ordering. The paper aims to show this ordering can be permanently inverted (a quantum Mpemba-type inversion) using feedback control, without altering the equilibrium state.
AI.method: A common quantum-jump feedback protocol exploiting collective compensation between monitored channels: feedback corrections cancel at equilibrium but stay active during relaxation. The authors prove that removing the slow-sector contribution of the initially higher-free-energy state, while retaining it for the comparison state, yields distinct asymptotic decay exponents. A thermal qutrit model realizes the mechanism via coherence interference.
AI.result: The free-energy ratio vanishes at long times, guaranteeing a permanent thermodynamic quantum Mpemba inversion. The thermal qutrit shows distinct detection thresholds for spectral selection and for exact slow-sector cancellation under feedback retuning.
AI.conclusion: Feedback-mediated mode reshaping enables permanent thermodynamic Mpemba inversion under the same controlled dynamics, with equilibrium Gibbs statistics preserved; the mechanism is experimentally accessible in a thermal qutrit.

title: Noise-resistant off-resonance π-rotation realized in an NMR system
summary: Precise manipulation of qubits (spins) requires strong suppression of noise arising from couplings between qubits and their environment, as well as from driving field fluctuations. We propose a double-pulse sequence and an eighteen-pulse sequence to realize a single spin pi-rotation under off-resonance conditions (instead of conventional on-resonance or near-resonance conditions). It is proved that the latter sequence performs much better than the former in simultaneously suppressing both dephasing and driving field noise. As a proof of principle, we experimentally demonstrate, by implementing both sequences in an NMR spin system with a polarized initial spin state, that the off-resonance pi-rotation fidelity reaches as high as 0.9992 +/- 0.0008 for the double-pulse sequence and 0.9997 +/- 0.0006 for the eighteen-pulse sequence. In addition, the noise-tolerance range of the eighteen-pulse sequence is about 20 percent of the driving field strength, approximately three times wider than that of the double-pulse sequence. Besides its potential application in the NMR community, our proposal provides an alternative practical way to accurately control qubits by suppressing the coexisting transversal and longitudinal noises.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a double-pulse and an eighteen-pulse sequence for single-spin π-rotation under off-resonance conditions, demonstrating that the eighteen-pulse sequence better suppresses both dephasing and driving-field noise, achieving fidelities up to 0.9997.
AI.motivation: Precise qubit (spin) manipulation requires strong suppression of noise from qubit-environment couplings and driving field fluctuations, motivating the search for pulse sequences that suppress coexisting transversal and longitudinal noises.
AI.method: Two pulse sequences—a double-pulse and an eighteen-pulse sequence—are designed to realize single-spin π-rotation under off-resonance conditions. Both are implemented in an NMR spin system with a polarized initial spin state as a proof of principle.
AI.result: Off-resonance π-rotation fidelity reaches 0.9992 ± 0.0008 for the double-pulse sequence and 0.9997 ± 0.0006 for the eighteen-pulse sequence; the noise-tolerance range of the eighteen-pulse sequence is about 20% of the driving field strength, roughly three times wider than that of the double-pulse sequence.
AI.conclusion: The eighteen-pulse sequence outperforms the double-pulse sequence in simultaneously suppressing dephasing and driving field noise. Beyond NMR applications, the proposal offers an alternative practical way to accurately control qubits by suppressing coexisting transversal and longitudinal noises.

title: QIAP: A Quantum-Inspired Authentication Protocol with BB84-Based Channel Monitoring
summary: Authentication in quantum-aware communication settings requires mechanisms that verify user legitimacy while also assessing whether the communication channel exhibits excessive disturbance. This paper presents QIAP, a stateful hybrid framework that combines classical commitment-based challenge-response authentication with BB84-based quantum-channel monitoring. QIAP uses a dual-branch verification structure inspired by rectilinear and diagonal basis selection. In the rectilinear branch, the prover opens a hash-based commitment and the verifier checks consistency with the registered round token. In the diagonal branch, the prover returns an HMAC tag bound to the verifier nonce, round identifier, and submitted commitment without disclosing the round-specific sub-secret. Under the stated hash, HMAC, freshness, secure-registration, protected-storage, and high-entropy-secret assumptions, QIAP provides computational resistance to the modeled wrong-secret and replay attempts and protects the long-term master secret from direct recovery. After successful authentication, the BB84 module estimates the quantum bit error rate (QBER) and aborts the session when the measured value reaches or exceeds the configured threshold. In the reported simulation, no successful authentication was observed among 1,000 tested wrong-secret attempts per branch. The baseline and full intercept-resend conditions produced mean QBER values of approximately 0.02 and 0.25, respectively. The classical authentication stage required approximately 0.6 ms, and the implemented authentication messages required approximately 113 bytes per round. These results indicate that QIAP can provide a lightweight hybrid framework for combining secret-based identity verification with QBER-based channel-disturbance assessment under the stated threat model.

AI.tldr: QIAP is a stateful hybrid authentication framework that combines classical commitment-based challenge-response authentication with BB84-based quantum-channel monitoring, achieving lightweight secret-based identity verification plus QBER-based disturbance assessment.
AI.motivation: Authentication in quantum-aware communication settings must verify user legitimacy while also assessing whether the channel exhibits excessive disturbance; existing approaches typically address only one of these concerns.
AI.method: QIAP uses a dual-branch verification structure inspired by rectilinear/diagonal basis selection. The rectilinear branch opens a hash-based commitment checked against the registered round token; the diagonal branch returns an HMAC tag bound to the verifier nonce, round identifier, and submitted commitment without revealing the round-specific sub-secret. Post-authentication, a BB84 module estimates QBER and aborts sessions at or above a configured threshold. Security relies on hash, HMAC, freshness, secure-registration, protected-storage, and high-entropy-secret assumptions.
AI.result: No successful authentication was observed among 1,000 tested wrong-secret attempts per branch. Baseline and full intercept-resend conditions yielded mean QBER of approximately 0.02 and 0.25. The classical authentication stage took approximately 0.6 ms, with authentication messages of approximately 113 bytes per round.
AI.conclusion: QIAP provides a lightweight hybrid framework combining secret-based identity verification with QBER-based channel-disturbance assessment under the stated threat model, offering computational resistance to modeled wrong-secret and replay attempts while protecting the long-term master secret.

title: Perfect discrimination of an orthogonal $2\otimes2$ basis may require collective separable measurements on two copies
summary: We consider an orthogonal basis of $\mathbb C^2\otimes\mathbb C^2$ with three entangled states and one product state. This basis is not perfectly distinguishable by LOCC or even by separable measurements when a single copy of the unknown state is available. We show that with two copies no adaptive separable protocol, which measures the copies one at a time, distinguishes the basis perfectly. We then show that a collective separable measurement on the two copies does. Whether two copies suffice for LOCC remains open.

AI.tldr: An orthogonal basis of C²⊗C² consisting of three entangled states and one product state is not perfectly distinguishable by one-copy LOCC or separable measurements, nor by any two-copy adaptive separable protocol; however, a two-copy collective separable measurement achieves perfect discrimination, while the two-copy LOCC case remains open.
AI.motivation: The paper studies the limitations and power of separable operations versus LOCC for distinguishing sets of quantum states, focusing on a specific orthogonal basis with entanglement structure that challenges single-copy protocols.
AI.method: The authors analyze an orthogonal basis of the two-qubit space C²⊗C² containing three entangled states and one product state, examining discriminability under LOCC, separable measurements, adaptive separable protocols, and collective separable measurements across one and two copies.
AI.result: The basis cannot be perfectly distinguished with a single copy by LOCC or separable measurements; no two-copy adaptive separable protocol distinguishes it, but a collective separable measurement on two copies achieves perfect discrimination. The two-copy LOCC question is left open.
AI.conclusion: Collective separable measurements can outperform adaptive separable protocols for this basis, highlighting a gap between adaptive and collective non-entangling strategies; whether LOCC with two copies suffices remains an open problem.

title: Device-to-protocol simulation of spectrally-resolved quantum photonic circuits
summary: Predicting quantum-photonic circuit performance requires retaining source and device physics without making photon-counting calculations prohibitively expensive. Here we present PhoQuS, a framework that combines frequency-resolved source models, electromagnetic compact models and spatially correlated fabrication variation to simulate quantum photonic circuits. Covariance-Gram reduction after full-resolution Gaussian propagation lowers readout cost while retaining dominant spectral correlations. For continuous-variable state preparation, spectral reduction accelerates photon counting by 60.4-fold in an approximate Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill circuit. Frequency-resolved modeling guides the use of cascaded squeezing with temporal walk-off compensation, yielding 0.99 fidelity to the single-mode circuit reference and 0.98 conditional purity in lossless simulations. For discrete-variable state preparation, simulations of three-photon Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger circuits across a virtual wafer show that component robustness alone does not predict circuit fidelity, which depends jointly on source spectra, circuit architecture and control. PhoQuS connects device physics to protocol-level performance through a unified workflow that retains spectral detail while reducing readout cost.

AI.tldr: PhoQuS is a simulation framework for quantum photonic circuits that unifies frequency-resolved source models, electromagnetic compact models, and spatially correlated fabrication variation, using Covariance-Gram reduction to cut photon-counting cost while preserving spectral correlations.
AI.motivation: Predicting quantum-photonic circuit performance requires retaining source and device physics, yet full photon-counting calculations become prohibitively expensive at full spectral resolution. A workflow is needed that keeps spectral detail without incurring prohibitive readout cost.
AI.method: PhoQuS combines frequency-resolved source models, electromagnetic compact models, and spatially correlated fabrication variation. After full-resolution Gaussian propagation, Covariance-Gram reduction is applied to lower readout cost while retaining dominant spectral correlations. It is applied to continuous-variable state preparation (approximate Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill circuit, cascaded squeezing with temporal walk-off compensation) and discrete-variable state preparation (three-photon GHZ circuits across a virtual wafer).
AI.result: Spectral reduction accelerates photon counting by 60.4-fold in an approximate GKP circuit. Frequency-resolved modeling guides cascaded squeezing with temporal walk-off compensation, achieving 0.99 fidelity to the single-mode circuit reference and 0.98 conditional purity in lossless simulations. In three-photon GHZ circuits across a virtual wafer, component robustness alone does not predict circuit fidelity, which depends jointly on source spectra, circuit architecture, and control.
AI.conclusion: PhoQuS links device physics to protocol-level performance in a unified workflow that preserves spectral detail while reducing readout cost, showing that circuit fidelity is jointly determined by source spectra, architecture, and control rather than component robustness alone.

title: Architectural Robustness to Label Noise Using Variational Quantum Circuits for Medical Image Classification
comment: Accepted at the Second AAAI Symposium on Quantum Information & Machine Learning (QIML), AAAI 2026 Fall Symposium Series. 8 pages, 1 figure
summary: Label noise is prevalent in medical image datasets, arising from observer disagreement and ambiguous cases and deep networks memorize the mislabeled examples at the cost of generalization. Current solutions such as loss correction and sample selection add training complexity and generally assume the noise rate is known or estimable. This paper investigates whether robustness can be obtained architecturally, by routing a frozen backbone's features through a low-dimensional bounded bottleneck and classifying them with a head whose function class is intrinsically smooth. Variational quantum circuits with angle encoding and a linear cost function realise exactly such a class. Their use in medical imaging, however, has been limited by the small number of qubits available on noisy intermediate-scale devices, which typically restricts inputs to low-resolution grayscale images. We therefore couple a frozen ImageNet-pretrained ViT-B/16 backbone to a trainable linear bottleneck and an eight-qubit variational quantum circuit, allowing 224x224 RGB inputs to be processed. Under clean labels the model leads five of six MedMNISTv2 benchmarks against published hybrid quantum-classical models, with margins of 17.4 and 15.7 percentages on BloodMNIST and PathMNIST. The advantage emerges under corrupted labels. At symmetric noise rates of 30% and 50% the model outperforms many published quantum and noise-robust classical baselines on all six datasets without any explicit noise-handling component. Against a control that shares the backbone, bottleneck, parameter count and optimizer and replaces only the circuit with a ReLU layer, it retains 89.75% accuracy on PathMNIST at 50% noise where the control falls to 78.96%. Direct measurement of training dynamics shows that this advantage is not an inability to fit corrupted labels, which the circuit retains, but greater stability under prolonged training on them.

AI.tldr: A frozen ViT-B/16 backbone feeding a trainable linear bottleneck and an 8-qubit variational quantum circuit yields architectural label-noise robustness in medical image classification without explicit noise-handling components.
AI.motivation: Label noise is prevalent in medical image datasets due to observer disagreement and ambiguous cases, and deep networks memorize mislabeled examples, harming generalization. Existing remedies (loss correction, sample selection) add training complexity and typically assume a known or estimable noise rate. This work asks whether robustness can instead be obtained architecturally. Quantum circuits are used because they have been limited in medical imaging by few qubits, restricting inputs to low-resolution grayscale images.
AI.method: The model couples a frozen ImageNet-pretrained ViT-B/16 backbone to a trainable low-dimensional linear bottleneck and an eight-qubit variational quantum circuit with angle encoding and a linear cost function, enabling 224x224 RGB inputs. A control replaces only the circuit with a ReLU layer while sharing backbone, bottleneck, parameter count and optimizer. Training dynamics are measured directly.
AI.result: Under clean labels the model leads five of six MedMNISTv2 benchmarks against published hybrid quantum-classical models (+17.4 and +15.7 percentage points on BloodMNIST and PathMNIST). At 30% and 50% symmetric noise it outperforms many published quantum and noise-robust classical baselines on all six datasets without any explicit noise-handling component. Against the ReLU control it retains 89.75% accuracy on PathMNIST at 50% noise where the control falls to 78.96%. Training dynamics show the circuit still fits corrupted labels but is more stable under prolonged training on them.
AI.conclusion: Noise robustness can be obtained architecturally via a bounded, intrinsically smooth function class (variational quantum circuit), not by an inability to fit corrupted labels but by greater training stability under them, without added loss-correction or sample-selection machinery or noise-rate assumptions.

title: Time-Frequency Continuous-Variable Quantum Teleportation with Single Photons
summary: Quantum teleportation, a key building block for quantum technologies, enables distant parties, Alice and Bob, to transfer an unknown quantum state using entanglement, local operations, and classical communication. In this work, we propose a quantum teleportation protocol for single-photon time-frequency continuous variables, where time is the time of arrival at a detector. We detail the operational requirements of the protocol, notably the nonlinear interactions needed for the photon-photon time-frequency entangling gate. By explicitly treating the detector position as the reference frame for time of arrival, we show that, even with ideal classical and quantum channels, the input-output fidelity is not unity unless the receiving party can correct the detector-position mismatch. This results in a trade-off between teleportation fidelity and the temporal bandwidth of the input photon wavepacket. The protocol itself can be used for remote detector synchronization. In particular, we show that time-frequency cat and Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill states provide an internal temporal ruler through fidelity revivals. We further derive the classical and best-copy fidelity thresholds for single-photon Gaussian wavepackets, finding that the relevant vacuum-equivalent shot noise is input-dependent, in contrast with quadrature-based continuous-variable quantum teleportation. Our proposal derives from a quantum theory of space-time events, whereafter we establish space as a reference for the time degree of freedom, thereby grounding our work in ongoing research on reference frames and superselection rules in quantum optics and quantum information. Beyond protocols harnessing time-frequency continuous variables of single photons, this work points toward remote synchronization in quantum communication architectures.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a quantum teleportation protocol for single-photon time-frequency continuous variables, treating detector position as the time-of-arrival reference frame, and shows fidelity is limited by detector-position mismatch, yielding a fidelity-bandwidth trade-off and applications in remote synchronization.
AI.motivation: Quantum teleportation is a foundational primitive for quantum technologies, but its realization with time-frequency continuous variables of single photons—where time is the arrival time at a detector—remains underexplored. The authors aim to ground teleportation in a quantum theory of space-time events, establishing space as a reference for the time degree of freedom and connecting to research on reference frames and superselection rules in quantum optics and quantum information.
AI.method: The authors design a teleportation protocol for single-photon time-frequency continuous variables, specifying operational requirements including nonlinear photon-photon time-frequency entangling gates. They explicitly treat detector position as the reference frame for time of arrival and analyze the resulting input-output fidelity under ideal classical and quantum channels. They derive classical and best-copy fidelity thresholds for single-photon Gaussian wavepackets and examine time-frequency cat and Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill states as internal temporal rulers via fidelity revivals.
AI.result: Even with ideal classical and quantum channels, input-output fidelity is not unity unless the receiving party corrects the detector-position mismatch, producing a trade-off between teleportation fidelity and the temporal bandwidth of the input photon wavepacket. Time-frequency cat and Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill states provide an internal temporal ruler through fidelity revivals. For single-photon Gaussian wavepackets, the classical and best-copy fidelity thresholds are derived, and the relevant vacuum-equivalent shot noise is input-dependent, contrasting with quadrature-based continuous-variable quantum teleportation.
AI.conclusion: The protocol enables remote detector synchronization and points toward remote synchronization in quantum communication architectures. In particular, time-frequency cat and GKP states offer an internal temporal ruler through fidelity revivals. The work establishes space as a reference for the time degree of freedom, grounding the proposal in reference-frame and superselection research, and extends beyond protocols harnessing time-frequency continuous variables of single photons.

title: Deterministic preparation of squeezed and non-Gaussian states in coupled qubit-boson systems
summary: Deterministic preparation of bosonic resource states is a central task in continuous-variable quantum information processing and quantum metrology. Here we develop a measurement-based imaginary time evolution (MITE) protocol for preparing squeezed and non-Gaussian states. The protocol combines ancilla-mediated weak measurements of the Hamiltonian with a conditional phase rotation that suppresses excited state trapping and stabilizes convergence toward the ground state. The method is potentially applicable in hybrid discrete variable-continuous variable (DV-CV) platforms, where the qubit acts as the measurement readout. We demonstrate deterministic convergence over a broad range of parameters and show that the performance degradation near the stability boundary is governed by the shrinking Bogoliubov quasiparticle gap. The same framework also extends to non-Gaussian bosonic resource states, including Schrödinger cat states and excited states of the single-mode squeezing Hamiltonian, which display Wigner negativity. The squeezed states remain robust under bosonic loss over experimentally relevant regimes.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a measurement-based imaginary time evolution (MITE) protocol to deterministically prepare squeezed and non-Gaussian bosonic resource states, using ancilla-mediated weak Hamiltonian measurements plus a conditional phase rotation. It shows convergence governed by the Bogoliubov quasiparticle gap and extends to cat states and excited squeezing states with Wigner negativity.
AI.motivation: Deterministic preparation of bosonic resource states is a central task in continuous-variable quantum information processing and quantum metrology, motivating a robust, deterministic preparation scheme applicable to hybrid DV-CV platforms.
AI.method: A measurement-based imaginary time evolution (MITE) protocol combining ancilla-mediated weak measurements of the Hamiltonian with a conditional phase rotation that suppresses excited state trapping and stabilizes convergence toward the ground state; the qubit serves as the measurement readout in hybrid DV-CV platforms.
AI.result: Deterministic convergence is demonstrated over a broad parameter range; performance degradation near the stability boundary is governed by the shrinking Bogoliubov quasiparticle gap. The framework extends to non-Gaussian states, including Schrödinger cat states and excited states of the single-mode squeezing Hamiltonian, which display Wigner negativity. Squeezed states remain robust under bosonic loss in experimentally relevant regimes.
AI.conclusion: MITE provides a deterministic route to squeezed and non-Gaussian bosonic resource states in hybrid DV-CV platforms, with convergence and robustness characterized by the Bogoliubov quasiparticle gap and loss tolerance.

title: Bootstrapping Classical and Quantum Query Lower Bounds for Finding Tarski Fixed Points
summary:
The Tarski fixed-point problem asks for a fixed point of a monotone map on a $k$-dimensional grid lattice of width $n$ and has applications in game theory, economics, and verification. Substantial gaps remain between the known upper and lower bounds on its quantum query complexity.
  We prove two hardness bootstrapping theorems for quantum query lower bounds. Starting from a hard instance family whose instances have pair-wise incomparable unique fixed points, and a lower bound established by the nonnegative adversary method, we bootstrap this lower bound by (i) a factor of $Ω(t)$ when the dimension is multiplied by $t$ and the width remains unchanged, and (ii) a factor of $Ω(\log m)$ when the width is multiplied by $m$ and the dimension is doubled. Applying these theorems, we obtain three consequences: (i) an $Ω(k\log^2 n)$ lower bound for $k\geq 4$, improving previously best-known classical and quantum lower bounds; (ii) for every fixed constant $α>0$, there exists a constant $δ(α)>0$ such that $Q_ε(\text{Tarski}(n,k))=Ω(kn^{δ(α)})$ whenever $k>n^α$, and in particular, an $Ω(kn^{0.0072})$ lower bound for $k>n^{2/203}$, the first lower bound with simultaneous linear dependence on the dimension and polynomial dependence on the width; and (iii) a superpolynomial lower bound of $(k/\log k)^{Ω(\log k)}$ for exponentially wide grids, where $n=2^{Θ(k)}$. The last result rules out a route to polynomial-time algorithms for simple stochastic games and ARRIVAL through generic polynomial-query black-box Tarski solvers.

AI.tldr: This paper proves two hardness bootstrapping theorems for quantum query lower bounds of the Tarski fixed-point problem, yielding improved and novel lower bounds, including an Ω(k log² n) bound, the first simultaneous linear-in-dimension and polynomial-in-width bound, and a superpolynomial bound that rules out certain polynomial-time algorithmic routes for simple stochastic games and ARRIVAL.
AI.motivation: The Tarski fixed-point problem has applications in game theory, economics, and verification, yet substantial gaps remain between known upper and lower bounds on its quantum query complexity. This work aims to close these gaps by establishing stronger lower bounds.
AI.method: The authors prove two hardness bootstrapping theorems for quantum query lower bounds. Starting from a hard instance family with pair-wise incomparable unique fixed points and a lower bound from the nonnegative adversary method, they bootstrap the bound by (i) a factor of Ω(t) when the dimension is multiplied by t with width unchanged, and (ii) a factor of Ω(log m) when the width is multiplied by m and the dimension is doubled.
