AI.result: Three consequences follow: (i) an Ω(k log² n) lower bound for k ≥ 4, improving prior classical and quantum bounds; (ii) for every fixed constant α > 0, a constant δ(α) > 0 exists such that Q_ε(Tarski(n,k)) = Ω(k n^{δ(α)}) whenever k > n^α, including Ω(k n^{0.0072}) for k > n^{2/203} — the first bound with simultaneous linear dependence on dimension and polynomial dependence on width; and (iii) a superpolynomial lower bound of (k/log k)^{Ω(log k)} for exponentially wide grids where n = 2^{Θ(k)}.
AI.conclusion: The superpolynomial lower bound for exponentially wide grids rules out a route to polynomial-time algorithms for simple stochastic games and ARRIVAL through generic polynomial-query black-box Tarski solvers.

title: Collective Floquet engineering between two distant superconducting artificial atoms
summary: A one-dimensional waveguide is a crucial medium for transferring propagating quantum information between remote qubits, yet the photon-mediated interaction is typically fixed by the static device geometry, qubit parameters, and their couplings to the transmission line. Such an interaction can be engineered to be coherent or dissipative via virtual- or real-photon exchange, respectively, yet its effective strength remains fixed in either case. Here we demonstrate dynamical control over this interaction by applying Floquet engineering to two superconducting qubits coupled to a waveguide terminated by a capacitive mirror. By positioning one qubit at an antinode and the other qubit at a node or an antinode of the resonant standing wave, we realize a Hermitian or non-Hermitian coupling between the two qubits. A periodic flux drive of the qubit frequencies then enables on-demand control of the coherent energy splitting and the collective decay. Our results establish Floquet engineering as a route to dynamically reshape both coherent and dissipative photon-mediated interactions between remote quantum emitters.

AI.tldr: Floquet engineering of two superconducting qubits coupled via a mirror-terminated waveguide enables dynamical, on-demand control over both coherent and dissipative photon-mediated interactions.
AI.motivation: A 1D waveguide is a key medium for transferring quantum information between remote qubits, but the photon-mediated interaction strength is normally fixed by static device geometry, qubit parameters, and line couplings. Although the interaction can be engineered to be coherent (virtual-photon exchange) or dissipative (real-photon exchange), its effective strength remains fixed in either regime, limiting tunability.
AI.method: Two superconducting qubits are coupled to a waveguide terminated by a capacitive mirror. One qubit is placed at an antinode and the other at either a node or an antinode of the resonant standing wave, yielding Hermitian or non-Hermitian qubit-qubit coupling. A periodic flux drive of the qubit frequencies (Floquet engineering) is applied to dynamically control the coupling.
AI.result: The periodic flux drive enables on-demand control of both the coherent energy splitting and the collective decay rate of the two qubits, realized in both the Hermitian and non-Hermitian coupling configurations.
AI.conclusion: Floquet engineering provides a route to dynamically reshape coherent and dissipative photon-mediated interactions between remote quantum emitters, overcoming the static limitation of conventional waveguide-mediated couplings.

title: Minimal Subsystems for Characterizing Genuine Multipartite Entanglement
summary: Genuine multipartite entanglement (GME) is a valuable resource for quantum technologies, but quantifying it in many-body systems can be demanding since measures defined through optimizations over bipartitions are often assumed to require large joint measurements and many measurement settings. We introduce the concepts of GME evaluation length and GME evaluation number, which capture, respectively, the largest subsystem that must be jointly measured and the number of distinct subsystems that need to be measured to evaluate multipartite entanglement measures defined via bipartition optimizations. Taking the genuine multipartite concurrence (GMC) as a canonical example, we show that, for $N$-qubit Haar-random pure states, the GMC can be evaluated using only $N$ single-qubit purity measurements. Thus, for typical many-body states, evaluating the GMC requires considering only the $N$ single-site bipartitions, rather than the exponentially many distinct bipartitions. We further corroborate this behavior numerically for physically accessible states generated by local random quantum circuits. Our results show that the practical cost of quantifying GME can be dramatically lower than suggested by its formal definition, establishing measurement complexity as a complementary operational lens for multipartite entanglement.

AI.tldr: Genuine multipartite entanglement measures defined via bipartition optimizations are typically assumed to need large joint measurements, but for typical many-body states only N single-qubit purity measurements suffice.
AI.motivation: Quantifying genuine multipartite entanglement (GME) in many-body systems is demanding because measures based on optimizations over bipartitions are assumed to require large joint measurements and many measurement settings. A framework is needed to characterize the actual measurement cost rather than the formal definition.
AI.method: The authors introduce GME evaluation length (largest subsystem that must be jointly measured) and GME evaluation number (number of distinct subsystems to be measured) for bipartition-optimized entanglement measures. Using the genuine multipartite concurrence (GMC) as a canonical example, they analyze N-qubit Haar-random pure states and verify the findings numerically for states generated by local random quantum circuits.
AI.result: For N-qubit Haar-random pure states, the GMC can be evaluated using only N single-qubit purity measurements, meaning only the N single-site bipartitions need to be considered instead of exponentially many distinct bipartitions. This behavior is corroborated numerically for physically accessible states from local random quantum circuits.
AI.conclusion: The practical cost of quantifying genuine multipartite entanglement can be dramatically lower than its formal definition suggests, establishing measurement complexity as a complementary operational lens for multipartite entanglement.

title: Classical and Quantum Information Measures Characterizing Convertibility: An Axiomatic Approach
comment: PhD thesis at the Centre for Quantum Technologies, National University of Singapore; contains corrections of some minor errors appearing in the published papers that this thesis is based on
summary: In this PhD thesis, we take an axiomatic approach to studying multivariate divergences, which are measures of the information content of a tuple of classical or quantum states. These divergences are studied in the context of large-sample and catalytic convertibility of tuples of states. This type of convertibility is characterized by the ordering of an axiomatically defined family of divergences. In this thesis, we identify this family of divergences explicitly for two scenarios, one classical and one quantum. In the classical setting, we show that the relevant divergences are certain generalizations of the bivariate Rényi divergences. Unlike previous studies, we do not require the distributions to have the same support, yielding interesting new divergences. In the quantum setting, we consider pairs of classical-quantum states with pure component states, and find that majorization is characterized by all $α$-$z$ relative entropies for $α<1$. This demonstrates the first operational interpretation of these relative entropies.

AI.tldr: This PhD thesis characterizes multivariate divergences governing convertibility of tuples of states, identifying generalized Rényi divergences classically and all α-z relative entropies quantumly.
AI.motivation: Multivariate divergences measure information content of tuples of classical or quantum states, and convertibility of such tuples is governed by an axiomatically defined family of divergences. Explicit identification of this family is lacking for the studied scenarios.
AI.method: An axiomatic approach to multivariate divergences, studied via large-sample and catalytic convertibility of state tuples. Divergences are explicitly identified in two settings: (1) classical, allowing distributions with unequal support; (2) quantum, for pairs of classical-quantum states with pure component states.
AI.result: Classically, the relevant divergences are generalizations of bivariate Rényi divergences, yielding new divergences when supports differ. Quantumly, majorization is characterized by all α-z relative entropies for α<1.
AI.conclusion: The thesis provides explicit characterizations of the divergence family determining convertibility, offering the first operational interpretation of α-z relative entropies.

title: Quantitative upper bounds for certain quantum channel divergences
summary: We show that completely positive maps can be decomposed into sums of submaps which are close in completely bounded trace norm but as far apart as possible in terms of geometric channel fidelity. We then show that this kind of behavior extends to a large class of quantum channel divergences. We construct quantitative norm estimates for quantum channel divergences in terms of the Arveson-Radon-Nikodym theorem.

AI.tldr: Completely positive maps decompose into submaps that are nearly identical in completely bounded trace norm yet maximally separated under geometric channel fidelity, and this phenomenon generalizes to many quantum channel divergences via Arveson-Radon-Nikodym norm estimates.
AI.motivation: Understanding how quantum channel distinguishability depends on the chosen divergence or metric is central to quantum information theory. The authors aim to expose a stark discrepancy between operator-norm-based notions of closeness and fidelity-based ones for completely positive maps.
AI.method: Decompose completely positive maps into sums of submaps and compare their behavior under completely bounded trace norm versus geometric channel fidelity. Generalize this behavior to a broad class of quantum channel divergences, and derive quantitative norm estimates for these divergences using the Arveson-Radon-Nikodym theorem.
AI.result: Completely positive maps admit decompositions into submaps that are close in completely bounded trace norm but as far apart as possible in geometric channel fidelity; this behavior extends to a large class of quantum channel divergences, with quantitative norm estimates established via Arveson-Radon-Nikodym.
AI.conclusion: Operator-norm closeness and fidelity-based similarity of quantum channels can diverge drastically, so the choice of channel divergence fundamentally affects conclusions about channel distinguishability. Arveson-Radon-Nikodym techniques provide a quantitative framework for bounding these divergences.

title: Metasurface quantum graphs for polarization-independent certified randomness
summary: Quantum random number generators are crucial for information security, yet existing implementations are hindered by bulky optics, device imperfections, and state alignment constraints. Here, using a compact metasurface platform, we achieve polarization-independent certified randomness by establishing a quantitative quantum graph framework. By mapping multi-channel nanophotonic responses onto graph vertices, we assign metasurface measurements an operational information-theoretic meaning, directly connecting weighted graph degrees to conditional min-entropy estimation. The resulting graph-certified measurements yield robust private randomness even under entanglement-based attacks without complex optics. Experimentally, we fabricate 4- and 6-channel dielectric metasurfaces to implement high-dimensional positive operator-valued measure graphs, successfully certifying randomness with heralded single photons and Poissonian light. By integrating complex quantum measurements into a single passive layer, our metasurface quantum graphs provide a scalable route for integrated quantum technologies.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a compact metasurface platform that achieves polarization-independent certified quantum randomness by mapping multi-channel nanophotonic responses onto graph vertices, directly linking weighted graph degrees to conditional min-entropy estimation.
AI.motivation: Existing quantum random number generators suffer from bulky optics, device imperfections, and state alignment constraints, limiting practical deployment.
AI.method: The authors establish a quantitative quantum graph framework in which multi-channel nanophotonic responses are mapped onto graph vertices, assigning metasurface measurements an operational information-theoretic meaning. They fabricate 4- and 6-channel dielectric metasurfaces implementing high-dimensional positive operator-valued measure (POVM) graphs, and certify randomness using heralded single photons and Poissonian light.
AI.result: The graph-certified measurements yield robust private randomness even under entanglement-based attacks without complex optics. Randomness is successfully certified with both heralded single photons and Poissonian light using the fabricated metasurfaces.
AI.conclusion: By integrating complex quantum measurements into a single passive layer, metasurface quantum graphs offer a scalable route for integrated quantum technologies and polarization-independent certified randomness.

title: Finite-time quantum equilibration from local correlations
summary: An isolated quantum system evolves reversibly, yet a small subsystem can lose nearly all information about its initial state. Conserved quantities may retain some of this information, depending on how strongly they overlap with local observables. Here we consider a subsystem in an arbitrary initial state coupled to a maximally mixed bath. We show that the worst-input mean-square equilibration error, maximised over window origins, is bounded from above and below by the mean square of a complete local autocorrelation, with the stationary part subtracted. A correlation record over a finite interval therefore controls the equilibration error in every interval of the same length. The result allows arbitrary degeneracies of energies and gaps. We apply it to two static Hamiltonian families. For fixed spin subsystems in the one-particle sector of a bounded-range periodic clock, fixed-accuracy thermalisation is guaranteed on windows that grow only slightly faster than linearly with system size, despite exponentially small positive energies. A random commuting model with logarithmic interaction range retains an extensive set of conserved observables. Its expected mean-square error is bounded by a finite-size term and an inverse-time term. The inverse-time dependence is unavoidable because of the initial transient. These examples show how local relaxation can coexist with exact conservation laws and a finely spaced spectrum.

AI.tldr: The paper bounds the worst-input mean-square equilibration error of a subsystem coupled to a maximally mixed bath by the mean square of a complete local autocorrelation (stationary part subtracted), valid despite arbitrary degeneracies and gaps, and applies this to two static Hamiltonian families exhibiting local relaxation coexisting with conserved quantities.
AI.motivation: An isolated quantum system evolves reversibly, yet small subsystems can lose nearly all initial-state information. Conserved quantities may retain some information depending on overlap with local observables, and it is unclear how equilibration error is controlled and how local relaxation can coexist with exact conservation laws and finely spaced spectra.
AI.method: Consider a subsystem in an arbitrary initial state coupled to a maximally mixed bath. Derive upper and lower bounds on the worst-input mean-square equilibration error, maximized over window origins, in terms of the mean square of a complete local autocorrelation with the stationary part subtracted. Allow arbitrary energy degeneracies and gaps. Apply the bound to two static Hamiltonian families: fixed spin subsystems in the one-particle sector of a bounded-range periodic clock, and a random commuting model with logarithmic interaction range.
AI.result: The worst-input mean-square equilibration error over all window origins is bounded above and below by the mean square of a stationary-subtracted complete local autocorrelation, so a correlation record over a finite interval controls the error in every interval of the same length, even with arbitrary degeneracies and gaps. For fixed spin subsystems in the one-particle sector of a bounded-range periodic clock, fixed-accuracy thermalisation is guaranteed on windows growing only slightly faster than linearly with system size, despite exponentially small positive energies. For the random commuting model with logarithmic interaction range, an extensive set of conserved observables persists, and the expected mean-square error is bounded by a finite-size term plus an inverse-time term, the latter unavoidable due to the initial transient.
AI.conclusion: The equilibration error of a subsystem coupled to a maximally mixed bath is tightly controlled by a stationary-subtracted complete local autocorrelation, holding under arbitrary degeneracies and gaps. Local relaxation can coexist with exact conservation laws and finely spaced spectra, as demonstrated by the periodic clock and random commuting model examples, with the inverse-time error dependence being an unavoidable consequence of the initial transient.

title: Pathfinder-BP: A Low-Latency Recursive Decoder for Topological Codes
summary: We propose Pathfinder-BP, a recursive decoder for topological quantum codes that combines belief propagation with controlled bit-flipping. An initial BP pass identifies and permanently fixes high-confidence errors. Upon convergence failure, the decoder recursively explores alternative error patterns by tentatively flipping low-confidence variables. On surface codes, Pathfinder-BP achieves a noise threshold and logical error rate comparable to minimum-weight perfect matching (MWPM). A crucial advantage of Pathfinder-BP is its highly parallelizable structure, which yields a worst-case decoding latency quasi-linear in the code distance, making it a suitable candidate for low-latency hardware implementation.

AI.tldr: Pathfinder-BP is a recursive decoder for topological quantum codes that combines belief propagation with controlled bit-flipping, achieving MWPM-comparable accuracy on surface codes with quasi-linear worst-case decoding latency.
AI.motivation: Existing decoders face a trade-off between accuracy and latency; minimum-weight perfect matching (MWPM) offers strong accuracy but limited parallelizability, which is problematic for low-latency hardware implementation.
AI.method: Pathfinder-BP uses an initial belief propagation (BP) pass to identify and permanently fix high-confidence errors; upon convergence failure, it recursively explores alternative error patterns by tentatively flipping low-confidence variables, yielding a highly parallelizable structure.
AI.result: On surface codes, Pathfinder-BP attains a noise threshold and logical error rate comparable to MWPM, with worst-case decoding latency quasi-linear in the code distance.
AI.conclusion: Pathfinder-BP achieves MWPM-level accuracy while offering a highly parallelizable decoder suitable for low-latency hardware implementation for topological quantum codes.

title: Benchmarking a randomized quantum algorithm for estimating expectation values of molecular observables
summary: Randomized quantum algorithms for the estimation of expectation values of molecular observables offer a promising route to early fault-tolerant quantum advantage by trading circuit depth for an increased number of samples. However, this begs the question whether the resulting measurement overhead remains feasible for industrially relevant molecular systems. In this work, we benchmark the randomized sampling algorithm of Wang et al. [1] through numerical simulations on a hydrogen molecule and resource estimates for various active spaces of the cytochrome P450, an industry-relevant system in the pharmaceutical industry. Our numerical simulations reveal that the analytical error bounds significantly overestimate the actual sampling error, whereas the analytical bound on the required imaginary evolution time is comparatively tight, exceeding a direct DMRG estimate by roughly 44% for the active space where the comparison is feasible. The measurement overhead nevertheless remains prohibitively high: even for the smallest active spaces, the expectation-value estimation alone requires around 1010 samples, scaling to beyond 1015 for the largest active spaces considered. These results suggest that substantial improvements in measurement strategies or algorithmic scaling are necessary before randomized early-fault-tolerant algorithms become competitive for industrial quantum chemistry applications.

AI.tldr: This work benchmarks the randomized sampling algorithm of Wang et al. for molecular expectation-value estimation via simulations of H2 and resource estimates for cytochrome P450 active spaces. It finds analytical error bounds overestimate actual sampling error, the imaginary-time bound is ~44% above a DMRG estimate, and the measurement overhead remains prohibitive (≈10^10 samples even for the smallest active spaces, exceeding 10^15 for the largest).
AI.motivation: Randomized quantum algorithms promise early fault-tolerant quantum advantage for molecular observables by trading circuit depth for more samples, but it is unclear whether the resulting measurement overhead is feasible for industrially relevant systems.
AI.method: Numerical simulations on a hydrogen molecule and resource estimates for various active spaces of cytochrome P450, an industry-relevant pharmaceutical system, benchmarking the randomized sampling algorithm of Wang et al.
AI.result: Analytical error bounds significantly overestimate the actual sampling error, while the analytical bound on required imaginary evolution time is relatively tight, exceeding a direct DMRG estimate by roughly 44% for the feasible comparison. Measurement overhead stays prohibitively high: ~10^10 samples for expectation-value estimation even in the smallest active spaces, scaling beyond 10^15 for the largest.
AI.conclusion: Substantial improvements in measurement strategies or algorithmic scaling are required before randomized early-fault-tolerant algorithms become competitive for industrial quantum chemistry applications.

title: Entanglement and parametric resonance in coupled oscillator systems
summary: We study a system of two quadratically-coupled harmonic oscillators, prepared respectively in the ground state and in a coherent state. This toy model can describe for instance the dynamics of one mode of a quantum field evolving in a harmonically-oscillating classical background. In such situations, it is well-known that, depending on the background oscillation amplitude and coupling strength, the system may exhibit parametric resonance. Using the Feynman-Vernon influence functional, we analyze the interplay between parametric resonance and quantum entanglement by perturbatively computing the purity of the mixed state resulting from tracing over one of the oscillators. We find a runaway behavior of the quantum entanglement between the two oscillators, as well as a rapid breakdown of the validity of perturbation theory, in regions of parametric instability. This provides a quantitative confirmation of various statements in the literature and is highly relevant to questions pertaining to the validity of the semiclassical approximation in coupled quantum-classical systems.

AI.tldr: A toy model of two quadratically-coupled oscillators (one in the ground state, one in a coherent state) explores whether parametric resonance drives runaway entanglement growth and breaks perturbative validity, with implications for the semiclassical approximation.
AI.motivation: This setup models a quantum field mode evolving in a harmonically-oscillating classical background, where parametric resonance is known to occur depending on amplitude and coupling strength. The authors want to quantify the interplay between parametric resonance and quantum entanglement, and probe the validity of semiclassical descriptions in coupled quantum-classical systems—issues raised qualitatively in prior literature.
AI.method: Using the Feynman-Vernon influence functional, they perturbatively compute the purity of the reduced mixed state obtained by tracing over one oscillator, tracking entanglement between the two quadratically-coupled oscillators.
AI.result: They find runaway (unbounded) growth of quantum entanglement between the two oscillators, along with a rapid breakdown of perturbation theory, in regions of parametric instability.
AI.conclusion: The results provide a quantitative confirmation of earlier qualitative claims and are highly relevant to questions about the validity of the semiclassical approximation in coupled quantum-classical systems.

title: QBFF: Deep Quantum Bottleneck for Automatic Speaker Verification Anti-Spoofing
comment: Accepted for publication at the 2026 IEEE 2nd International Conference on Quantum Artificial Intelligence (QAI)
summary: A central goal of quantum machine learning is to identify applications in which small quantum circuits can improve task performance while remaining executable on real hardware. We investigate deepfake (synthetic) speech detection, a largely unexplored application in this area, where reliable confidence scores are as important as discrimination performance because deployment decisions are made at fixed thresholds and overconfident errors can be costly. We introduce QBFF, which routes a compressed speech representation through a small 8-qubit variational circuit (VQC) used as a drop-in bottleneck, with a matched classical bottleneck as the control. The quantum circuit yields better-calibrated confidence in most matched comparisons, including out-of-distribution evaluation, though the downstream deployment-cost benefit is model-dependent. We then run the same circuit on a real IBM quantum processor. To our knowledge, this is the first anti-spoofing pipeline to run on a QPU; hardware execution demonstrates feasibility, with lower subset EER and $C_{llr}$ but higher mean actDCF than the matched classical reference. Together, these results show that hardware-executable quantum bottlenecks can improve score reliability, with gains that vary by evaluation setting.

AI.tldr: QBFF routes a compressed speech representation through an 8-qubit variational quantum circuit as a bottleneck for deepfake speech detection, improving confidence calibration and achieving the first anti-spoofing pipeline execution on a real QPU.
AI.motivation: Quantum machine learning needs applications where small quantum circuits improve task performance while remaining executable on real hardware. Deepfake/synthetic speech detection is largely unexplored in this context, and it uniquely demands reliable confidence scores—not just discrimination—because deployment decisions use fixed thresholds and overconfident errors are costly.
AI.method: The authors introduce QBFF, which passes a compressed speech representation through a small 8-qubit variational quantum circuit (VQC) serving as a drop-in bottleneck. A matched classical bottleneck is used as the control. The same circuit is also executed on a real IBM quantum processor.
AI.result: The quantum circuit yields better-calibrated confidence in most matched comparisons, including out-of-distribution evaluation, though the downstream deployment-cost benefit is model-dependent. On real hardware, execution is feasible, showing lower subset EER and C_llr but higher mean actDCF than the matched classical reference.
AI.conclusion: Hardware-executable quantum bottlenecks can improve score reliability in anti-spoofing, with gains that vary by evaluation setting. This is, to the authors' knowledge, the first anti-spoofing pipeline run on a QPU.

title: Magic-Free Certification of Logical Error Rates in Universal Fault-Tolerant Circuits
summary: As quantum hardware enters the fault-tolerant regime, algorithms are beginning to be executed on encoded qubits, yet scalable certification of how well they run remains an open problem. Here we introduce magic-free certification, a certification protocol for universal fault-tolerant circuits that consumes no magic, the resource that generally places them beyond efficient classical simulation and is by far the most expensive element of a fault-tolerant computation. The protocol is code- and decoder-agnostic, runs interleaved with the target circuit on the same device, and has a sample complexity that grows linearly with the number of logical qubits and non-Clifford gates while remaining decoupled from the logical error rate itself. Given a predefined error tolerance $p_L^*$, the protocol determines at a chosen confidence level whether the device executes the target circuit at a logical error rate below $p_L^*$. The method relies on trap circuits, copies of the target with every magic state replaced by a stabilizer state, whose outcomes are deterministic and which, being indistinguishable from the target to stochastic Pauli noise, fail at the same rate. We illustrate the protocol in Steane-code simulations of a magic state injection gadget and a quantum Fourier transform.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces magic-free certification, a code- and decoder-agnostic protocol that certifies logical error rates of universal fault-tolerant circuits without consuming magic states, using trap circuits to bound error rates at linear sample complexity.
AI.motivation: As quantum hardware approaches the fault-tolerant regime, algorithms run on encoded qubits, but scalable verification of how well they execute remains unsolved. Existing certification methods typically consume magic states, the most expensive resource in fault-tolerant computation, and often scale poorly or depend on specific codes/decoders.
AI.method: The protocol interleaves with the target circuit on the same device and is code- and decoder-agnostic. It uses trap circuits: copies of the target in which every magic state is replaced by a stabilizer state, yielding deterministic outcomes. These traps are indistinguishable from the target under stochastic Pauli noise, so they fail at the same rate, enabling certification of the logical error rate against a tolerance p_L* at a chosen confidence level.
AI.result: Sample complexity grows linearly with the number of logical qubits and non-Clifford gates, and is decoupled from the logical error rate. The protocol is demonstrated in Steane-code simulations of a magic state injection gadget and a quantum Fourier transform.
AI.conclusion: Magic-free certification provides a scalable, resource-efficient way to verify fault-tolerant quantum circuits without consuming magic states, applicable across codes and decoders and validated on representative gadgets and algorithms.

title: Quantum state texture of maximal-resource Fourier states under Hawking radiation
summary: Quantum state texture (QST) is a recently proposed quantum resource that characterizes the nonuniformity of a density matrix in a given computational basis. In the resource theory of QST, the Fourier states f_k are maximally resourceful states, attaining the maximum QST measure. We study the QST behavior of three maximally resourceful states in a two-mode Dirac field under Hawking radiation from a Schwarzschild black hole, using a fidelity-based measure. We consider three cases: only mode B undergoes radiation, only mode A undergoes radiation, and both modes undergo radiation simultaneously. Our results show that for single-mode radiation, if the mode unaffected by radiation is orthogonal to the single-mode textureless state, the QST of the overall output state remains maximal and is independent of the Hawking temperature; we call this phenomenon orthogonality protection. When both modes undergo radiation simultaneously, orthogonality protection vanishes, and the QST of all three Fourier states decreases with increasing Hawking temperature. Notably, the QST measure of f_3 under two-mode radiation is higher than that under only mode B radiation, indicating that QST can be redistributed among modes: QST gained by one mode under radiation can partially compensate for QST lost by the other. We further provide a general resource-theoretic explanation of orthogonality protection, showing that this phenomenon is independent of the specific form of the QST measure. These results reveal how QST degrades under Hawking radiation and provide a new perspective on the redistribution of quantum resources in black hole backgrounds.

AI.tldr: This paper studies the behavior of quantum state texture (QST) for three maximally resourceful Fourier states in a two-mode Dirac field under Hawking radiation, revealing "orthogonality protection" under single-mode radiation and QST redistribution under two-mode radiation.
AI.motivation: QST is a recently proposed quantum resource characterizing the nonuniformity of a density matrix in a given computational basis, with Fourier states being maximally resourceful. Understanding how such quantum resources degrade or redistribute in relativistic settings—particularly under Hawking radiation—remains an open question, motivating a systematic study of QST dynamics in black hole backgrounds.
AI.method: The authors analyze three maximally resourceful Fourier states (f_k) in a two-mode Dirac field under Hawking radiation from a Schwarzschild black hole, using a fidelity-based QST measure. Three scenarios are considered: only mode B radiates, only mode A radiates, and both modes radiate simultaneously. A general resource-theoretic argument is also developed to explain orthogonality protection.
AI.result: For single-mode radiation, when the non-radiating mode is orthogonal to the single-mode textureless state, the QST of the overall output state remains maximal and is independent of the Hawking temperature—a phenomenon termed orthogonality protection. When both modes radiate, orthogonality protection vanishes and QST for all three Fourier states decreases with increasing Hawking temperature. Notably, the QST of f_3 under two-mode radiation exceeds that under only mode B radiation, showing QST can be redistributed among modes, with gains in one mode partially compensating losses in the other.
AI.conclusion: The study reveals how QST degrades under Hawking radiation and demonstrates a redistribution mechanism of quantum resources across modes. A general resource-theoretic explanation confirms that orthogonality protection is independent of the specific QST measure, offering a new perspective on quantum resource behavior in black hole backgrounds.

title: Bell's go theorem: regaining local causality with a new notion of realism
comment: The core argument is told without mathematics in "A simple story" (Sec. I); the models proving the main result are in Secs. III F and IV B (Figs. 2 and 4). 43 pages, 6 figures
summary: Bell's theorem is popularly stated as the inconsistency of quantum theory with local realism. Realism is here formalized by the ontological models framework, where elements of reality are points of a measurable space and probabilities obey the Kolmogorov axioms. In the Bell scenario, locally causal ontological models posit a common cause supporting a global valuation, a joint assignment of outcomes to all measurements at once, across incompatible contexts. Within this notion of realism, Bell's theorem makes any realist explanation of the quantum predictions conspiratorial: any mechanism, whether superluminal, superdeterministic, or retrocausal, must be finely tuned so as never to manifest operationally. We redefine realism through a new ontological framework that generalizes the standard one. The elements of reality, which we call records, are no longer points but relational parts of a point-free generalization of a topological space (sublocales of a locale). A record shared by two incompatible contexts establishes the sameness of a measurement across them, without such pairwise identities composing into a global valuation, and the common cause is then a web of such records. Within this framework, Bell's no-go theorem becomes a go theorem: local causality, restated for records, is no longer at odds with the quantum statistics. This is possible because modularity, the inclusion-exclusion law of classical probability, fails across incompatible contexts, so that the probability theory generalizes Kolmogorov's. We exhibit explicit models reproducing several quantum strategies, including the optimal CHSH violation. More broadly, locally causal models of this kind attain every Bell-CHSH value up to the algebraic maximum. A realist explanation of the quantum predictions need not be conspiratorial; every causal influence posited by these models is reflected in the operational predictions.

AI.tldr: The paper redefines realism using a point-free (locale/sublocale) ontological framework where "records" are relational rather than points, turning Bell's no-go theorem into a go theorem: local causality restated for records is compatible with quantum statistics, reproducing the optimal CHSH violation and all Bell-CHSH values up to the algebraic maximum.
AI.motivation: In the standard ontological models framework, realism is formalized via points of a measurable space with Kolmogorov probabilities. Under this notion, Bell's theorem forces any locally causal realist explanation of quantum predictions to be conspiratorial—requiring fine-tuned mechanisms (superluminal, superdeterministic, or retrocausal) that never manifest operationally. The authors aim to escape this conspiratorial conclusion by redefining realism itself.
AI.method: They introduce a generalized ontological framework replacing point-based reality with "records," which are relational parts of a point-free generalization of a topological space (sublocales of a locale). A record shared by two incompatible contexts establishes sameness of a measurement across them without composing into a global valuation; the common cause becomes a web of such records. Local causality is restated for records, and the probability theory generalizes Kolmogorov's by allowing modularity (the inclusion-exclusion law) to fail across incompatible contexts.
AI.result: Bell's no-go theorem becomes a go theorem: local causality, restated for records, is no longer at odds with quantum statistics. They exhibit explicit models reproducing several quantum strategies, including the optimal CHSH violation. More broadly, locally causal models of this kind attain every Bell-CHSH value up to the algebraic maximum.
AI.conclusion: A realist explanation of quantum predictions need not be conspiratorial; every causal influence posited by these record-based models is reflected in the operational predictions, eliminating the fine-tuning demanded under standard realism.

title: Towards the Geometry of Quantum Optical Measurements: Kraus Trajectories in the Instrumental Weyl-Heisenberg Group Manifold
summary: Since ancient Greek times, geometry has been a method by which humans can make inferences, by the use of similar triangles, about the world far beyond their immediate senses. Similarity plays an equally important role in quantum measurement, except that instead of triangles, the similarity is between the infinitesimal generators of rotation, canonical transformation, or some other virtual symmetry. For many quantum optical measurements of a single mode, these generators produce Kraus operators that are contained within a twelve-dimensional Lie group: the Instrumental Weyl-Heisenberg group manifold ($\mathrm{IWH}^{\textbf{12}}$). In particular, $\mathrm{IWH}^{\textbf{12}}$ is general enough to include all diffusively generated 'dyne measurements. In this paper, $\mathrm{IWH}^{\textbf{12}}$ will be used to develop two more general classes of 'dyne measurement: one that interpolates between diffusive homodyne and diffusive heterodyne (``slomodyne'') and one that adds to 'dyne measurements adaptive squeezing and displacement. Our analysis uses an approach known as the Instrument Manifold Program (IMP). In particular, a Harish-Chandra-like decomposition of $\mathrm{IWH}^{\textbf{12}}$ is used to calculate the vielbein transformation from a right-invariant basis to the corresponding coordinate basis, allowing us to universally and autonomously navigate $\mathrm{IWH}^{\textbf{12}}$ and locate the Kraus-operator of whatever selective process is being considered as it evolves in time according to the measurement record.

AI.tldr: The paper exploits the twelve-dimensional Instrumental Weyl-Heisenberg group manifold to define two generalized classes of continuous quantum measurements: one interpolating between diffusive homodyne and heterodyne detection ("slomodyne"), and one incorporating adaptive squeezing and displacement into 'dyne measurements, using the Instrument Manifold Program.
AI.motivation: Similarity is a fundamental inferential tool in geometry and also in quantum measurement, where the relevant similarity is between infinitesimal generators of rotation, canonical transformation, or virtual symmetries. Many single-mode quantum optical measurements produce Kraus operators contained in a twelve-dimensional Lie group, making a unified geometric treatment desirable for generalizing measurement schemes.
AI.method: The Instrumental Weyl-Heisenberg group manifold (IWH^12) is employed via the Instrument Manifold Program (IMP). A Harish-Chandra-like decomposition of IWH^12 is used to compute the vielbein transformation from a right-invariant basis to the corresponding coordinate basis, enabling autonomous navigation of the manifold and identification of the Kraus operator for varying selective processes as they evolve with the measurement record.
AI.result: Two more general classes of 'dyne measurement are developed: (1) "slomodyne," interpolating between diffusive homodyne and diffusive heterodyne, and (2) a class adding adaptive squeezing and displacement to 'dyne measurements. The vielbein transformation allows universal, autonomous navigation of IWH^12.
AI.conclusion: IWH^12 is sufficiently general to encompass all diffusively generated 'dyne measurements, and the IMP-based decomposition provides a unified framework for locating the Kraus operator of arbitrary selective processes evolving in time according to the measurement record.

title: Emergent quantum algebras in dissipative time crystals
summary: Strong dynamical symmetries provide an algebraic description of persistent oscillations in open quantum systems governed by the Lindblad equation. For finite-dimensional systems with a full-rank stationary state, such symmetries are necessary and sufficient for non-decaying oscillatory modes to appear in the Liouvillian's spectrum. These modes can be directly constructed by acting on stationary states with the identified symmetry operators. Here we establish an asymptotic counterpart of this algebra for collective spins. Taking a single spin $S$ in a magnetic field, subject to dissipation through linear jump operators, we identify the exact conditions on the field and dissipative couplings under which non-decaying oscillatory modes emerge as $S \rightarrow \infty$. We then write down a simple, closed form for the corresponding `symmetry' operator which can be applied to the steady state to construct these modes, which are eigenvectors of the Liouvillian, with imaginary eigenvalues, up to $O(1/S)$ corrections. A second operator, an emergent conserved quantity, completes the algebra, and its slow relaxation determines how quantum noise selects the stationary state. The construction can be directly extended to a pair of interacting spins sharing a common reservoir, with the resulting quantum algebra making the entanglement during a quench analytically accessible.

AI.tldr: The paper establishes an asymptotic (large-spin) counterpart of strong dynamical symmetries for collective spins obeying a Lindblad master equation, deriving exact conditions for persistent oscillatory modes, explicit symmetry operators, and an emergent conserved quantity.
AI.motivation: Strong dynamical symmetries are known to fully characterize non-decaying oscillatory modes in finite-dimensional open quantum systems with full-rank stationary states, but this algebraic framework is tied to finite dimensions. Collective-spin systems, where the spin length S acts as a control parameter, lack an analogous description of their asymptotic symmetry structure, motivating an extension of the symmetry algebra to the large-S limit.
AI.method: A single spin S in a magnetic field with dissipation via linear jump operators is analyzed. Exact conditions on the field and dissipative couplings for the emergence of non-decaying oscillatory modes as S→∞ are identified. A closed-form symmetry operator acting on the steady state to produce Liouvillian eigenvectors with imaginary eigenvalues (up to O(1/S) corrections) is constructed, together with a second operator—an emergent conserved quantity—completing the algebra.
AI.result: Exact conditions on field and dissipative couplings are obtained for persistent oscillatory modes in the S→∞ limit. A simple closed-form symmetry operator generates Liouvillian eigenvectors with imaginary eigenvalues up to O(1/S) corrections. A companion emergent conserved quantity completes the algebra, and its slow relaxation rate governs how quantum noise selects the stationary state. The construction extends to two interacting spins sharing a common reservoir, rendering quench entanglement analytically accessible.
AI.conclusion: An asymptotic dynamical symmetry algebra for collective spins is established, generalizing strong dynamical symmetries beyond finite dimensions. It provides explicit operators for constructing non-decaying oscillatory modes and an emergent conserved quantity controlling stationary-state selection, with direct extension to interacting spin pairs and their quench entanglement.

title: Closed-form construction of exceptional points in a two-parametric PT-symmetric large-matrix model
summary: Stable bound states living on a discrete one-dimensional N-point lattice are assumed generated by a certain two-parametric PT symmetric potential $V=V(A,B)$. At any $N$, the coordinates $A=A^{(EP)}$ and $B=B^{(EP)}$ of the Kato's exceptional point (marking the phase-transition instant of the loss of stability) are defined, exactly, via roots of a certain elementary quartic polynomial.

AI.tldr: For a two-parameter PT-symmetric potential on a discrete 1D N-point lattice, the exceptional-point (stability-loss transition) coordinates A^(EP), B^(EP) are obtained exactly as roots of an elementary quartic polynomial, for any N.
AI.motivation: Stable bound states on a discrete one-dimensional N-point lattice generated by a two-parametric PT-symmetric potential V(A,B) need a precise characterization of where stability is lost—i.e., the Kato exceptional point marking the phase-transition instant.
AI.method: The exceptional-point coordinates A=A^(EP) and B=B^(EP) are determined exactly via the roots of an elementary quartic polynomial, for arbitrary lattice size N.
AI.result: Exact, closed-form exceptional-point locations A^(EP), B^(EP) are defined through quartic-polynomial roots at any N.
AI.conclusion: The PT-symmetry phase transition (loss of stability) of the discrete-lattice bound states is analytically captured by an elementary quartic, valid for all N.

title: Bosonic Quantum Conditional Mutual Information and Bose-Einstein Condensation
summary: This article aims to introduce the bosonic asymmetric quantum conditional mutual information (QCMI), $I_{B}(A; B|C)$, as a rigorously defined information-theoretic quantity for continuous-variable (bosonic) systems. After defining $I_{B}(A; B|C)$ through quantum instruments on infinite-dimensional Fock spaces, we prove that Bose-Einstein condensation (BEC) induces a logarithmic divergence $ I_{B}(A; B|C) \geq α\log_2 (N_{0}^C+1)$, which further establishes $I_{B}(A; B|C)$ as a quantum-information order parameter for BEC with power-law scaling near the critical point. We provide the complete five-step proof of this result, connecting measurement back-action, off-diagonal long-range order, and Jensen's inequality. In the condensed phase, the effective causal propagation velocity is set by the Bogoliubov sound speed $c_s$ in the long-wavelength limit, and vanishes continuously at the superfluid--Mott-insulator transition. Applications to composite bosons, the BEC--BCS crossover, and a quantum-gas-microscope measurement protocol are presented. Finally, we demonstrate how the reduced bosonic QCMI serves as a finite-size scaling probe analogous to the Binder cumulant.

AI.tldr: The paper defines a bosonic asymmetric quantum conditional mutual information $I_B(A;B|C)$ for continuous-variable systems and proves it diverges logarithmically under Bose-Einstein condensation, making it a quantum-information order parameter with power-law scaling near criticality.
AI.motivation: Continuous-variable (bosonic) systems lack a rigorously defined information-theoretic order parameter for phase transitions such as Bose-Einstein condensation, motivating a quantum-information characterization of condensation.
AI.method: $I_B(A;B|C)$ is defined via quantum instruments on infinite-dimensional Fock spaces. A complete five-step proof establishes the logarithmic divergence $I_B(A;B|C) \\geq \\alpha \\log_2(N_0^C+1)$ by connecting measurement back-action, off-diagonal long-range order, and Jensen's inequality.
AI.result: BEC induces a logarithmic divergence of $I_B(A;B|C)$, qualifying it as a quantum-information order parameter with power-law scaling near the critical point. In the condensed phase the effective causal propagation velocity is set by the Bogoliubov sound speed $c_s$ in the long-wavelength limit and vanishes continuously at the superfluid--Mott-insulator transition.
AI.conclusion: The bosonic QCMI serves as a finite-size scaling probe analogous to the Binder cumulant, with applications to composite bosons, the BEC--BCS crossover, and a quantum-gas-microscope measurement protocol.

title: Reverse quantum aging: Restoring rhythmicity from quantum aging state
summary: Quantum aging transition has recently been reported, whereby the oscillatory dynamics of a network of globally coupled quantum self-sustained oscillators is degraded sharply when the fraction of inactive nodes exceeds a critical value. Here we explore the reverse process: the revival of rhythmic dynamics from an aged state in a quantum oscillator network by introducing a controlled incoherent single-boson pumping channel. Using a self-consistent quantum master equation in the Lindblad form for globally coupled active--inactive quantum Stuart--Landau oscillators, we show that increasing the pumping strength progressively suppresses the aging transition and eventually eliminates it, restoring rhythmicity even when all oscillators are inactive. Remarkably, complete compensation of the coupling-induced dissipative loss is not required; a substantially weaker pumping strength is sufficient to eliminate the aging transition. We show that the revival is governed by a redistribution of the Fock-state population of the inactive oscillators toward higher-occupation states. Our results establish controlled incoherent pumping as an effective mechanism for restoring dynamical robustness in quantum oscillator networks.

AI.tldr: This work demonstrates that controlled incoherent single-boson pumping can revive rhythmic dynamics in a quantum oscillator network that has undergone an aging transition, without needing to fully compensate the dissipative loss.
AI.motivation: Quantum aging transition—the sharp degradation of oscillatory dynamics when the fraction of inactive nodes in a globally coupled quantum self-sustained oscillator network exceeds a critical value—has recently been reported. The reverse process, i.e., reviving rhythmicity from an aged state, remained unexplored. This paper addresses whether and how such a revival can be achieved.
AI.method: The authors study globally coupled active–inactive quantum Stuart–Landau oscillators using a self-consistent quantum master equation in Lindblad form. They introduce a controlled incoherent single-boson pumping channel and analyze its effect on the aging transition, examining the dependence on pumping strength and the underlying Fock-state population dynamics of the inactive oscillators.
AI.result: Increasing the pumping strength progressively suppresses the aging transition and eventually eliminates it, restoring rhythmicity even when all oscillators are inactive. Notably, complete compensation of the coupling-induced dissipative loss is not required—a substantially weaker pumping strength suffices to eliminate the aging transition. The revival is governed by a redistribution of the Fock-state population of the inactive oscillators toward higher-occupation states.
AI.conclusion: Controlled incoherent pumping is established as an effective mechanism for restoring dynamical robustness in quantum oscillator networks, enabling revival of rhythmic dynamics from an aged state.

title: Euler's thirty-six officers need not all be entangled: real AME(4,6), families and classification
comment: 9 pages, 3 figures, 2 tables; gtihub repo is https://github.com/palashpandya/real-ame46
summary: Absolutely maximally entangled states of four six-level systems, AME$(4,6)$, are the quantum solutions of Euler's problem of the thirty-six officers. Until recently all reported solutions were complex, and it was conjectured that no real orthogonal 2-unitary matrix of order $36$ exists. We give real AME$(4,6)$ states with $60$ non-zero coefficients in $\{\pm1,\sqrt2\}/\sqrt{72}$. Of their thirty-six officers, $12$ are classical, as some must be whenever fewer than $72$ coefficients are non-zero. They lie in the $-1$ eigenspace of an order-$4$ local symmetry, and on their support the AME conditions become linear. We derive two closed-form families of AME$(4,6)$ states that meet at one of these states: a $10$-parameter family that is supported on $72$ basis states, and an $11$-parameter family on $60$ basis states. At each of its two ends the first family loses $12$ coefficients, and the AME states on the remaining $60$ basis states form an $11$-parameter family: the second family at one end, and an analogous family at the other. These two $60$-term families contain $4096$ real AME states up to diagonal local unitaries, $1024$ of which are limits of the first family. They fall into exactly $20$ classes under local unitaries and permutations of the parties, and we certify their separation with interval arithmetic.

AI.tldr: The paper constructs real Absolutely Maximally Entangled states AME$(4,6)$—quantum solutions to Euler's thirty-six officers problem—with 60 nonzero coefficients in $\{\pm1,\sqrt2\}/\sqrt{72}$, derives two closed-form families (a 10-parameter/72-term family and an 11-parameter/60-term family) meeting at one such state, and classifies the resulting real AME states.
AI.motivation: AME$(4,6)$ states correspond to the quantum solution of Euler's thirty-six officers problem, and previously all reported solutions were complex. It had been conjectured that no real orthogonal 2-unitary matrix of order 36 exists. The work aims to resolve this by exhibiting real solutions and characterizing them.
AI.method: The authors construct real AME$(4,6)$ states supported on 60 basis states, exploiting an order-4 local symmetry whose $-1$ eigenspace contains the states and on whose support the AME conditions become linear. They derive two closed-form parameterized families: a 10-parameter family on 72 basis states and an 11-parameter family on 60 basis states, meeting at a common state, with the first family losing 12 coefficients at each end. Classification is performed via interval arithmetic.
AI.result: Real AME$(4,6)$ states with 60 nonzero coefficients in $\{\pm1,\sqrt2\}/\sqrt{72}$ are obtained; 12 of their 36 officers are classical, as required whenever fewer than 72 coefficients are nonzero. The two 60-term families contain 4096 real AME states up to diagonal local unitaries, 1024 of which are limits of the first family, falling into exactly 20 classes under local unitaries and party permutations, with separation certified by interval arithmetic.
AI.conclusion: The conjecture that no real orthogonal 2-unitary matrix of order 36 exists is refuted: real AME$(4,6)$ states are constructed explicitly via two intersecting closed-form families, and the space of 60-term real AME states is fully classified into 20 equivalence classes.

title: Fisher-Information Certification from Bell Statistics: CHSH Bounds, Information Loss, and Finite-Data Guarantees
summary: Bell-test data are typically used to certify nonlocal correlations, while quantum metrology is concerned with the sensitivity of measurement statistics to unknown parameters. Here we connect these tasks at the level of experimentally accessible Bell statistics. Using standard moment-based Fisher-information inequalities, we derive lower bounds on the classical Fisher information directly from Bell scores and their parameter dependence, without requiring full state tomography. For CHSH measurements we establish a hierarchy between the information contained in the full outcome record, the set of individual correlators, and the compressed Bell parameter, thereby quantifying the metrological cost of data compression. In polarization-phase sensing, this hierarchy reveals a Bell-metrology tradeoff: the point of maximal CHSH violation need not maximize, and can even suppress, the Fisher information carried by the Bell score itself. We further derive finite-sample lower-confidence bounds from coincidence counts and analyze the effects of biased marginals, accidental coincidences, visibility loss, and multipair emission. The framework provides a practical route for extracting metrological guarantees from Bell-type experiments using only standard correlation measurements.

AI.tldr: The paper links Bell-test statistics to quantum metrology by deriving Fisher-information lower bounds directly from measured Bell scores and their parameter dependence, revealing a tradeoff between maximal CHSH violation and metrological sensitivity.
AI.motivation: Bell-test data are conventionally used to certify nonlocal correlations, while quantum metrology focuses on how sensitive measurement statistics are to unknown parameters. These two tasks are usually treated separately, and there is a need to connect them using only experimentally accessible Bell statistics rather than full state tomography.
AI.method: The authors apply standard moment-based Fisher-information inequalities to derive lower bounds on the classical Fisher information directly from Bell scores and their parameter dependence, without full state tomography. For CHSH measurements they establish a hierarchy among the information in the full outcome record, the individual correlators, and the compressed Bell parameter. They also derive finite-sample lower-confidence bounds from coincidence counts and analyze biased marginals, accidental coincidences, visibility loss, and multipair emission.
AI.result: A hierarchy is established quantifying the metrological cost of data compression. In polarization-phase sensing, this hierarchy reveals a Bell-metrology tradeoff: the point of maximal CHSH violation need not maximize, and can even suppress, the Fisher information carried by the Bell score itself. Finite-sample lower-confidence bounds are obtained, and the effects of several experimental imperfections are characterized.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a practical route for extracting metrological guarantees from Bell-type experiments using only standard correlation measurements.

title: Realistic simulation of universal multiport interferometers with losses within a Gaussian formalism
summary: Photonic technologies are among the leading platform contenders for demonstrating quantum advantage. Nevertheless, photon losses represent the major hurdle for the realization of a fault-tolerant optical quantum computer, and the need for an accurate characterization of this phenomenon is crucial for classical simulations of quantum algorithms on noisy backends. The noisy regime would require the simulation of the algorithm on a Fock backend or rather assuming the a priori hypothesis on the uniformity of the optical losses, which may lead to wrong predictions about the outcome from the algorithm on a cerain hardware. We propose a Gaussian model that can reproduce a lossy dynamics through the experimental characterization of imperfect interferometers, yielding the corresponding mean vector and the covariance matrix. Such model can be adapted to any continuous-variable architecture (spatial or time-bin encoded) and for both the Gaussian boson sampling or general-dyne based algorithms. Eventually, we quantify the drift of optical losses from being uniform throughout the multiport interferometer by a numerical simulation. This work proposes a blueprint for future characterizations, tailor-suited for specific devices and architectures, as well as for potential error correction and mitigation techniques, and it paves the way for realistic simulations of quantum algorithms on NISQ optical platforms.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a Gaussian model that reproduces lossy dynamics via experimental characterization of imperfect interferometers, providing mean vector and covariance matrix, adaptable to any continuous-variable architecture. It quantifies the drift of optical losses from uniformity, offering a blueprint for device-specific characterization, error mitigation, and realistic NISQ optical simulations.
AI.motivation: Photon losses are the major hurdle for fault-tolerant optical quantum computing. Accurate loss characterization is crucial for classically simulating quantum algorithms on noisy backends, but the noisy regime typically requires Fock-backend simulation or assumes uniform losses, which can yield wrong predictions about algorithm outcomes on actual hardware.
AI.method: The authors construct a Gaussian model that reproduces lossy dynamics through experimental characterization of imperfect interferometers, yielding the corresponding mean vector and covariance matrix. The model is adaptable to any continuous-variable architecture (spatial or time-bin encoded) and supports both Gaussian boson sampling and general-dyne-based algorithms.
AI.result: A numerical simulation quantifies the drift of optical losses from the assumption of uniformity across the multiport interferometer, demonstrating the deviation from the uniform-loss hypothesis.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a blueprint for future characterizations tailored to specific devices and architectures, useful for error correction and mitigation techniques, and paves the way toward realistic simulations of quantum algorithms on NISQ optical platforms.

title: The Quantum Character Transform
summary: Bastidas et al. (2025) highlighted the importance of exploiting group symmetries to reduce computational overhead and unify simulation methods across both condensed matter physics and ab initio quantum chemistry. I discuss the discrete character transform, which is the group Fourier transform restricted to $Z(\mathbb{C}[G])$, the center of the group algebra, where class functions form a commutative convolution algebra and irreducible characters are its spectral basis. The normalized character table of a non-abelian group can be obtained through a restriction operator, which means an efficient quantum character transform for any finite group with an efficient quantum Fourier transform. I give complementary quantum algorithms for class convolution based on direct class-sum block encoding and spectral implementation in the character basis, explaining their applications to symmetry-adapted many-body dynamics, molecular and spectroscopic symmetry analysis, and quantum walks, as well as characterizing the central information used in hidden-subgroup problems, including its limitations for graph isomorphism.

AI.tldr: This work introduces the discrete character transform as the group Fourier transform restricted to the center of the group algebra, and provides efficient quantum algorithms for class convolution, with applications to symmetry-adapted many-body dynamics, molecular spectroscopy, quantum walks, and hidden-subgroup problems.
AI.motivation: Building on Bastidas et al. (2025), who emphasized exploiting group symmetries to reduce computational overhead and unify simulation methods across condensed matter physics and ab initio quantum chemistry, the paper aims to develop a symmetry-based transform framework that unifies quantum algorithms across these domains.
AI.method: The author discusses the discrete character transform, defined as the group Fourier transform restricted to Z(C[G]), the center of the group algebra, where class functions form a commutative convolution algebra and irreducible characters serve as its spectral basis. The normalized character table of a non-abelian group is obtained via a restriction operator, enabling an efficient quantum character transform for any finite group possessing an efficient quantum Fourier transform. Complementary quantum algorithms for class convolution are given based on direct class-sum block encoding and spectral implementation in the character basis.
AI.result: The paper delivers complementary quantum algorithms for class convolution and characterizes the central information used in hidden-subgroup problems, including its limitations for graph isomorphism.
AI.conclusion: The discrete character transform provides a unified group-symmetry framework supporting symmetry-adapted many-body dynamics, molecular and spectroscopic symmetry analysis, and quantum walks, while clarifying what central information can and cannot resolve in hidden-subgroup problems.

title: Geodesic steering for rapid dissipative entanglement distribution
summary: We describe an optimal-control strategy designed to accelerate the dissipative preparation of complex, highly entangled quantum many-body states. Analogous to optimal steering of isolated quantum systems, our scheme identifies control pulses that guide the evolution of open quantum systems along trajectories of instantaneous steady states while minimizing leakage resulting from non-adiabatic transitions. In many cases of interest, these control parameters can be derived analytically and without the need for computationally expensive numerical simulations of the full many-body master equation. We apply this technique for the preparation of bi- and multipartite entangled states in qubit systems coupled to a common photonic waveguide or a distributed squeezed reservoir. In both scenarios, our optimal-control strategy significantly outperforms the bare relaxation dynamics after a quench, reducing preparation times of near-maximally entangled states by orders of magnitude. This drastic speedup makes dissipative entanglement distribution protocols compatible with high-fidelity quantum information processing applications and illustrates more broadly the potential of leakage minimization for accelerating reservoir-engineering schemes.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces an optimal-control strategy to accelerate dissipative preparation of highly entangled quantum many-body states by steering open quantum systems along instantaneous steady-state trajectories while minimizing non-adiabatic leakage, achieving orders-of-magnitude speedup in entanglement preparation.
AI.motivation: Dissipative reservoir-engineering schemes can prepare entangled quantum many-body states, but the bare relaxation dynamics after a quench are typically slow, limiting compatibility with high-fidelity quantum information processing applications. There is a need to accelerate these protocols without relying on computationally expensive numerical simulations of the full many-body master equation.
AI.method: The authors design an optimal-control strategy analogous to optimal steering of isolated quantum systems. They identify control pulses that guide the evolution of open quantum systems along trajectories of instantaneous steady states while minimizing leakage from non-adiabatic transitions. In many cases of interest, the control parameters are derived analytically, avoiding expensive numerical simulation of the full many-body master equation. The technique is applied to prepare bi- and multipartite entangled states in qubit systems coupled to a common photonic waveguide or a distributed squeezed reservoir.
AI.result: In both the common photonic waveguide and distributed squeezed reservoir scenarios, the optimal-control strategy significantly outperforms the bare relaxation dynamics after a quench, reducing preparation times of near-maximally entangled states by orders of magnitude.
AI.conclusion: The drastic speedup makes dissipative entanglement distribution protocols compatible with high-fidelity quantum information processing applications and more broadly illustrates the potential of leakage minimization for accelerating reservoir-engineering schemes.

title: Direct polarisation-state reconstruction with a temporal pointer: accessible states, resolution and optimal coupling
summary: Weak measurements are used to amplify small signals, to address foundational questions, and to characterise quantum states without tomography. In direct state reconstruction each amplitude of the state vector is proportional to a single complex weak value, which for a temporal pointer is read from the mean arrival time and the mean frequency of the postselected pulse. Such an experiment requires three quantities to be fixed, the coupling, the angular resolution demanded of the reconstruction, and the set of states over which the method remains usable, and these are commonly set by the available apparatus rather than derived. We derive all three for a Gaussian temporal pointer and an arbitrary postselection state. The states that cannot be reconstructed form a spherical cap centred on the state orthogonal to the postselection, whose geodesic half-angle follows from the largest of three independent thresholds and involves no adjustable parameter. Two states are distinguishable only if they differ by more than a minimal step fixed by the coupling, by the number of incident photons and by the sensitivity of the weak value along the path followed. For an inversion at first order in the coupling the systematic and statistical errors are opposed and fix an optimal coupling that varies as the inverse sixth root of the number of incident photons, whereas an exact inversion at finite coupling removes the systematic error, the remaining bound being one on the two-centroid readout rather than on the inversion, since below an amplitude equal to a quarter of the coupling two states give the same pair of centroids while their profiles differ. These results allow a direct reconstruction experiment to be dimensioned before the apparatus is assembled.

AI.tldr: The paper derives, for a Gaussian temporal pointer with arbitrary postselection, the three key parameters of direct weak-value state reconstruction: the usable state set (a spherical cap with geodesic half-angle from three thresholds), the minimal distinguishable step between states (set by coupling, photon number, and weak-value sensitivity), and the optimal coupling (varying as the inverse sixth root of incident photons), enabling experiment dimensioning prior to assembly.
AI.motivation: In direct state reconstruction, each amplitude of the state vector is proportional to a single complex weak value read from the mean arrival time and mean frequency of the postselected pulse. Such experiments require three quantities to be fixed—the coupling, the angular resolution demanded of the reconstruction, and the set of states over which the method remains usable—but these are commonly set by the available apparatus rather than derived. The paper aims to derive all three so that a direct reconstruction experiment can be dimensioned before the apparatus is assembled.
AI.method: The authors analytically derive the three parameters for a Gaussian temporal pointer and an arbitrary postselection state. They characterize the reconstructable states as a spherical cap centred on the state orthogonal to the postselection, whose geodesic half-angle follows from the largest of three independent thresholds with no adjustable parameter. They determine the minimal distinguishable step between two states from the coupling, the number of incident photons, and the sensitivity of the weak value along the path followed. They analyze both a first-order inversion in the coupling and an exact inversion at finite coupling.
AI.result: The states that cannot be reconstructed form a spherical cap centred on the state orthogonal to the postselection, with a geodesic half-angle determined by the largest of three independent thresholds and involving no adjustable parameter. Two states are distinguishable only if they differ by more than a minimal step fixed by the coupling, the number of incident photons, and the weak-value sensitivity along the path. For a first-order inversion, the systematic and statistical errors are opposed and fix an optimal coupling varying as the inverse sixth root of the number of incident photons. An exact inversion at finite coupling removes the systematic error, leaving a bound on the two-centroid readout rather than on the inversion; below an amplitude equal to a quarter of the coupling, two states give the same pair of centroids while their profiles differ.
AI.conclusion: The derived thresholds, minimal step, and optimal coupling allow a direct weak-value reconstruction experiment to be dimensioned before the apparatus is assembled, replacing apparatus-imposed settings with analytically derived ones for a Gaussian temporal pointer and arbitrary postselection.

title: Geomagic Square Representation of a Real AME$(4, 6)$ State
comment: 6 pages, 2 figures, 1 table. Scripts and data: https://github.com/matrix-toolbox/AME_4_6
summary: Seeking a pictorial representation of four-party absolutely maximally entangled (AME) states of local size six, we independently construct a real AME$(4,6)$ state from a table of signed Pauli matrices. Its two-unitary matrix has $60$ nonzero entries, equal to $1$ or $\pm 1/\sqrt{2}$. A locally equivalent representative yields a genuine geomagic square, where every row, column and main diagonal tiles a hexagon and all $36$ pieces are pairwise non-congruent. Colors, shapes and hatching retain the full tensor, allowing its reconstruction from the picture.

AI.tldr: A real four-party absolutely maximally entangled AME(4,6) state is constructed from signed Pauli matrices, and a locally equivalent representative is shown to correspond to a genuine geomagic square whose 36 hexagon tiles are all pairwise non-congruent.
AI.motivation: The paper seeks a pictorial representation of four-party absolutely maximally entangled (AME) states with local dimension six. The goal is to visualize a real AME(4,6) state as an intuitive geometric object, extending the role of magic squares as pictures of multipartite entanglement.
AI.method: The authors independently construct a real AME(4,6) state from a table of signed Pauli matrices. Its two-unitary matrix has 60 nonzero entries, each equal to 1 or ±1/√2. A locally equivalent representative of this state is then identified and encoded pictorially using colors, shapes, and hatching to retain the full tensor.
AI.result: The locally equivalent representative yields a genuine geomagic square in which every row, column, and main diagonal tiles a hexagon, and all 36 pieces are pairwise non-congruent. The color, shape, and hatching encoding preserves the full tensor, enabling reconstruction of the state from the picture.
AI.conclusion: The real AME(4,6) state admits a genuine geomagic square representation, providing a pictorial encoding of four-party AME states of local size six. This establishes a geometric visualization of multipartite entanglement with all tiles distinct and the tensor fully recoverable from the image.

title: Thermal aliases in quantum noise: sampling clocks and pulse widths
summary: Can collective quantum-noise measurements distinguish different mode temperatures from one common temperature when the coupling spectrum is unknown? For stationary Gaussian oscillator environments, we derive a sharp bandwidth threshold for an exact thermal alias on the integer-time sampling lattice. The threshold depends on temperature order through the quantum response. For frequencies within the first alias period, fixing sufficient integer-time correlations makes one additional fractional-time fluctuation observation enough to exclude every common-temperature fit. A calibrated second pulse width provides another route through the same collective port: both widths must probe one spectrum and retain their measured variance scales. For a specified two-mode example, continuous-frequency certificates cover all common temperatures and uncertainty in a shared pulse ramp. A binary-readout protocol combines randomly interleaved matched references with collective-variance and coherence checks to handle Gaussian oscillator loss and predictable readout drift. The selected fractional-clock and two-width designs require approximately $3.8\times10^7$ and $1.6\times10^8$ outcomes for at most 5\% type-I error and at least 95\% power on the stated alternative class. These theoretical and numerical acquisition guarantees assume independently validated preparation, spectral support and control specifications; validation costs are additional. The result identifies which new observation makes thermal-model testing informative when mode-resolved access is unavailable.

AI.tldr: For stationary Gaussian oscillator environments with an unknown coupling spectrum, the authors derive a sharp bandwidth threshold for an exact thermal alias on the integer-time sampling lattice, showing that one additional fractional-time fluctuation observation (or a calibrated second pulse width) suffices to rule out all common-temperature fits when integer-time correlations are sufficiently fixed. They give sample-complexity guarantees for a binary-readout protocol and identify the minimal new observation that makes thermal-model testing informative without mode-resolved access.
AI.motivation: Collective quantum-noise measurements normally can only access a single aggregated port, so it is unclear whether they can distinguish distinct mode temperatures from a common temperature when the coupling spectrum is unknown. A common-temperature fit could masquerade as a genuine multi-temperature signature (a "thermal alias"), and it is not known which supplementary observation is minimal and sufficient to break this degeneracy. The paper aims to identify the observation that makes thermal-model testing informative under unknown coupling and limited mode-resolved access.
