AI.method: The paper analyzes stationary Gaussian oscillator environments and derives an aliasing condition on the integer-time sampling lattice, obtaining a sharp bandwidth threshold whose value depends on temperature order via the quantum response. It then constructs two certification routes through the same collective port: (i) a fractional-clock design adding one fractional-time fluctuation observation to fixed integer-time correlations, and (ii) a two-width design using a calibrated second pulse width, requiring both widths to probe one spectrum and retain their measured variance scales. A specified two-mode example yields continuous-frequency certificates covering all common temperatures and shared-pulse-ramp uncertainty. A binary-readout protocol interleaves randomly matched references with collective-variance and coherence checks to handle Gaussian oscillator loss and predictable readout drift.
AI.result: The analysis identifies a sharp bandwidth threshold for an exact thermal alias, with the threshold governed by temperature order through the quantum response. Within the first alias period, fixing sufficient integer-time correlations plus one fractional-time fluctuation observation excludes every common-temperature fit. For the selected fractional-clock and two-width designs, approximately 3.8×10^7 and 1.6×10^8 outcomes are required for at most 5% type-I error and at least 95% power on the stated alternative class. Continuous-frequency certificates cover all common temperatures and shared-pulse-ramp uncertainty in the two-mode example.
AI.conclusion: Collective quantum-noise measurements can distinguish mode temperatures from a common temperature even with an unknown coupling spectrum, provided one targeted extra observation is added to sufficient integer-time correlations: either a fractional-time fluctuation sample or a calibrated second pulse width. The results pin down the minimal new observation that renders thermal-model testing informative when mode-resolved access is unavailable. The acquisition guarantees are theoretical and assume independently validated preparation, spectral support, and control specifications; validation costs are additional.

title: Photon-stimulated decay of $χ$-matched ancillas causes unheralded bit flips in bosonic codes
comment: 27 pages, 15 figures. Code and data: https://github.com/gulkanov/bosonoise
summary: Bosonic codes often read out their syndrome with a transmon ancilla whose computational levels $g$ and $f$ have equal parity and matched dispersive shifts: a decay $f\to e$ is then heralded and leaves the code intact, while the direct $f\to g$ is forbidden by parity. We show that the photons of the code open this decay at first order in the ancilla's decay rate. Dressing by the code mode lets the charge noise that limits the ancilla's $T_1$ drive a photon-stimulated Raman decay $|f,n\rangle\to|g,n+1\rangle$, at $(n+1)(χ_{ge}/2g_{01})^2$ times the $f\to e$ rate for a smooth noise spectrum. When the matching is set by the detuning, the decay costs $\approxΓ_{fe}/α$ per gate and photon, whatever the coupling strength; a deliberate mismatch or matching by a drive lowers this cost, and a qubit ancilla has no such channel. The opened decay is unheralded and flips a cat with probability $\approx 1/2$; being first order, it overtakes the second-order double decay $f\to e\to g$ as the ancilla improves. In a microscopic model of the Ocelot repetition cat code, it makes the bit-flip floor of the gates grow linearly with the cat size, by a factor 1.2-1.7 from four to ten photons, which would limit the noise bias to $\sim 10^3$. The published gate data end at four photons and do not yet test this growth.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies a first-order photon-stimulated Raman decay channel that opens the nominally parity-forbidden f→g transition of a transmon ancilla used to read out bosonic codes, and shows it degrades the noise bias of the Ocelot repetition cat code, growing linearly with cat size.
AI.motivation: Bosonic codes rely on transmon ancillas whose g and f levels are parity-matched, so that f→e is heralded and benign while f→g is forbidden by parity. This parity protection is assumed to keep the code intact during syndrome readout. The authors question whether the code's own photons can break this protection by opening the forbidden decay at first order in the ancilla decay rate, a mechanism not previously accounted for in error budgets.
AI.method: Analytical treatment of the dressed ancilla-code system: the code mode dresses the ancilla, allowing charge noise (which limits ancilla T1) to drive a photon-stimulated Raman transition |f,n⟩→|g,n+1⟩. The authors compute the rate as (n+1)(χ_ge/2g_01)^2 times the f→e rate for a smooth noise spectrum, and analyze the cost per gate and photon (≈Γ_fe/α) under detuning-matched conditions, with variants for deliberate mismatch or drive-based matching. They compare to the second-order double decay f→e→g and note a qubit ancilla has no such channel.
AI.result: The opened decay is unheralded and flips a cat with probability ≈1/2. Being first order, it overtakes the second-order double decay as the ancilla improves. In a microscopic model of the Ocelot repetition cat code, it makes the bit-flip floor of the gates grow linearly with cat size, by a factor 1.2–1.7 from four to ten photons, which would limit the noise bias to ∼10^3. Published gate data end at four photons and do not yet test this growth.
AI.conclusion: Parity protection of transmon ancillas in bosonic-code readout is not absolute: code photons open a first-order f→g Raman decay that is unheralded and scales unfavorably with cat size, imposing a linear growth of the bit-flip floor and a bias ceiling of ∼10^3 for the Ocelot repetition cat code. The effect is reduced by deliberate mismatch or drive-based matching, and is absent for qubit ancillas. Existing experiments at four photons cannot yet confirm the predicted scaling.

title: Entanglement Sudden Death in Gapped Ground States
summary: Spatial sudden death of entanglement refers to the disappearance of quantum correlations between subsystems after a certain distance called the entanglement length. Specifically, given a density matrix $ρ_{ABC}$ on a tripartite system $ABC$ with $B$ spatially separating $A$ and $C$, the entanglement length is the distance $\ell(A,C)$ after which the reduced density matrix $ρ_{AC}$, given by tracing out the $B$ subsystem, is separable. We show in the case of gapped ground states in any dimension that the entanglement length is finite on finite subsystems. Restricting to one-dimensional systems, we prove that normal matrix product states have a finite entanglement length independent of $A$ and $C$, and that a finite pure state with such uniform entanglement length has a matrix product state representation with bond dimension independent of $A$ and $C$. Consequently, in one dimension, entanglement length distinguishes matrix product states from all other pure states.

AI.tldr: The paper proves that spatial entanglement sudden death occurs for gapped ground states in any dimension and that, in 1D, finite uniform entanglement length exactly characterizes matrix product states among pure states.
AI.motivation: Quantum correlations between subsystems can vanish beyond a finite distance ("entanglement length") when an intervening subsystem is traced out. Whether this spatial sudden death is generic and how it relates to tensor-network representations was unclear, especially for gapped ground states.
AI.method: The authors analyze reduced density matrices ρ_AC obtained by tracing out a spatially separating subsystem B from tripartite states ρ_ABC. They establish bounds on the entanglement length for gapped ground states in arbitrary dimension, then restrict to one-dimensional systems to study normal matrix product states and general pure states.
AI.result: For gapped ground states in any dimension, the entanglement length is finite on finite subsystems. In one dimension, normal matrix product states have a finite entanglement length independent of A and C; conversely, a pure state with such uniform finite entanglement length admits an MPS representation with bond dimension independent of A and C.
AI.conclusion: Spatial entanglement sudden death is a robust feature of gapped ground states, and in one dimension entanglement length provides a sharp operational criterion distinguishing matrix product states from all other pure states.

title: Enhanced Quantum Metrology via Saddle-Point Scrambling in Phase Space
summary: Nonlinear effects are widely utilized in quantum metrology to enhance measurement precision by leveraging complex dynamical behaviors. Here, we propose a quantum scrambling-integrated scheme that optimizes the selection of initial states and parameter encoding by exploiting the nonlinear dynamical trajectories and their geometric properties in phase space. We consider a two-mode Bose-Einstein condensate as a typical example. Within a certain parameter range, using uncorrelated spin coherent states located at saddle points and separatrices enables the measurement precision to reach the Heisenberg scaling. An analytical expression for the quantum Fisher information under long-time evolution is provided, and our analysis further reveals that the enhancement mechanism is governed by the sensitivity of the energy spectrum to parameter variations. Compared to the criticality-enhanced protocol that requires parameters to approach the critical point, our scheme offers a distinct advantage in its applicability over a broader range of parameters. Moreover, this scheme can also be applied to models that include one- and two-axis countertwisting interactions and chaotic dynamics. This Letter offers a new perspective for advancing the application of nonlinear dynamics to enhance the parameter estimation precision in quantum systems.

AI.tldr: A quantum scrambling-integrated scheme exploits nonlinear phase-space trajectories and their geometry to select optimal initial states and encoding, achieving Heisenberg-scaling precision in a two-mode BEC over a broad parameter range.
AI.motivation: Nonlinear effects can enhance quantum metrology via complex dynamics, but existing criticality-enhanced protocols require parameters to be tuned close to a critical point, limiting their applicability. A scheme that achieves high precision over a broader parameter range is needed.
AI.method: The authors propose a quantum scrambling-integrated scheme that optimizes initial-state selection and parameter encoding by leveraging nonlinear dynamical trajectories and their geometric properties in phase space. A two-mode Bose-Einstein condensate is used as the typical example, with uncorrelated spin coherent states placed at saddle points and separatrices. They derive an analytical expression for the quantum Fisher information under long-time evolution and analyze the enhancement mechanism.
AI.result: Within a certain parameter range, uncorrelated spin coherent states at saddle points and separatrices enable measurement precision reaching the Heisenberg scaling. The enhancement is governed by the sensitivity of the energy spectrum to parameter variations. The scheme works over a broader parameter range than criticality-enhanced protocols and also applies to one- and two-axis countertwisting interactions and chaotic dynamics.
AI.conclusion: The proposed scrambling-integrated scheme offers a distinct advantage in applicability over a wider parameter range and provides a new perspective for advancing nonlinear-dynamics-based enhancement of parameter estimation precision in quantum systems.

title: Optical Detection of Coherent Nuclear Spin Control in a Molecular System at Room Temperature
summary: Molecular systems with optically addressable electron spins are emerging as versatile quantum sensing platforms, offering tunable qubit properties and molecular-scale spatial control. Owing to their longer lifetimes, coupled nuclear spins provide an attractive resource for enhancing sensing performance. For molecular spin systems, the ability to initialise, coherently control and readout nuclear spins at room temperature is crucial for realising such benefits. Here, we present the first optical detection of nuclear magnetic resonance and coherent nuclear spin control with a molecular system at room temperature. Specifically, we demonstrate optically detected Rabi oscillations of $^{14}$N nuclear spins in the photoexcited triplet state of the organic chromophore 6,13-diazapentacene. The strong hyperfine coupling between the electronic spin and $^{14}$N nuclei enhances the nuclear Rabi frequency, enabling fast coherent nuclear-spin rotations. This work lays the foundation for leveraging nuclear spins as memories for enhanced molecular-based quantum sensing.

AI.tldr: First room-temperature optical detection of NMR and coherent nuclear spin control in a molecular system, demonstrated via optically detected Rabi oscillations of 14N nuclear spins in the photoexcited triplet state of 6,13-diazapentacene.
AI.motivation: Molecular systems with optically addressable electron spins are emerging quantum sensing platforms, and coupled nuclear spins offer longer lifetimes that could enhance sensing performance. However, realizing these benefits in molecular spin systems requires the ability to initialize, coherently control, and read out nuclear spins at room temperature.
AI.method: Optical detection of nuclear magnetic resonance combined with coherent nuclear spin control using a molecular system at room temperature. Optically detected Rabi oscillations of 14N nuclear spins are measured in the photoexcited triplet state of the organic chromophore 6,13-diazapentacene.
AI.result: Optically detected Rabi oscillations of 14N nuclear spins were achieved at room temperature. Strong hyperfine coupling between the electronic spin and 14N nuclei enhances the nuclear Rabi frequency, enabling fast coherent nuclear-spin rotations.
AI.conclusion: This work lays the foundation for leveraging nuclear spins as quantum memories for enhanced molecular-based quantum sensing.

title: Architecting Instruction Execution for Scalable Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing
summary: Scaling fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC) requires orchestrating millions of operations continuously across a tightly coupled classical-quantum control stack. A critical challenge in this orchestration is determining the optimal hardware-software boundary, i.e., the Quantum Instruction Set Architecture (QISA). We focus on cryogenic, fixed-connectivity qubit platforms, such as superconducting and topological Majorana qubits. For these, existing QISA choices either operate at too low a level, violating cryogenic thermal budgets at scale, or at too high a level, imposing unrealizable complexity on the control engine. To reason about these tradeoffs, we introduce the ARIES instruction set hierarchy, which categorizes QISAs into distinct abstraction levels. To systematically evaluate these levels, we develop an end-to-end evaluation toolflow featuring a cycle-accurate classical driver and hardware engine simulator. Using eight quantum applications across superconducting and topological qubit platforms, we measure instruction bandwidth, transceiver power dissipation, and measurement processing overheads. We demonstrate that while physical-level abstractions exceed the thermal limits of dilution refrigerators by orders of magnitude, canonical-level abstractions significantly underestimate hardware routing congestion and execution runtimes. Our Level 4 QISA (local logical operations) offers an optimal architectural balance. As quantum hardware platforms scale toward FTQC in the coming years, our findings provide concrete architectural guidance for the design of their classical control stacks and instruction interfaces.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the ARIES instruction set hierarchy for categorizing Quantum Instruction Set Architectures (QISAs) and an end-to-end evaluation toolflow to identify the optimal hardware-software boundary for cryogenic, fixed-connectivity qubit platforms scaling toward fault-tolerant quantum computing.
AI.motivation: Scaling FTQC requires orchestrating millions of operations continuously across a tightly coupled classical-quantum control stack. A critical challenge is determining the optimal QISA boundary. For cryogenic, fixed-connectivity platforms (superconducting, topological Majorana qubits), existing QISA choices are flawed: they either operate at too low a level, violating cryogenic thermal budgets at scale, or at too high a level, imposing unrealizable complexity on the control engine. A principled framework is needed to reason about these tradeoffs.
AI.method: The authors introduce the ARIES instruction set hierarchy, categorizing QISAs into distinct abstraction levels. To evaluate them systematically, they develop an end-to-end evaluation toolflow with a cycle-accurate classical driver and hardware engine simulator. They assess eight quantum applications across superconducting and topological qubit platforms, measuring instruction bandwidth, transceiver power dissipation, and measurement processing overheads.
AI.result: Physical-level abstractions exceed the thermal limits of dilution refrigerators by orders of magnitude, while canonical-level abstractions significantly underestimate hardware routing congestion and execution runtimes. The Level 4 QISA (local logical operations) offers an optimal architectural balance.
AI.conclusion: The Level 4 QISA provides optimal architectural balance for cryogenic, fixed-connectivity platforms. As quantum hardware scales toward FTQC, these findings offer concrete architectural guidance for designing classical control stacks and instruction interfaces.

title: Cyclotomic Structure and Exact Recurrences in Floquet Many-Body Quantum Dynamics
summary: Periodically driven quantum systems exhibit a wide range of complex dynamics, including chaos. Yet, at special parameter values, their evolution can recur exactly. Several quantum protocols have recently been proposed that exploit exact Floquet recurrences to demonstrate genuine quantum advantage. Such recurrences can be studied through the arithmetic structure of the Floquet unitary. In this work, we establish a necessary and sufficient arithmetic criterion for exact recurrence and determine the minimal recurrence period when one exists. Because recurrence is a global property of the unitary, it holds for every initial state. Applying our framework requires only knowledge of the number field associated with the Hamiltonian parameters. We demonstrate the method using the kicked Ising chain, establishing exact recurrences in both Clifford and non-Clifford regimes. We further show that, in the recurrent non-Clifford regime, magic--a resource for quantum computation--is generated at intermediate times and undergoes exact periodic revivals enforced by the recurrence of the full Floquet unitary. By connecting number theory, quantum many-body dynamics, and quantum information, our work shows that exact recurrence extends beyond Clifford circuits and opens new avenues for magic generation and quantum hardware benchmarking.

AI.tldr: The paper establishes a necessary and sufficient arithmetic criterion for exact Floquet recurrence and identifies the minimal recurrence period, using number fields associated with Hamiltonian parameters. It applies this to the kicked Ising chain, finding exact recurrences in both Clifford and non-Clifford regimes, and shows that in the recurrent non-Clifford regime, magic is generated at intermediate times and undergoes exact periodic revivals.
AI.motivation: Periodically driven quantum systems can exhibit exact recurrences at special parameter values, and several quantum protocols exploit these recurrences for quantum advantage. However, a complete characterization of when exact recurrence occurs and how to determine the minimal recurrence period was lacking.
AI.method: The authors analyze the arithmetic structure of the Floquet unitary, establishing a necessary and sufficient arithmetic criterion for exact recurrence based on the number field associated with the Hamiltonian parameters, and derive the minimal recurrence period when one exists.
AI.result: The framework yields exact recurrences in the kicked Ising chain for both Clifford and non-Clifford regimes; in the recurrent non-Clifford regime, magic is generated at intermediate times and exhibits exact periodic revivals driven by the recurrence of the full Floquet unitary.
AI.conclusion: Exact recurrence is a global property valid for every initial state and extends beyond Clifford circuits; the number-theoretic framework connects number theory, quantum many-body dynamics, and quantum information, offering new avenues for magic generation and quantum hardware benchmarking.

title: On the Computational Complexity of Blind Quantum Machine Learning
summary:
Can quantum advantages in computational efficiency coexist with quantum advantages in privacy? In this paper, we construct and use MasonQ, a universal brickwork transpiler, to answer this question with a resounding yes. We approach this question by bridging two seemingly disparate paradigms: universal blind quantum computation (UBQC), based on measurement-based quantum computation, and quantum machine learning (QML) algorithms such as the Harrow-Hassidim-Lloyd (HHL) algorithm and quantum recommendation systems.
  We provide new upper bounds on the depth of UBQC brickwork graphs, establishing that $D = \mathcal{O}(ωn)$, where $ω$ is the circuit width and $n$ its computational gate complexity. This is enabled by our newly developed transpiler MasonQ, which maps arbitrary quantum circuits to computational brickwork graph states. Given an optimal Qiskit circuit as input, we prove optimality (up to logarithmic corrections) of the MasonQ transpiler in terms of asymptotic scaling of the total brickwork graph width and depth after decomposition into bricks, enabling systematic cost analyses of blind implementations in near-term experiments and asymptotic regimes.
  Leveraging MasonQ, we derive depth bounds for several representative blind quantum machine learning (B-QML) algorithms, including the quantum Fourier transform, the HHL algorithm, recommendation systems, and quantum transformers. Lastly, we analyze concrete resource estimates for near-term demonstrations of blind quantum machine learning. We propose a minimal B-QML implementation requiring only a $12$ qubit quantum server.
  To the best of our knowledge, MasonQ is the first functional and optimal universal circuit-to-brickwork-graph transpiler to implement the full brickwork transpilation process from first principles.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces MasonQ, a universal circuit-to-brickwork-graph transpiler, and uses it to show that quantum advantages in computational efficiency and privacy can coexist, providing depth bounds for blind quantum machine learning algorithms and near-term resource estimates.
AI.motivation: The central question is whether quantum computational-efficiency advantages can coexist with quantum privacy advantages. The authors aim to bridge two seemingly disparate paradigms: universal blind quantum computation (UBQC), grounded in measurement-based quantum computation, and quantum machine learning (QML) algorithms such as HHL and quantum recommendation systems.
AI.method: They construct and employ MasonQ, a universal brickwork transpiler that maps arbitrary quantum circuits to computational brickwork graph states. They derive new upper bounds on the depth of UBQC brickwork graphs, establishing D = O(ωn), where ω is the circuit width and n the computational gate complexity. Given an optimal Qiskit circuit, they prove optimality (up to logarithmic corrections) of MasonQ in terms of asymptotic scaling of total brickwork graph width and depth after decomposition into bricks. They then apply MasonQ to derive depth bounds for representative blind QML (B-QML) algorithms—quantum Fourier transform, HHL, recommendation systems, and quantum transformers—and analyze concrete near-term resource estimates.
AI.result: MasonQ yields the depth bound D = O(ωn) for UBQC brickwork graphs and is proven optimal up to logarithmic corrections in asymptotic width and depth scaling. Applying it to B-QML algorithms produces depth bounds for QFT, HHL, recommendation systems, and quantum transformers. Resource analysis identifies a minimal B-QML implementation requiring only a 12-qubit quantum server.
AI.conclusion: Quantum advantages in computational efficiency and privacy can coexist, answered affirmatively. MasonQ is, to the authors' knowledge, the first functional and optimal universal circuit-to-brickwork-graph transpiler implementing the full brickwork transpilation process from first principles, enabling systematic cost analyses of blind implementations in near-term and asymptotic regimes.

title: Programmable Floquet Response for Quantum Sensing
summary: Quantum sensing is typically based on phase accumulation and is therefore fundamentally tied to the coherence time of the sensing system. Here we introduce an alternative sensing paradigm based on programmable Floquet locking in periodically driven two-level systems. We show that periodic control generates an effective Floquet locking field whose orientation and amplitude depend on global offset, allowing information to be encoded in the driven population relaxation dynamics, not in the integrated phase. By controlling transfer between distinct Floquet locking manifolds, external perturbations can be mapped onto engineered relaxation responses whose characteristics are programmable through the driving sequence. We numerically demonstrate this approach for both DC and frequency-selective AC sensing, and show that temporal encoding of the response can provide enhanced precision in the presence of slow instrumental fluctuations. These results illustrate the potential of programmable Floquet responses and open the way to exploring new sensing strategies in driven quantum systems.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a quantum sensing paradigm based on programmable Floquet locking in periodically driven two-level systems, encoding information in driven population relaxation dynamics rather than accumulated phase, and demonstrates enhanced precision for DC and AC sensing.
AI.motivation: Conventional quantum sensing relies on phase accumulation, which is fundamentally limited by the coherence time of the sensing system. This coherence constraint motivates the search for alternative sensing paradigms that decouple sensing performance from coherence time.
AI.method: The authors introduce programmable Floquet locking in periodically driven two-level systems. Periodic control generates an effective Floquet locking field whose orientation and amplitude depend on the global offset. Information is encoded in the driven population relaxation dynamics instead of the integrated phase. By controlling transfer between distinct Floquet locking manifolds, external perturbations are mapped onto engineered relaxation responses programmable via the driving sequence.
AI.result: Numerical demonstrations show the approach works for both DC and frequency-selective AC sensing. Temporal encoding of the response provides enhanced precision in the presence of slow instrumental fluctuations.
AI.conclusion: The results illustrate the potential of programmable Floquet responses and open the way to exploring new sensing strategies in driven quantum systems.

title: Bosonic unstructured search: quantum enhancement without entanglement
summary: We consider unstructured search using multimode bosonic quantum systems under energy constraints. The task is to locate an unknown marked mode among $N$ possibilities using arbitrary control, subject to a time-averaged mean-boson-number budget $n_{\text{b}}\gg 1$. We analyze a continuous-time phase-shift oracle of strength $B_{0}$, with cost given by the total oracle time, and a discrete oracle with fixed phase $φ_{0}$, with cost given by the number of queries. We give algorithms that identify the target with query complexity $O(\sqrt{N}/{n_{\text{b}}}B_{0})$ for continuous-time oracles or $O(\sqrt{N}/n_{\text{b}} |{\sin(φ_{0}/{2})}|)$ for discrete oracles with $n_{\text{b}} |{\sin(φ_{0}/{2})}|=O(1)$. In contrast, for discrete oracles with $n_{\text{b}} |{\sin(φ_{0}/{2})}|=Ω(1)$, we provide an algorithm using $O(\max\{1,\sqrt{N/n_{\text{b}}|{\sin(φ_{0}/{2})}|}\})$ queries. We also prove matching lower bounds on the query complexity, showing that these algorithms are asymptotically optimal. Furthermore, we show that, in the absence of loss, non-Gaussianity is necessary to achieve the optimal joint query scaling in $N$ and $n_{\text{b}}$, but entanglement is not. Under uniform boson loss at rate $γ$, we prove a query lower bound of $Ω( γN / n _{\text{b}} B_{0}^{2} )$, attained for $γ= Ω(B_{0} \sqrt{n _{\text{b}}/N})$ using coherent-state probes. Finally, we propose experimental implementations using multipass optical microscopy or superconducting circuits as potential routes to speeding up imaging or device calibration with a low boson-number budget.

AI.tldr: The paper studies unstructured search with multimode bosonic quantum systems under a mean-boson-number budget, derives asymptotically optimal query-complexity algorithms and matching lower bounds for continuous-time and discrete oracles, examines non-Gaussianity/entanglement requirements and loss effects, and proposes experimental implementations.
AI.motivation: Unstructured search is a central quantum-information primitive, but its behavior in bosonic systems constrained by finite energy and photon loss is less understood. The authors aim to characterize how a time-averaged mean-boson-number budget affects the optimal search cost and what physical resources are required for achieving the best joint scaling in the number of modes and the boson budget.
AI.method: The task is to identify an unknown marked mode among N possibilities using arbitrary bosonic control. Two oracle models are analyzed: a continuous-time phase-shift oracle of strength B0, with cost equal to total oracle time, and a discrete oracle of fixed phase φ0, with cost equal to the number of queries. Algorithms are constructed and accompanied by matching lower bounds. The role of non-Gaussianity and entanglement is studied in the lossless case, and uniform boson loss at rate γ is analyzed, with a coherent-state protocol attaining the lossy lower bound in a specified regime.
AI.result: For continuous-time oracles the query complexity is O(√N/(n_b B0)); for discrete oracles with n_b|sin(φ0/2)|=O(1) it is O(√N/(n_b|sin(φ0/2)|)), whereas for n_b|sin(φ0/2)|=Ω(1) an algorithm uses O(max{1,√(N/(n_b|sin(φ0/2)|))}) queries. Matching lower bounds establish asymptotic optimality. Without loss, non-Gaussianity is necessary for optimal joint query scaling in N and n_b, while entanglement is not. Under uniform loss at rate γ, a lower bound Ω(γN/(n_b B0^2)) is proved, attained for γ=Ω(B0√(n_b/N)) using coherent-state probes.
AI.conclusion: Energy-constrained bosonic unstructured search admits asymptotically optimal algorithms whose scaling depends on whether the oracle is continuous-time or discrete. Non-Gaussianity is a necessary resource for optimal joint scaling, but entanglement is not; loss imposes a fundamental query lower bound that coherent states can saturate in a certain regime. The results suggest experimental routes via multipass optical microscopy or superconducting circuits for low-boson-budget imaging and device calibration.

title: Fractional and quantum Latin squares: real solutions of quantum 36 officers problem
summary: A Latin square can be extended by replacing its symbols with probabilities or quantum states. We relate these two extensions through explicit examples, from classical and fractional Latin squares to quantum Latin squares and a real solution of Euler's quantum 36 officers problem. A simultaneous cyclic-shift ansatz on a four-torus of tensor coefficients gives a real absolutely maximally entangled (AME) state of four six-level systems. A local orthogonal change of basis yields a representative with 96 nonzero amplitudes. Two single-party arrays obtained from the corresponding quantum orthogonal Latin square yield fractional Latin squares. Signs matter: comparison with the independent real construction of Bruzda and its sign variant distinguishes three local-unitary classes, two of which have identical probabilities. We extend this probability representation to existing seven- and nine-party AME states with six levels each. Their amplitude matrices reveal 48 complex Hadamard blocks of order $3^3$ and six of order $6^4$, respectively. These constructions separate what can be read from a probability picture from the coherent conditions responsible for maximal entanglement.

AI.tldr: This paper connects classical/fractional Latin squares, quantum Latin squares, and absolutely maximally entangled (AME) states, giving a real AME state of four six-level systems via a cyclic-shift ansatz and analyzing its local-unitary classes and probability picture.
AI.motivation: Latin squares can be extended by replacing symbols with probabilities (fractional Latin squares) or quantum states (quantum Latin squares). The paper aims to relate these two extensions explicitly and to use them to construct and characterize AME states, especially real solutions of Euler's quantum 36 officers problem, distinguishing coherent conditions from probability-level information.
AI.method: A simultaneous cyclic-shift ansatz on a four-torus of tensor coefficients is used to construct a real AME state of four six-level systems. A local orthogonal basis change yields a representative with 96 nonzero amplitudes. Single-party arrays from the corresponding quantum orthogonal Latin square give fractional Latin squares. Comparisons with Bruzda's independent real construction and its sign variant are used to distinguish local-unitary classes. The probability representation is extended to existing seven- and nine-party six-level AME states.
AI.result: The construction produces a real AME state of four six-level systems, with a 96-nonzero-amplitude representative after local orthogonal change of basis. Two single-party arrays yield fractional Latin squares. Sign choices distinguish three local-unitary classes, two sharing identical probabilities. The probability representation extended to seven- and nine-party six-level AME states reveals 48 complex Hadamard blocks of order 3^3 and six of order 6^4, respectively.
AI.conclusion: The results separate what can be inferred from a probability picture from the coherent conditions responsible for maximal entanglement, clarifying the relationship between fractional Latin squares, quantum Latin squares, and AME states across four-, seven-, and nine-party six-level systems.

title: Moving quantum sensors
summary: We investigate whether controlled motion of a quantum sensor offers a metrological advantage in a field-detection task. We consider a localized field of known strength $B$ occupying an unknown contiguous region making up a fraction $1/N$ of the total search space, with a qubit sensor controlled for a total time $T$ to maximize the probability of detecting the field. We study the regime in which the characteristic timescale of the field is slow compared to the time to move the sensor between any two regions, and we distinguish classical motion, where the sensor follows a definite trajectory, from quantum motion, where the sensor can be in a coherent superposition of locations. For a single classically moving sensor, we derive an optimal multi-stop protocol and obtain the exact maximum detection probability. Allowing coherent spatial superposition maps the single-sensor problem onto Hamiltonian search and reduces the interrogation time for successfully detecting the field from $Θ(N/B)$ to $Θ(\sqrt{N}/B)$. We then extend the problem to $M$ sensors and identify a hierarchy of optimal time scalings for constant success probability determined by the available spatial and inter-sensor quantum resources. Unentangled coherently moving sensors achieve $T=Θ(\sqrt{N/M}/B)$ by searching disjoint regions in parallel, while entanglement among the sensors can further enhance the effective field coupling and achieve $T=Θ(\sqrt{N}/(MB))$. Matching lower bounds establish the optimality of these scalings in the presence of arbitrary controls and ancilla systems. Our results separate the roles of classical motion, spatial coherence, and entanglement in spatial field detection.

AI.tldr: Optimal quantum search for a localized field: classically moving qubit needs Θ(N/B) time, coherent spatial superposition reduces it to Θ(√N/B) (Hamiltonian search), and with M sensors, unentangled sensors reach Θ(√(N/M)/B) while entangled sensors reach Θ(√N/(MB)), with matching lower bounds proving optimality.
AI.motivation: To determine whether controlled motion of a quantum sensor confers a metrological advantage in field detection, and to disentangle the distinct roles of classical motion, spatial coherence, and entanglement in spatial field detection.
AI.method: Model a localized known-strength field B occupying an unknown contiguous region of fraction 1/N of the search space, detected by a qubit sensor controlled over total time T. Work in the slow-field regime (field timescale ≫ inter-region travel time). Derive an optimal multi-stop protocol for a single classically moving sensor; map the coherent-superposition case onto Hamiltonian search; extend to M sensors and derive matching lower bounds under arbitrary controls and ancilla systems.
AI.result: Exact maximum detection probability for the single classically moving sensor. Coherent superposition reduces interrogation time from Θ(N/B) to Θ(√N/B). For M sensors: unentangled coherent motion yields T=Θ(√(N/M)/B) via parallel disjoint-region search, and entanglement enhances effective field coupling to T=Θ(√N/(MB)). Matching lower bounds confirm optimality.
AI.conclusion: Quantum resources yield provable metrological advantages: spatial coherence alone upgrades classical search to Hamiltonian-search scaling, and inter-sensor entanglement further improves time scaling. The results cleanly separate the contributions of classical motion, spatial coherence, and entanglement.

title: Error-Corrected QRAM Queries with One-Fault-Tolerant \texttt{CSWAP} Gates
summary: Quantum random-access memory (QRAM) enables coherent queries to classical data. However, the \(O(N)\) qubits required for a memory with \(N=2^n\) addresses make QRAM appear vulnerable to noise. Though bucket-brigade routing provides intrinsic noise resilience to reduce the error in QRAM, improving the fidelity of QRAM queries is still an important and challenging problem. We introduce a low-overhead protection framework for bucket-brigade QRAM with two complementary components. First, we propose a one-fault-tolerant repeat-until-success logical controlled-SWAP gate using the \([[4,2,2]]\) code under erasure noise channel. Interleaved erasure checks and local recovery correct every single erasure, so the leading logical failure probability is second order in the physical erasure error rates. Second, we exploit validity constraints of bucket-brigade routing to define local parity checks directly on the router states, without adding extra data qubits to create code redundancy. Under bit-flip noise, minimum-weight perfect matching with noiseless syndrome measurements corrects single interior faults, while open spatial boundaries retain a first-order contribution in the residual bit-flip rate. Monte Carlo simulations confirm quadratic suppression for the protected controlled-SWAP and improved depth scaling for decoded QRAM router-state snapshots. The two codes admit a concatenated realization in which the inner code supplies erasure protection and the outer code optionally corrects interior logical bit flips. Together, these results show how routing constraints and a protected non-Clifford routing gate can improve QRAM reliability under biased and erasure-dominant noise.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a low-overhead two-component protection framework for bucket-brigade QRAM, combining a one-fault-tolerant logical controlled-SWAP gate with routing-constraint-based parity checks.
AI.motivation: QRAM requires O(N) qubits for N=2^n addresses, making it vulnerable to noise; although bucket-brigade routing offers intrinsic noise resilience, improving QRAM query fidelity remains an important and challenging problem.
AI.method: The framework has two complementary codes: (1) a one-fault-tolerant repeat-until-success logical controlled-SWAP gate using the [[4,2,2]] code under erasure noise, with interleaved erasure checks and local recovery; (2) local parity checks defined directly on router states via validity constraints of bucket-brigade routing, avoiding extra data qubits, decoded by minimum-weight perfect matching with noiseless syndrome measurements. The two codes admit a concatenated realization (inner code for erasure protection, outer code optionally for interior logical bit flips).
AI.result: Under erasure noise, the leading logical failure probability is second order in physical erasure rates (every single erasure corrected). Under bit-flip noise, single interior faults are corrected, while open spatial boundaries retain a first-order contribution in residual bit-flip rate. Monte Carlo simulations confirm quadratic suppression for the protected controlled-SWAP and improved depth scaling for decoded QRAM router-state snapshots.
AI.conclusion: Routing constraints combined with a protected non-Clifford routing gate can improve QRAM reliability under biased and erasure-dominant noise.

title: Fermionic non-Gaussianity via computable measures and experimentally accessible bounds
summary: Interacting fermions owe both their non-trivial correlations and their computational power to their departure from Gaussianity. Yet, quantifying that departure geometrically faces two challenges: the Gaussian manifold is non-convex, and perturbative treatments are confined to weak interactions. Here, we introduce a geometric measure of fermionic non-Gaussianity, the fidelity distance of a target state to the manifold of fermionic Gaussian states. We construct an iteration formalism to numerically access it, applicable also at strong coupling. Further, we prove a sharpened operator Jensen inequality, of interest in its own right. We use it to derive a witness that involves only two- and four-point fermionic correlators. Numerical benchmarks on the one-dimensional Fermi--Hubbard model show that the quality of the witness improves with system size and, for strong coupling, is tighter than antiflatness. Our results open a scalable route to charting non-Gaussianity of strongly-interacting fermionic quantum simulators.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a geometric measure of fermionic non-Gaussianity defined as the fidelity distance from a target state to the manifold of fermionic Gaussian states, with an iteration formalism to compute it even at strong coupling, and a two- and four-point correlator witness derived from a sharpened operator Jensen inequality.
AI.motivation: Interacting fermions derive their non-trivial correlations and computational power from departing from Gaussianity, but quantifying this departure geometrically is hard because the Gaussian manifold is non-convex and perturbative methods only work for weak interactions.
AI.method: The authors define a geometric measure (fidelity distance to the fermionic Gaussian state manifold), construct an iteration formalism to numerically access it applicable at strong coupling, and prove a sharpened operator Jensen inequality used to derive a witness involving only two- and four-point fermionic correlators.
AI.result: Numerical benchmarks on the one-dimensional Fermi–Hubbard model show the witness quality improves with system size and, at strong coupling, is tighter than antiflatness.
AI.conclusion: The results provide a scalable route to charting non-Gaussianity in strongly-interacting fermionic quantum simulators.

title: Quantum Reference Frames in terms of Tetrads
summary:
We adapt to the context of quantum theory the treatment, familiar in relativity theory, of a reference frame as a tetrad. Since a tetrad is a set of four orthonormal vectors at a spacetime point, it encodes a timelike direction, three orthogonal spatial directions, and units; and so it gives a configuration in spacetime (a spatial orientation and state of motion) of an idealized infinitesimal apparatus (``rulers and a clock"). So a natural ``first guess" is that the state of a quantum reference frame should be an assignment of complex amplitudes to a set of tetrads. We develop this idea, in terms of bundles over spacetime of bases of the tangent spaces.
  This paper is a companion to two other papers. It emphasises the main conceptual aspects of our proposal, while the other two papers give physical details. It also explains the main contrast between those two papers. Namely: (i) the first considers a single spacetime geometry, so that a quantum reference frame, on our proposal, gives a superposition of perspectives on that geometry; while (ii) the second considers the spacetime manifold with no geometry given a priori, which will imply that a quantum reference frame, on our proposal, can describe a superposition of perspectives on a superposition of geometries---not ``just" a superposition of perspectives on a single geometry. The main mathematical idea for representing this contrast will be choosing between (i) the orthonormal frame bundle, for a given spacetime geometry; (ii) the frame bundle in the usual sense of containing all bases of all spacetime points' tangent spaces.

AI.tldr: This companion paper presents the conceptual core of a proposal treating a quantum reference frame as a quantum state over tetrads, formulated via bundles of tangent-space bases over spacetime, and contrasts two frameworks: superpositions of perspectives on a single geometry versus on a superposition of geometries.
AI.motivation: Relativity theory already treats a reference frame as a tetrad (four orthonormal vectors encoding a timelike direction, three spatial directions, and units), which gives the configuration of an idealized infinitesimal apparatus of rulers and a clock. The paper's motivation is to adapt this familiar tetrad treatment to quantum theory, so as to give a principled notion of a quantum reference frame, and to clarify the conceptual differences between two companion papers that develop the physical details.
AI.method: The authors take a "first guess" that the state of a quantum reference frame is an assignment of complex amplitudes to a set of tetrads, since a tetrad encodes an orientation and state of motion of an infinitesimal apparatus. They develop this idea in terms of bundles over spacetime of bases of the tangent spaces. To represent the contrast between the two companion papers, they choose between (i) the orthonormal frame bundle for a given spacetime geometry and (ii) the frame bundle in the usual sense, containing all bases of all spacetime points' tangent spaces.
AI.result: The conceptual analysis yields a clear contrast: (i) the first companion paper considers a single spacetime geometry, so a quantum reference frame gives a superposition of perspectives on that geometry; (ii) the second companion paper considers the spacetime manifold with no geometry given a priori, so a quantum reference frame can describe a superposition of perspectives on a superposition of geometries—not merely a superposition of perspectives on a single geometry. The mathematical vehicle for this contrast is the choice between the orthonormal frame bundle and the general frame bundle.
AI.conclusion: A quantum reference frame is naturally modeled as a quantum state over tetrads, expressed through bundles of tangent-space bases. The choice of bundle—orthonormal frame bundle versus the general frame bundle—encodes whether one is dealing with superpositions of perspectives on a single geometry or on a superposition of geometries. This paper emphasizes the main conceptual aspects, while the two companion papers supply the physical details.

title: Quantum Cryptography and Autoformalization in Lean
summary: Quantum key distribution provides secure communication by relying on physics principles and mathematical reasoning. Security proofs across the field can contain gaps, often between individually valid theorems integrated under mismatched assumptions. We produce an end-to-end security theorem formalized in the Lean proof assistant, eliminating hidden hypotheses by building only on Lean's standard axioms. Our proof covers composable security of the entanglement-based qubit BB84 protocol against coherent attacks by the postselection technique, accounting for finite block size, and is written in a language that enforces local operations and classical communication to help ensure a faithful representation of the protocol. The proof itself was enabled by LLM-based autoformalization, and with the proof complete, we used the same pipeline as a discovery machine, reducing the finite-size penalty on the key rate. Our work sets a reproducible standard for security arguments in quantum cryptography and shows how formal proof engines can accelerate discovery across quantum information science.

AI.tldr: The paper delivers an end-to-end, machine-checked security proof of the entanglement-based qubit BB84 quantum key distribution protocol in the Lean proof assistant, relying only on standard axioms, and uses the formalization pipeline to improve the finite-size key rate.
AI.motivation: Security proofs in quantum key distribution can harbor gaps where individually valid theorems are combined under mismatched assumptions, leaving hidden hypotheses that undermine end-to-end guarantees. The authors aim to eliminate such hidden assumptions and establish a rigorous, reproducible standard for security arguments in quantum cryptography.
AI.method: They formalize a complete security theorem in the Lean proof assistant, building solely on Lean's standard axioms. The proof covers composable security of the entanglement-based qubit BB84 protocol against coherent attacks via the postselection technique, accounts for finite block size, and is expressed in a language that enforces local operations and classical communication to faithfully represent the protocol. LLM-based autoformalization enabled the proof, and the same pipeline was then used as a discovery tool.
AI.result: The work produces an end-to-end, gap-free formalized security theorem for the protocol, and the formalization pipeline reduced the finite-size penalty on the key rate.
AI.conclusion: The paper sets a reproducible standard for security arguments in quantum cryptography and demonstrates that formal proof engines can accelerate discovery across quantum information science.

title: Ghost unitaries for loss-resilient photonic resource-state generation
summary: Entangled few-photon states, such as Bell and Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ) states, are central resources for discrete-variable photonic quantum information processing. In many architectures, these states are generated probabilistically by first heralding single photons from biphoton sources and then interfering them in linear-optical circuits. In this work, we show that the entanglement structure of said biphoton sources can be directly exploited for noise-engineering to deliver higher quality resource states. Using the transpose identity of multi-mode squeezed vacuum states, we introduce "ghost-unitary" implementations in which the target resource-generation interferometer is applied to the heralding modes rather than to the delivered resource modes. When the dominant imperfection is interferometric loss, this relocation converts direct amplitude damping of the output into false-positive heralding events that require both higher-pair emission and photon loss. In the low-squeezing regime, these events are parametrically suppressed, yielding higher-fidelity conditional resource states. We analyze this mechanism for single-qubit states, two-photon NOON states, Bell states, and a family of $n$-qubit GHZ states, as well as for single-qubit teleportation and type-I-fusion-based resource growth. Across these examples, we delineate finite parameter regimes in which ghost-unitary implementations outperform direct implementations, with particular relevance to frequency-bin photonics where active linear-optical transformations can be relatively lossy. We also prove that, in the setting considered here, the direct implementation of the $n$-GHZ family delivers identically damped outputs: equivalent to the ideal state followed by uniform amplitude damping. This extends the known $n=2,3$ cases and provides a structural result of independent interest for photonic quantum information processing.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that the entanglement structure of biphoton sources can be exploited for noise-engineering: by moving the resource-generation interferometer onto the heralding modes ("ghost-unitary" implementation), interferometric loss is converted into false-positive heralding events that are parametrically suppressed in the low-squeezing regime, yielding higher-fidelity conditional few-photon entangled states.
AI.motivation: Entangled few-photon states (Bell, GHZ) are key resources for discrete-variable photonic quantum information processing, but in typical architectures they are generated probabilistically by heralding single photons from biphoton sources and interfering them in linear-optical circuits. Interferometric loss limits the fidelity of these conditionally prepared resource states, and there is a need for schemes that mitigate this dominant imperfection without changing the underlying resource-generation circuit.
AI.method: Using the transpose identity of multi-mode squeezed vacuum states, the authors introduce "ghost-unitary" implementations where the target resource-generation interferometer is applied to the heralding modes instead of the delivered resource modes. They analyze how interferometric loss, which normally produces direct amplitude damping of the output, is relocated into false-positive heralding events requiring both higher-pair emission and photon loss. They study this mechanism for single-qubit states, two-photon NOON states, Bell states, a family of n-qubit GHZ states, single-qubit teleportation, and type-I-fusion-based resource growth, comparing ghost-unitary versus direct implementations across finite parameter regimes.
AI.result: False-positive heralding events arising from relocated interferometric loss are parametrically suppressed in the low-squeezing regime, delivering higher-fidelity conditional resource states. Finite parameter regimes are identified in which ghost-unitary implementations outperform direct implementations, with particular relevance to frequency-bin photonics where active linear-optical transformations are relatively lossy. Additionally, the authors prove that direct implementation of the n-GHZ family yields identically damped outputs—equivalent to the ideal state followed by uniform amplitude damping—extending the known n=2,3 cases.
AI.conclusion: Relocating the resource-generation interferometer to the heralding modes via ghost-unitary implementations provides a practical noise-engineering route to higher-quality photonic resource states, especially for frequency-bin platforms with lossy active linear optics. The structural result on uniform amplitude damping of n-GHZ states is of independent interest for photonic quantum information processing.

title: Optical interferometric tools for probing memory effects
summary: Recent efforts to detect non-Markovian memory have become increasingly important, motivated by the broad relevance of memory effects in quantum information processing, metrology, and thermodynamic engines. Here, we show that interferometric methods, particularly the phase shift and visibility, provide an experimentally accessible framework for probing environmental effects and witnessing non-Markovian dynamics. Specifically, suitably constructed witness operators enable the detection of non-Markovianity through measurable phase shifts in the interference pattern. Furthermore, we prove that the interferometric visibility is monotonically non-increasing under incoherent CP-divisible (Markovian) dynamics. Consequently, any revival of the optimized visibility constitutes a sufficient signature of information backflow and hence non-Markovianity. The effectiveness of the proposed phase-based and visibility approaches is illustrated for representative examples of non-Markovian dynamics. Our results offer a simple and experimentally feasible framework for probing memory effects, with potential applications in quantum sensing and noisy intermediate-scale quantum devices.

AI.tldr: The paper presents interferometric methods—phase shift and visibility—as experimentally accessible witnesses of non-Markovian quantum dynamics, proving that visibility is monotonically non-increasing under incoherent CP-divisible dynamics so that visibility revival signals information backflow.
AI.motivation: Detecting non-Markovian memory is increasingly important because memory effects are broadly relevant to quantum information processing, metrology, and thermodynamic engines. A simple, experimentally feasible framework for probing environmental effects and witnessing non-Markovian dynamics is therefore desired.
AI.method: The authors employ interferometric techniques, specifically measurable phase shifts and visibility of the interference pattern, and construct suitable witness operators. They prove a monotonicity property of interferometric visibility under incoherent CP-divisible (Markovian) dynamics and illustrate the phase-based and visibility-based approaches on representative non-Markovian examples.
AI.result: Suitably constructed witness operators detect non-Markovianity via measurable phase shifts in the interference pattern. Interferometric visibility is monotonically non-increasing under incoherent CP-divisible dynamics, so any revival of the optimized visibility is a sufficient signature of information backflow and thus non-Markovianity. The approaches are shown to work on representative non-Markovian dynamics.
AI.conclusion: The results provide a simple and experimentally feasible framework for probing memory effects, with potential applications in quantum sensing and noisy intermediate-scale quantum devices.

title: Krylov Complexity and Quantum Many-body Scars in Non-Hermitian Kinetically Constrained Models
summary: Thermalization in closed quantum systems and its breakdown are central to understanding the emergence of statistical behavior in isolated many-body systems. Kinetic constraints can hinder thermalization by restricting the allowed dynamics and giving rise to non-ergodic behavior. While various aspects of ergodicity breaking in kinetically constrained models have been extensively studied in Hermitian systems, their behavior in non-Hermitian kinetically constrained models remains less explored. In particular, the inequivalence of left and right eigenstate ensembles in non-Hermitian systems raises the question of whether they exhibit qualitatively different dynamical and eigenstate properties. In this work, we study non-Hermitian generalizations of the paradigmatic PXP and PPXPP models, focusing on their Krylov complexity, eigenstate structure, and dynamics. By exploiting the Arnoldi's algorithm, we find distinct behavior of Krylov complexity in the left and right eigenstate ensembles as non-Hermiticity is increased: in the right ensemble, it exhibits persistent oscillations with an increasing period, while in the left ensemble, it gradually saturates. The characteristic arch-shaped profile of the Arnoldi coefficients is also modified differently in the two ensembles, with a Hermitian-like arch re-emerging in the left ensemble at large non Hermiticity. Additionally, in the non-Hermitian PXP model, the right ensemble retains the characteristic scar structure, while the left ensemble develops additional non-scar eigenstates with anomalously low entanglement and large overlap with the vacuum state. These findings reveal that non-Hermiticity can affect Krylov dynamics and eigenstate structure differently in the left and right ensembles, demonstrating the need to treat them separately when characterizing non-Hermitian kinetically constrained systems.

AI.tldr: This work studies non-Hermitian generalizations of the PXP and PPXPP kinetically constrained models, showing that left and right eigenstate ensembles exhibit qualitatively different Krylov complexity, Arnoldi coefficient profiles, and eigenstate structures as non-Hermiticity increases.
AI.motivation: Kinetic constraints can hinder thermalization in closed quantum systems, and ergodicity breaking has been well studied in Hermitian kinetically constrained models. However, the non-Hermitian case is less explored, and the inequivalence of left and right eigenstate ensembles in non-Hermitian systems raises the question of whether they display qualitatively different dynamical and eigenstate properties.
AI.method: The authors study non-Hermitian generalizations of the paradigmatic PXP and PPXPP models, focusing on Krylov complexity, eigenstate structure, and dynamics, using Arnoldi's algorithm to analyze the left and right eigenstate ensembles.
AI.result: As non-Hermiticity increases, Krylov complexity behaves distinctly in the two ensembles: the right ensemble shows persistent oscillations with increasing period, while the left ensemble gradually saturates. The characteristic arch-shaped Arnoldi coefficient profile is modified differently, with a Hermitian-like arch re-emerging in the left ensemble at large non-Hermiticity. In the non-Hermitian PXP model, the right ensemble retains the scar structure, whereas the left ensemble develops additional non-scar eigenstates with anomalously low entanglement and large overlap with the vacuum state.
AI.conclusion: Non-Hermiticity affects Krylov dynamics and eigenstate structure differently in the left and right ensembles, demonstrating that these ensembles must be treated separately when characterizing non-Hermitian kinetically constrained systems.

title: Generating Superposition of Transverse Ising Ground States by Quantum Interaction
summary: We investigate superpositions of quantum Ising ground states generated through a quantum interaction, in which the nearest-neighbor coupling strength is promoted to an operator acting on a central auxiliary spin. We prepare the central spin in a superposition, which allows the chain to evolve coherently under different effective interaction strengths. The states are prepared by adiabatic evolution of the joint system comprising the central spin and the many-body spin chain, followed by a measurement on the central spin and post-selection of a specific outcome. It is possible to prepare superpositions of transverse-field quantum Ising ground states belonging to the three magnetic phases, namely, the paramagnetic, ferromagnetic, and anti-ferromagnetic phases. For a spin-1/2 central system, it is possible to prepare superpositions of ground states belonging to any two phases, while for the spin-1 case, the superpositions may contain three ground states, each belonging to one of the three phases. We analytically derive expressions for the magnetization, spin correlations, and entanglement of such states. The magnetization and spin correlations show distinct features in different superposition sectors. The nearest-neighbor entanglement is largest where the transverse field and Ising interaction compete, and its behavior differs from that of the magnetic observables. We also derive the quantum Fisher information relevant to estimating the Ising interaction strength. And it exhibits multiple peaks near the critical points of the constituent ground states, with the maximum value showing Heisenberg scaling, for the parameters and system sizes examined.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes preparing quantum superpositions of transverse-field Ising ground states from different magnetic phases via an auxiliary central spin, and analytically characterizes their magnetization, correlations, entanglement, and metrological quantum Fisher information.
AI.motivation: Ground states of the quantum Ising model belong to distinct magnetic phases (paramagnetic, ferromagnetic, anti-ferromagnetic). Creating coherent superpositions of ground states from different phases is physically intriguing and potentially useful for quantum technologies and metrology, motivating a scheme that controllably superposes such many-body states.
AI.method: The nearest-neighbor Ising coupling is promoted to an operator acting on a central auxiliary spin, which is prepared in a superposition so the chain evolves coherently under different effective interaction strengths. States are produced by adiabatic evolution of the joint central-spin-plus-chain system, followed by a measurement on the central spin and post-selection. Analytical expressions are derived for magnetization, spin correlations, nearest-neighbor entanglement, and quantum Fisher information for estimating the Ising interaction strength.
AI.result: Superpositions of Ising ground states spanning all three magnetic phases can be prepared: a spin-1/2 central system enables superpositions of any two phases, while a spin-1 central system enables superpositions of all three. Magnetization and spin correlations display distinct features across superposition sectors; nearest-neighbor entanglement is maximal where transverse field and Ising interaction compete and behaves differently from magnetic observables. The quantum Fisher information shows multiple peaks near the constituent critical points, with maximum value exhibiting Heisenberg scaling for the studied parameters and system sizes.
AI.conclusion: Auxiliary-spin-mediated adiabatic preparation with post-selection provides a viable route to phase superpositions of quantum Ising ground states, whose magnetic, entanglement, and metrological properties are analytically tractable and include Heisenberg-limited sensitivity near criticality.

title: Periodic-Pulse Control of Collective Emission and Photon Statistics in Interacting Quantum Emitters
summary: We investigate the collective emission spectra and photon correlations of two identical dipole-dipole-coupled emitters under continuous-wave (CW) and periodic pulsed driving. Our results show that a periodic train of instantaneous $π_x$ pulses can generate emission spectra whose dominant features closely resemble those obtained under CW excitation. We find that the structure of the collective emission spectra reflects the interplay among the resonance conditions, dipole-dipole coupling, and the inter-pulse delay $τ_D$. We further demonstrate that finite-duration $π_x$ pulses with sufficiently high Rabi frequencies can closely reproduce the ideal instantaneous-pulse limit. In contrast to the emission spectra, the photon correlations $g^{(2)}(t,τ)$ are governed primarily by $τ_D$ and, unlike under CW driving, become increasingly insensitive to the resonance conditions in the short-pulse limit. These results establish periodic pulsed driving as a versatile means of tailoring both the emission spectra and the photon statistics of coupled two-emitter systems.

AI.tldr: Periodic π_x pulse trains can reproduce CW-like collective emission spectra in two dipole-coupled emitters, while photon correlations are governed mainly by the inter-pulse delay and become insensitive to resonance conditions in the short-pulse limit.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to determine how periodic pulsed driving, compared with continuous-wave excitation, shapes the collective emission spectra and photon correlations of two identical dipole-dipole-coupled emitters, and whether pulsed driving can serve as a flexible control tool for their optical properties.
AI.method: The authors analyze two identical dipole-dipole-coupled emitters driven by continuous-wave (CW) excitation and by periodic trains of instantaneous π_x pulses. They also examine finite-duration π_x pulses with sufficiently high Rabi frequencies to assess how closely they approach the ideal instantaneous-pulse limit, tracking the roles of resonance conditions, dipole-dipole coupling, and inter-pulse delay τ_D.
AI.result: A periodic train of instantaneous π_x pulses produces emission spectra whose dominant features closely resemble those under CW excitation. The collective emission spectral structure reflects the interplay of resonance conditions, dipole-dipole coupling, and τ_D. Finite-duration π_x pulses with high enough Rabi frequencies closely reproduce the ideal instantaneous-pulse limit. Photon correlations g^(2)(t,τ) are governed primarily by τ_D and, unlike under CW driving, become increasingly insensitive to resonance conditions in the short-pulse limit.
AI.conclusion: Periodic pulsed driving is established as a versatile means of tailoring both the emission spectra and the photon statistics of coupled two-emitter systems.

title: A Controlled Null Result for Per-Gate Riemannian Optimization in VQE
summary: Parametrized gates in a variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) live on a product of unitary groups, which makes Riemannian optimization a natural candidate for improving training. We test this candidate in the clean per-gate setting: each single-qubit gate is optimized directly on U (2) and compared with Adam on an unconstrained Euler-angle chart representing the same physical gate, initialized from the same unitaries and tuned with a separate learning-rate sweep. On a validated hydrogen-chain benchmark, we find no measurable practical advantage from the Riemannian machinery. The direct manifold optimizer and the Euler-coordinate baseline are interleaved in final error and success rate; the classical coordinate baseline is not slower in iterations on the successful cells; and the choices of Riemannian metric, retraction, and momentum vector transport do not change the conclusion. We also identify four failure modes that can manufacture an apparent positive result: a trivial product-state benchmark, a projected-matrix Adam baseline that discards most of its own step, a non-unitary inherited Cayley retraction that lets the reported energy pass below the variational minimum, and a learning-rate grid whose optimum sits at its boundary. Each failure mode produced a plausible multi-seed result in our own workflow before being caught. The practical output of this paper is therefore a controlled null result and a validation checklist for VQE optimizer comparisons.

AI.tldr: A controlled study finds no practical advantage of Riemannian optimization over an Euler-angle Adam baseline in per-gate VQE training, and documents four failure modes that can fabricate false positives in such comparisons.
AI.motivation: Parametrized gates in VQE live on a product of unitary groups, so Riemannian optimization appears a natural way to improve training; the authors test whether this apparent theoretical fit yields real practical gains.
AI.method: Clean per-gate comparison: each single-qubit gate optimized directly on U(2) versus Adam on an unconstrained Euler-angle chart of the same physical gate, with identical initialization and separate learning-rate sweeps. Ablations cover choice of Riemannian metric, retraction, and momentum vector transport, evaluated on a validated hydrogen-chain benchmark. Four suspected failure modes are also isolated and diagnosed.
AI.result: No measurable practical advantage from Riemannian machinery: final error and success rate are interleaved between the two optimizers, the coordinate baseline is not slower in iterations on successful cells, and metric/retraction/transport choices do not alter the conclusion. Four false-positive generators identified: trivial product-state benchmark, projected-matrix Adam discarding most of its step, non-unitary inherited Cayley retraction allowing energy below the variational minimum, and a learning-rate grid optimum at its boundary—each initially producing plausible multi-seed results.
AI.conclusion: The paper's contribution is a controlled null result plus a validation checklist for VQE optimizer comparisons.

title: Distributed quantum phase sensing using an SU(1,1) Perelomov coherent state in a Mach-Zehnder interferometer network
summary: We present a theoretical study of distributed quantum sensing using a reconfigurable network of $N$ Mach--Zehnder interferometers to simultaneously estimate weighted linear combinations of relative phase shifts. The proposed scheme relies on injecting a Perelomov coherent state, generated from the SU(1,1) group representation, into one port of a passive quantum circuit while the remaining modes are initialized in the vacuum state, thereby establishing non-trivial quantum correlations among the sensors. Based on multi-parameter quantum estimation theory, our analysis shows that this entangled strategy outperforms the standard shot-noise limit and asymptotically achieves the Heisenberg limit. Furthermore, we highlight the crucial role of the first beam splitter's asymmetry; specifically, the optimal transmission coefficient that maximizes sensitivity corresponds to its maximum imbalance. Compared to a separable approach utilizing the same total average photon number, the entangled strategy yields a more efficient use of quantum resources, guaranteeing an accuracy gain between $1$ and $N$. This demonstrates that the entangled strategy is systematically superior to its separable counterpart. Ultimately, these results illustrate the potential of entangled distributed quantum sensor networks for high-precision measurements and provide clear guidelines for optimizing interferometric architectures in quantum metrology.

AI.tldr: The paper theoretically studies distributed quantum sensing with a reconfigurable network of N Mach-Zehnder interferometers, showing that injecting a Perelomov coherent state (SU(1,1)) enables Heisenberg-limited estimation of weighted linear combinations of phase shifts, with optimal sensitivity achieved at maximum first-beam-splitter imbalance.
AI.motivation: Distributed quantum sensing aims to estimate multiple parameters across sensor networks with higher precision than classical or separable strategies; the paper seeks to characterize an entangled strategy's resource efficiency and provide design guidelines for interferometric architectures.
AI.method: A reconfigurable network of N Mach-Zehnder interferometers is modeled, with a Perelomov coherent state generated from the SU(1,1) representation injected into one port of a passive circuit while other modes start in vacuum, creating quantum correlations among sensors. Multi-parameter quantum estimation theory is applied to evaluate sensitivity and compare entangled versus separable approaches at fixed total average photon number.
AI.result: The entangled strategy surpasses the shot-noise limit and asymptotically reaches the Heisenberg limit. The optimal transmission coefficient of the first beam splitter corresponds to its maximum imbalance. Compared with a separable strategy using the same total average photon number, the entangled approach guarantees an accuracy gain between 1 and N.
AI.conclusion: Entangled distributed quantum sensor networks offer systematically superior resource efficiency over separable counterparts and are promising for high-precision measurement, with the first beam splitter's asymmetry providing a clear optimization rule for interferometric architectures in quantum metrology.

title: Imaging the topological sign of a Dirac mass with spin-polarized tunneling
summary: A Dirac mass is characterized not only by its magnitude but also by its sign, which influences the Berry curvature, Hall response, and the propagation direction of chiral boundary modes. However, local spectroscopy of magnetic topological surfaces has so far accessed only the gap magnitude $|M|$. Here we show how the topological sign of $M$ can be determined locally. We first establish the sign information that spin-resolved tunneling can access and the reference required to obtain an absolute Hall sign. Although spin--orbital entanglement generally obscures the relation between measured spin and Dirac pseudospin, crystalline rotation symmetry alleviates this ambiguity at the band edge. On a $C_3$ axis, an axial tip couples to a fully spin-polarized state whose tunneling asymmetry directly reveals the sign of the occupied-band Berry curvature, independent of orbital composition. We further show that the zeroth Landau level provides an independent mass-sign measurement with an unpolarized tip, while opposite domains and their chiral domain-wall modes provide self-consistency checks. These results pave the way for imaging the locations where the topological character changes within a material, rather than merely identifying where a spectral gap appears.

AI.tldr: This work proposes local experimental protocols to determine the topological sign of a Dirac mass, not just its magnitude, using spin-resolved and Landau-level tunneling on C3-symmetric surfaces.
AI.motivation: A Dirac mass is defined by both magnitude and sign; the sign controls Berry curvature, the Hall response, and the propagation direction of chiral boundary modes. Yet local surface spectroscopy of magnetic topological materials has only been able to measure the gap magnitude |M|, leaving the sign undetermined locally. Absolute Hall-sign determination also requires a known reference, which had not been established.
AI.method: The authors analyze the sign information accessible via spin-resolved tunneling and identify the reference needed for an absolute Hall sign. Because spin-orbital entanglement generally blurs the relation between measured spin and Dirac pseudospin, they invoke crystalline rotation symmetry to lift this ambiguity at the band edge. On a C3 rotation axis, an axially oriented tip couples to a fully spin-polarized state, so the tunneling asymmetry directly reports the sign of the occupied-band Berry curvature irrespective of orbital composition. They also consider the zeroth Landau level as an independent mass-sign probe usable with an unpolarized tip, plus opposite domains and their chiral domain-wall modes as self-consistency checks.
AI.result: On a C3 axis, an axial tip's tunneling asymmetry reveals the sign of the occupied-band Berry curvature independently of orbital composition. The zeroth Landau level supplies a separate mass-sign measurement with an unpolarized tip. Opposite domains and their chiral domain-wall modes serve as consistency verifications.
AI.conclusion: Topological sign of the Dirac mass can be measured locally, enabling imaging of where topological character changes inside a material rather than simply mapping where a spectral gap opens.

title: A three-eighths upper bound on the stabilizer-rank exponent of face-center magic states
summary: We give an explicit construction proving that the exact stabilizer rank of $m$ copies of the qubit face-center magic state is $O(2^{3m/8})$. Two symmetry-related fifteen-term identities combine into a twenty-four-term decomposition at twelve copies.
