These transitions act as local spectral references: gravitational redshift changes the photon's detuning from each resonance, yielding large differences in reflection amplitude, hence substantial visibility loss and interferometric phase shift even for centimetre-scale height differences. They quantify experimental requirements and assess feasibility with current or near-term technology.
AI.result: Substantial visibility loss and interferometric phase shift are predicted already for centimetre-scale height differences, avoiding the kilometre-scale optical paths required by geometric-accumulation schemes. The experimental requirements are quantified and implementation appears feasible with current or near-term technology.
AI.conclusion: Spectral enhancement via ultranarrow atomic transitions offers a route to tabletop optical tests of the interplay between quantum mechanics and general relativity.

title: Theory of Trotter Error with Variable-Weight Schedules
summary: Trotterization is a widely used algorithm for simulating quantum evolutions and consists of approximating a target unitary through a local linear decomposition of its generator that is repeated over $N$ steps. We introduce {scheduled trotterization}, a variable-weight modification in which the coefficients of the local linear decomposition are allowed to change from step to step. Using the geometry of the Lie group of unitary operators, we express the global endpoint error as a product of transported local defects, whose leading terms are obtained by two applications of the Baker-Campbell-Hausdorff formula, one inside each local step and one between different transported defects, separating the internal Trotter error from the external accumulation error. While we recover recent tighter bounds on the global approximation error when the weights are held fixed, the new framework allows us to propose a weight-varying schedule that significantly decreases the global error. For exact infinitesimal synthesis, we prove that this improves the usual fixed-weight $O(N^{-1})$ behavior to $O(N^{-2})$, without changing the basic pulse skeleton. We also extend the framework to imperfect infinitesimal synthesis, as arises in quantum gate synthesis problems, where admissible coefficients may only approximate the desired local corrections. In this case, the error is controlled by a local covering parameter measuring the quality of the available coefficient set. Numerical experiments for random $\SU(2)$ targets further support the predicted theoretical improvements. The results suggest a novel perspective for the analysis of Trotter errors, which can be treated as schedulable quantities to be coherently canceled at the endpoint.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces scheduled Trotterization, a variable-weight modification of standard Trotterization in which the coefficients of the local decomposition of the generator are allowed to change at each step. By leveraging the geometry of the Lie group of unitary operators, the error is expressed as a product of transported local defects, separating internal Trotter error from external accumulation error. A weight-varying schedule is shown to reduce the global error, improving the usual O(N^{-1}) convergence to O(N^{-2}) for exact infinitesimal synthesis without altering the pulse skeleton.
AI.motivation: Trotterization is a standard approach for simulating quantum evolutions by approximating a target unitary with a local linear decomposition of its generator repeated over N steps. Conventional Trotterization keeps the coefficients of this decomposition fixed, which limits accuracy at finite N. The authors seek a systematic way to reduce the global approximation error without changing the underlying pulse structure, treating Trotter errors as schedulable quantities that can be coherently canceled at the endpoint.
AI.method: The authors introduce scheduled Trotterization, allowing step-dependent coefficients in the local decomposition. Using the geometry of the unitary Lie group, they factor the global endpoint error into a product of transported local defects. Two applications of the Baker-Campbell-Hausdorff formula—one within each local step, one between transported defects—yield the leading error terms, cleanly separating internal Trotter error from external accumulation error. They then design weight-varying schedules to cancel global error and extend the framework to imperfect infinitesimal synthesis via a local covering parameter that measures the quality of the available coefficient set.
AI.result: The framework recovers recent tighter bounds on global approximation error for fixed weights. With a weight-varying schedule, the global error is significantly decreased: for exact infinitesimal synthesis, the fixed-weight O(N^{-1}) behavior is improved to O(N^{-2}) without changing the basic pulse skeleton. For imperfect infinitesimal synthesis, error is controlled by the local covering parameter. Numerical experiments on random SU(2) targets confirm the predicted theoretical improvements.
AI.conclusion: Scheduled Trotterization offers a novel perspective in which Trotter errors are treated as schedulable quantities that can be coherently canceled at the endpoint. By allowing step-dependent coefficients, the method improves convergence orders and mitigates global accumulation error, with extensions to imperfect synthesis. The approach provides a geometric framework for analyzing and reducing Trotter errors and is supported by both theory and numerical evidence.

title: Methods for Automated Equivalence Checking of Quantum Error-Correction Codes
comment: 22 pages, 16 main text + 2 references + 4 appendix, 19 figures
summary: Quantum error-correction code and circuit construction is an active field of research, motivating automated methods for identifying equivalent designs. We develop and evaluate automated strategies for deciding whether two descriptions of quantum error-correction codes are equivalent under specified transformations. We formalize permutation equivalence for stabilizer and CSS codes and local-Clifford equivalence for stabilizer codes within a unified framework that separates physical from representation freedom. We develop three decision strategies (group-action search, isomorphism-based methods, and constraint solving), together with invariants and signatures for preprocessing. The empirical evaluation shows that no paradigm dominates across equivalence notions, code families, and parameter ranges. We therefore combine their complementary strengths in input-dependent hybrid checkers following a staged Refute-Refine-Decide architecture. Mean hybrid runtimes remain below 10 s for most evaluated structured-code cases with $n \leq 37$; for inequivalent code instances with $n=144$, they are about 310 s for permutation and 16 s for local-Clifford equivalence.

AI.tldr: This paper develops and evaluates automated methods for deciding equivalence between quantum error-correction code descriptions under specified transformations, and combines complementary strategies into hybrid checkers.
AI.motivation: Quantum error-correction code and circuit construction is active research, motivating automated methods to identify equivalent designs. No single existing paradigm suffices across equivalence notions, code families, and parameter ranges.
AI.method: The authors formalize permutation equivalence for stabilizer and CSS codes and local-Clifford equivalence for stabilizer codes in a unified framework separating physical from representation freedom. They develop three decision strategies (group-action search, isomorphism-based methods, constraint solving), plus invariants and signatures for preprocessing, and combine them in input-dependent hybrid checkers using a staged Refute-Refine-Decide architecture.
AI.result: Empirically, no paradigm dominates across equivalence notions, code families, and parameter ranges. Mean hybrid runtimes remain below 10 s for most structured-code cases with n ≤ 37; for inequivalent instances with n = 144, about 310 s for permutation and 16 s for local-Clifford equivalence.
AI.conclusion: Combining complementary equivalence-checking strategies via an input-dependent, staged hybrid architecture yields practical automated equivalence checking for quantum error-correction codes where no single paradigm is universally dominant.

title: PPVM: A Circuit Simulation Framework for Digital Twins of Quantum Processors
comment: 20 pages, 8 figures, 1 table. Code available at https://github.com/QuEraComputing/ppvm
summary: Quantum computers are approaching the early fault-tolerant regime. Verifying the next generation of quantum hardware requires joint emulation of the quantum processor, hardware noise, and classical control and decoding logic. We introduce the Programmable Pauli Virtual Machine (PPVM), an open-source framework for digital twins of quantum processors. PPVM unifies Pauli propagation and generalized tableau simulation under a common abstraction within a single virtual machine. Its bytecode supports arbitrary classical control flow, with measurement-conditioned feed-forward available in the generalized tableau backend. For neutral-atom hardware, we derive independent and correlated atom-loss channels and integrate them into both backends. We demonstrate loss-aware magic state distillation on over a thousand physical qubits and integration with classical decoding through Bloqade QEC Studio.

AI.tldr: PPVM is an open-source virtual machine framework that unifies Pauli propagation and generalized tableau simulation to digitally twin next-generation quantum processors, with hardware noise (including neutral-atom loss) and classical control/decoding support.
AI.motivation: Verifying next-generation quantum hardware in the approaching early fault-tolerant regime requires joint emulation of the quantum processor, hardware noise, and the classical control and decoding logic, which existing tools do not address in a unified manner.
AI.method: The authors introduce the Programmable Pauli Virtual Machine (PPVM), which unifies Pauli propagation and generalized tableau simulation under a common abstraction within a single virtual machine. Its bytecode supports arbitrary classical control flow, with measurement-conditioned feed-forward enabled in the generalized tableau backend. For neutral-atom hardware, they derive independent and correlated atom-loss channels and integrate them into both backends.
AI.result: The framework is demonstrated via loss-aware magic state distillation on more than a thousand physical qubits, and integration with classical decoding through Bloqade QEC Studio.
AI.conclusion: PPVM provides a unified, open-source digital-twin platform for quantum processors that combines multiple simulation backends with realistic noise modeling and classical decoding integration, supporting verification of early fault-tolerant hardware.

title: Resource-based reliability of quantum-coherent devices
summary: Quantum devices can lose the resource needed for a specified function without entering a fixed failure subspace. We propose a resource-based reliability framework for this situation, quantifying the remaining task-relevant resource relative to a stated ideal capacity. The resource measure is selected through its operational connection to the task and the allowed operations. We develop this approach for a trusted quantum random-number generator and a calibrated two-port interferometer. Relative-entropy coherence determines the optimal asymptotic yield of standard coherent qubits under incoherent operations for the former, while logarithmic $l_1$ coherence quantifies the fringe resource of the latter and determines its calibrated correct-port probability. An exactly solvable multi-spin spin-boson model illustrates how environmental records affect these resources at the same isolated-spin dephasing strength. Collective noise preserves coherence within magnetization sectors for product inputs, but enhances the decay of Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger branch coherence. Finite-record simulations connect the resource definitions to measurement counts and show that increasing the sample size reduces statistical fluctuations without eliminating bias from an incorrect many-spin noise model. The resulting framework provides a task-specific route to reliability assessment when a fixed failure projector is insufficient, while keeping retained resource capacity distinct from a classical survival probability.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a resource-based reliability framework for quantum devices that lose functional capability without entering a fixed failure subspace, quantifying remaining task-relevant resource relative to an ideal capacity, and applies it to a quantum random-number generator, a calibrated interferometer, and a multi-spin spin-boson model.
AI.motivation: Standard reliability assessment relies on a fixed failure subspace, but quantum devices can lose the resource required for a specified function without entering such a subspace, so this criterion is insufficient. A task-specific measure of retained functional resource is needed.
AI.method: The authors define a resource-based reliability framework quantifying remaining task-relevant resource relative to a stated ideal capacity, with the resource measure chosen by its operational connection to the task and the allowed operations. They apply it to a trusted quantum random-number generator (relative-entropy coherence as optimal asymptotic yield of standard coherent qubits under incoherent operations), a calibrated two-port interferometer (logarithmic l1 coherence as fringe resource and calibrated correct-port probability), and an exactly solvable multi-spin spin-boson model, with finite-record simulations linking resource definitions to measurement counts.
AI.result: Relative-entropy coherence determines the optimal asymptotic yield of standard coherent qubits under incoherent operations; logarithmic l1 coherence quantifies the interferometer fringe resource and determines its calibrated correct-port probability. In the spin-boson model, at the same isolated-spin dephasing strength, collective noise preserves coherence within magnetization sectors for product inputs but enhances decay of Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger branch coherence. Increasing sample size lowers statistical fluctuations but does not remove bias from an incorrect many-spin noise model.
AI.conclusion: The framework offers a task-specific route to reliability assessment when a fixed failure projector is insufficient, while keeping retained resource capacity distinct from a classical survival probability.

title: Towards an autonomous optomechanical Maxwell Demon engine
summary: We present a fully autonomous model of a mechanical Maxwell demon engine that converts heat absorbed by a qubit into population inversion in an attached quantum battery. A damped mechanical oscillator acts as a pointer that incorporates the essential demon function of information acquisition about the qubit state and subsequent feedback into the system dynamics, replacing external measurements and control operations. This is achieved by means of a Holstein-type Hamiltonian, which makes the pointer's equilibrium position depend on the qubit state and thereby induces a state-dependent resonance shift. The mechanism enables a selective energy transfer to an attached spin system that acts as the quantum battery. We derive both local and global Lindblad master equations for the coupled system and identify the parameter regimes in which the engine operates efficiently. The figure of merit is the resulting steady-state population inversion of the battery, quantified in terms of ergotropy. Based on these results, we discuss the necessary conditions for practical implementations of the demon engine on realistic experimental platforms.

AI.tldr: A fully autonomous mechanical Maxwell demon converts qubit-absorbed heat into population inversion (ergotropy) in an attached quantum battery, using a damped Holstein-type oscillator as a self-measuring pointer instead of external measurement/feedback.
AI.motivation: Standard Maxwell demon engines rely on explicit external measurements and feedback control, which limits their autonomy and practicality. This work aims to realize the demon's information-acquisition and feedback functions intrinsically via a physical pointer, enabling a fully autonomous quantum heat engine.
AI.method: The system is modeled by a Holstein-type Hamiltonian in which a damped mechanical oscillator (pointer) couples to a qubit such that the pointer's equilibrium position depends on the qubit state, inducing a state-dependent resonance shift. This enables selective energy transfer to an attached spin system serving as the quantum battery. Local and global Lindblad master equations are derived for the coupled system to identify efficient operating regimes.
AI.result: The engine's performance is quantified by the steady-state population inversion of the battery, measured via ergotropy. Parameter regimes yielding efficient operation are identified, and the necessary conditions for practical experimental implementation are discussed.
AI.conclusion: A mechanical oscillator can autonomously perform the demon's measurement and feedback roles, allowing heat-to-population-inversion conversion in a quantum battery without external control, with experimentally relevant conditions outlined for realization.

title: Experimental Benchmarking of a 256-Qubit Room-Temperature NV-Diamond Quantum Processor with an Optically Programmable Biomolecular Quantum Bus
summary: We report Zeus-256, a room-temperature nitrogen-vacancy (NV) diamond processor with 256 simultaneously active processor-level logical qubits arranged in a 16 x 16 array. Each logical qubit combines an NV electron-spin ensemble with nuclear-spin memory and ancillary resources. OpenQASM 2.0 circuits are transpiled into RFSoC-controlled microwave, radio-frequency, optical, timing, measurement and bus-configuration sequences. An optically programmable proprietary protein-chromophore layer with an internal metastable-triplet spin mediator provides a reconfigurable biomolecular quantum bus for local and long-range interactions. Benchmarks cover QFT, GHZ entanglement, Grover search, arithmetic, variational, neural-network, graph-state and Shor-family circuits. Factor recovery is reported for 11 integers of 8-84 bits, with 10 attempts per instance; the 84-bit endpoint uses 256 qubits and 40,250,342 reported gates, with a reported execution time of 551.694 ms. Bell-CHSH measurements yield S = 2.8008 +/- 0.0446. Three-qubit Grover search returns the marked state in 958 of 1,024 shots (93.55%), compared with an ideal reference of 94.53%. A separate 30,000-shot population-and-parity protocol yields fixed-phase GHZ+ fidelity of 99.8960%, an estimated standard error of 0.2885 percentage points and a conservative physical 95% interval of [98.2342%, 100%]. Timing metrics are partial and do not establish quantum advantage. Scaling to 9,984 processor-level logical qubits is an engineering target, distinct from the demonstrated register.

AI.tldr: Zeus-256 is a room-temperature NV-diamond processor demonstrating a 16x16 array of 256 simultaneously active logical qubits, benchmarked across QFT, Grover, GHZ, neural-network and Shor-family circuits, including factor recovery for integers up to 84 bits, though claimed timing metrics are explicitly partial and do not establish quantum advantage.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate a scalable, room-temperature logical-qubit architecture that combines NV electron-spin ensembles with nuclear-spin memory and a reconfigurable biomolecular quantum bus, and to benchmark it against a broad suite of quantum algorithms including large-integer factoring. The paper signals ambition toward an engineering target of 9,984 logical qubits.
AI.method: A 256 logical-qubit processor is arranged as a 16x16 array, each logical qubit coupling an NV electron-spin ensemble with nuclear-spin memory and ancillary resources. OpenQASM 2.0 circuits are transpiled into RFSoC-controlled microwave, RF, optical, timing, measurement and bus-configuration sequences. An optically programmable protein-chromophore layer with an internal metastable-triplet spin mediator acts as a reconfigurable biomolecular quantum bus for local and long-range interactions. Benchmarks include QFT, GHZ entanglement, Grover search, arithmetic, variational, neural-network, graph-state and Shor-family circuits; Bell-CHSH, population-and-parity GHZ fidelity, and multi-shot Grover protocols are reported.
AI.result: Factor recovery is reported for 11 integers of 8-84 bits (10 attempts each); the 84-bit endpoint uses 256 qubits, 40,250,342 reported gates, and a reported execution time of 551.694 ms. Bell-CHSH yields S = 2.8008 +/- 0.0446. Three-qubit Grover returns the marked state in 958/1,024 shots (93.55%) versus an ideal 94.53%. A 30,000-shot population-and-parity protocol gives fixed-phase GHZ+ fidelity of 99.8960%, standard error 0.2885 pp, and a conservative physical 95% interval of [98.2342%, 100%].
AI.conclusion: The processor demonstrates broad algorithmic benchmarking at room temperature with high reported GHZ fidelity and competitive Grover performance. However, the authors explicitly note that timing metrics are partial and do not establish quantum advantage, and that scaling to 9,984 processor-level logical qubits is an engineering target distinct from the demonstrated register. Claims should therefore be read as a platform demonstration rather than a verified computational-speedup result.

title: A complete quantum process model for physically realistic photo-detection in the joint photon-number and spectral degrees of freedom
summary: Photo-detection is a fundamental component of experimental photonics, yet theoretical models often treat detectors solely in the photon-number basis, neglecting other relevant degrees of freedom such as spectral characteristics. We present a complete quantum process model for physically realistic photodetection that incorporates both photon-number effects and frequency-dependent detector response, described through explicitly derived Kraus operators in the operator-sum representation. This formalism accommodates realistic inefficiencies, models detection within finite spectral windows, and can be directly substituted for idealized models in quantum optical analyses. The model leads to identifying the suitable detection window of the detectors relative to the spectral distribution of incident photons and conversely, in order to maximize the observability of quantum effects.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a complete quantum process model for realistic photodetection that combines photon-number effects with frequency-dependent detector response via explicitly derived Kraus operators, enabling optimal matching of detection windows to incident photon spectra.
AI.motivation: Existing theoretical models of photodetection treat detectors solely in the photon-number basis, neglecting other relevant degrees of freedom such as spectral characteristics, which limits their physical realism.
AI.method: The authors construct a quantum process model using the operator-sum representation, deriving explicit Kraus operators that incorporate both photon-number effects and frequency-dependent detector response, accommodating realistic inefficiencies and finite spectral detection windows.
AI.result: The formalism can directly replace idealized models in quantum optical analyses and identifies the suitable detection window of detectors relative to the spectral distribution of incident photons.
AI.conclusion: Matching the detection window to the incident photon spectrum maximizes the observability of quantum effects.

title: V-type Atomic Variance Squeezing
comment: Corresponding author: Zhao-Yang Tong. This preprint is submitted to quant-ph
summary: Variance squeezing of a V-type atom interacting with a dissipative cavity is investigated. First, the influence of atomic initial state parameters on the variance squeezing is explored. The results show that the atomic variance squeezing switches alternately between Sx and Sy as the initial state parameter alpha sweeps from -pi to pi. The two squeezing intervals are symmetric about alpha = pi/4, each with a width of pi/2. For alpha = pi/14, only the Sx component can generate variance squeezing and will eventually disappear with time evolution due to unavoidable environmental noise. Then, the influence of system parameters on the variance squeezing is also studied. It is found that, the optical variance squeezing depth of Sx is determined solely by the atomic initial parameters and is independent of the system parameters. Both weak cavity-environment coupling and atom-cavity detuning can significantly enhance the robustness of the Sx variance squeezing. The SGI parameter has an extremely weak influence on variance squeezing. These results are beneficial for high-precision quantum communication applications.

AI.tldr: This paper studies variance squeezing in a V-type atom inside a dissipative cavity, showing that squeezing alternates between Sx and Sy with the atomic initial parameter and that cavity-environment coupling and detuning enhance Sx squeezing robustness.
AI.motivation: Variance squeezing is a key resource for high-precision quantum communication, motivating a detailed understanding of how atomic initial states and system parameters govern squeezing in a realistic dissipative cavity.
AI.method: The authors investigate a V-type atom interacting with a dissipative cavity, examining the dependence of variance squeezing on the atomic initial state parameter alpha and on system parameters such as cavity-environment coupling, atom-cavity detuning, and the SGI parameter.
AI.result: Squeezing switches alternately between Sx and Sy as alpha sweeps from -pi to pi, with two squeezing intervals symmetric about alpha = pi/4, each of width pi/2. For alpha = pi/14, only Sx squeezes and it vanishes over time due to environmental noise. The Sx squeezing depth depends solely on atomic initial parameters, independent of system parameters; weak cavity-environment coupling and detuning greatly enhance Sx squeezing robustness, while the SGI parameter has negligible influence.
AI.conclusion: The Sx variance squeezing depth is fixed by atomic initial conditions, and its robustness can be significantly improved by weak cavity-environment coupling and atom-cavity detuning, findings useful for high-precision quantum communication applications.

title: Beyond Gaussian Entanglement: Practical Criteria for Polynomially Excited Quantum States
summary: Polynomial excitations consisting of creation and annihilation operators are studied. Subsystem entanglement is proven produced and preserved by such manipulations. NPT entanglement already present between any two subsystems of a general pure or mixed multipartite Gaussian state is preserved under all polynomial excitations. Nevertheless, these excitations can create NPT entanglement between initially separable subsystems, implying that the number of NPT entangled pairs cannot decrease. Polynomial excitations of a wide class of initially separable pure states are considered. For these states, the method reduces the infinite-dimensional positivity problem to a finite-dimensional one: after partial transposition, NPT entanglement is equivalent to a corresponding bilinear representation matrix not being positive semi-definite. Furthermore, using symplectic diagonalization and spectral decomposition, an explicit transformation is constructed between the Fock-space and position representations. It is applied to quadratic excitations of a three-mode mixed Gaussian state. The behavior of the NPT entanglement is tracked between subsystems as a function of a parameter $κ$, which tunes the non-locality of the excitation, and quantum negativity is evaluated. Under a chosen quadratic Hamiltonian, the resulting unitary time evolution maintains NPT entanglement for long intervals, interrupted only by short periods of PPT states. Finally, a closed analytical expression is derived for the covariance matrix of a general quadratic operator for an arbitrary number of degrees of freedom in phase space. Our framework directly connects mathematical foundations, theoretical modeling, and experimentally feasible implementations.

AI.tldr: This work analyzes how polynomial excitations (built from creation and annihilation operators) generate and preserve subsystem entanglement in multipartite Gaussian states, reducing an infinite-dimensional positivity problem to a finite-dimensional one and linking theory to feasible implementations.
AI.motivation: Understanding whether and how experimentally realizable operations—polynomial excitations of bosonic modes—produce or preserve entanglement is key to quantum information with continuous variables. The paper aims to establish general entanglement-preservation and entanglement-creation results, and to bridge abstract mathematical foundations with theoretical modeling and experimental implementation.
AI.method: Polynomial excitations composed of creation and annihilation operators are studied. For a broad class of initially separable pure states, the infinite-dimensional positivity problem (after partial transposition) is reduced to a finite-dimensional one, where NPT entanglement is equivalent to a bilinear representation matrix not being positive semi-definite. Symplectic diagonalization and spectral decomposition are used to construct an explicit transformation between Fock-space and position representations. Quantum negativity is evaluated as a function of a parameter κ tuning the non-locality of the excitation. A closed analytical expression is derived for the covariance matrix of a general quadratic operator for arbitrary degrees of freedom in phase space.
AI.result: Subsystem entanglement is shown to be produced and preserved under polynomial excitations. NPT entanglement existing between any two subsystems of a general pure or mixed multipartite Gaussian state is preserved under all polynomial excitations, and such excitations can create NPT entanglement between initially separable subsystems, so the number of NPT entangled pairs cannot decrease. For the considered separable pure states, NPT entanglement corresponds to a finite-dimensional bilinear representation matrix failing to be positive semi-definite. In a three-mode mixed Gaussian state under a quadratic excitation, NPT entanglement between subsystems is tracked versus κ and quantum negativity computed; under a chosen quadratic Hamiltonian the resulting unitary time evolution maintains NPT entanglement over long intervals, interrupted only by short PPT periods.
AI.conclusion: Polynomial excitations universally preserve existing NPT entanglement and can generate new NPT entanglement, making non-decreasing numbers of NPT entangled pairs. The framework provides a finite-dimensional criterion for entanglement, explicit Fock-to-position transformations, and closed-form covariance-matrix expressions, directly connecting mathematical foundations, theoretical modeling, and experimentally feasible implementations.

title: Unequal Coherent Ergotropy at Equal Interferometric Visibility and Energy in Quantum-Controlled Interferometers
comment: 20 pages, 6 figures and 1 table. Comments are welcome
summary: The ergotropy, or unitarily extractable work, of a quantum system naturally splits into incoherent and coherent contributions, respectively set by population inversion and coherences in the energy eigenbasis. We show that this split makes the coherent ergotropy of a Mach--Zehnder qubit sensitive to path predictability that the output interference fringes do not reveal. We send the path qubit, prepared as a thermal quantum battery, through two quantum-controlled interferometers built from the same elements, a fixed beam splitter and a beam splitter coherently controlled to be present or absent, differing only in the order in which these two act. The two arrangements share identical visibility, stored energy, and incoherent ergotropy at every point in the parameter space. Yet, for work extracted from the output battery alone, placing the controlled beam splitter first never yields less coherent ergotropy, and at fixed visibility and interferometric phase the difference is governed by the path predictability that this ordering creates. The same expression reappears as a purity deficit on the beam-splitter controller, so the work advantage comes with a Landauer bound on the cost of locally resetting the controller that is never larger at the same temperature. We further examine the effects of decoherence on the battery and consider a relativistic realization in which a Wigner rotation correlates the particle's spin with its path. Tracing out the spin decoheres the battery and allows the two arrangements to exhibit different coherent ergotropies even in regimes where their non-relativistic counterparts coincide. These results show that interference visibility is not a complete measure of the coherence available as work.

AI.tldr: The coherent ergotropy of a Mach-Zehnder qubit is shown to be sensitive to path predictability that interference visibility does not capture; two element-identical interferometers differing only in beam-splitter order share visibility, stored energy, and incoherent ergotropy, yet differ in coherent ergotropy, with the advantage tied to a controller purity deficit and a bounded reset cost.
AI.motivation: Ergotropy splits into incoherent (population inversion) and coherent (energy-basis coherences) contributions, but standard interferometric visibility is widely used as the indicator of available coherence. The paper questions whether visibility is a complete measure of coherence usable as work, motivating a setting where two physically comparable interferometers can be distinguished by coherent ergotropy despite identical visibility.
AI.method: A path qubit prepared as a thermal quantum battery is sent through two quantum-controlled Mach-Zehnder interferometers constructed from the same elements: a fixed beam splitter and a beam splitter coherently controlled to be present or absent, differing only in the order of these two operations. Coherent and incoherent ergotropy are evaluated across parameter space, and the resulting work difference between orderings is expressed in terms of path predictability. Decoherence on the battery is additionally analyzed, and a relativistic realization is considered in which a Wigner rotation correlates the particle's spin with its path, with the spin traced out.
AI.result: The two arrangements share identical visibility, stored energy, and incoherent ergotropy at every point in parameter space. For work extracted from the output battery alone, placing the controlled beam splitter first never yields less coherent ergotropy, and at fixed visibility and interferometric phase the difference is governed by the path predictability created by the ordering. The same expression appears as a purity deficit on the beam-splitter controller, so the work advantage carries a Landauer reset bound that is never larger at the same temperature. Under decoherence, and in the relativistic Wigner-rotation realization, tracing out the spin decoheres the battery and lets the two arrangements exhibit different coherent ergotropies even where their non-relativistic counterparts coincide.
AI.conclusion: Interference visibility is not a complete measure of the coherence available as work. Coherent ergotropy can distinguish interferometric arrangements that visibility, stored energy, and incoherent ergotropy cannot, with the ordering advantage controlled by path predictability and accompanied by a temperature-dependent Landauer cost on resetting the controller.

title: Experimental Realization of a C-Shunt Flux-Qubit Coupler for Controlled-Z Gates between Transmons
summary: Fast entangling gates and low-interaction idling require distinct operating conditions in superconducting quantum processors. We experimentally realize a transmon-C-shunt-transmon (TCT) device in which a flux-tunable, three-junction capacitively shunted flux-qubit coupler connects two transmon data qubits. The C-shunt coupler provides a flux-tunable, positively anharmonic spectrum for tailoring the interactions between the data qubits. Conditional Ramsey and swap measurements identify an idle region with near-zero residual ZZ interaction strength and suppressed transverse exchange. At this bias, simultaneous single-qubit interleaved randomized benchmarking yields X-gate fldelities above 99.7%, consistent with individual operation. A 45 ns nonadiabatic controlled-Z (CZ) gate achieves an interleaved randomized benchmarking fldelity estimate of 99.23(15)%. Numerical simulations identify coupler energy relaxation as an important limitation on CZ-gate fldelity and indicate that extending the coupler lifetime can improve gate performance. These results demonstrate the experimental feasibility of C-shunt flux-qubit couplers for combining low-interaction idling with fast entangling operations between transmon qubits.

AI.tldr: A transmon-C-shunt-transmon device uses a flux-tunable C-shunt three-junction coupler to combine low-residual-ZZ idling with a 45 ns CZ gate at 99.23% fidelity, with coupler relaxation identified as the main fidelity limiter.
AI.motivation: Fast entangling gates and low-interaction idling demand conflicting operating conditions in superconducting quantum processors, creating a need for a coupler that can be tuned between a strongly interacting and a nearly non-interacting regime.
AI.method: The device (TCT) links two transmon data qubits via a flux-tunable, three-junction capacitively shunted flux-qubit coupler, whose positively anharmonic, flux-tunable spectrum tailors inter-qubit interactions. Conditional Ramsey and swap measurements locate the idle bias; simultaneous single-qubit interleaved randomized benchmarking (IRB) characterizes X-gate fidelities; a 45 ns nonadiabatic CZ gate is benchmarked via IRB; numerical simulations assess the fidelity bottleneck.
AI.result: An idle region with near-zero residual ZZ interaction and suppressed transverse exchange is identified. Simultaneous single-qubit IRB gives X-gate fidelities above 99.7%, matching individual operation. The 45 ns nonadiabatic CZ gate reaches an IRB fidelity of 99.23(15)%. Simulations pinpoint coupler energy relaxation as a key CZ-fidelity limitation and suggest that longer coupler lifetime would improve gate performance.
AI.conclusion: C-shunt flux-qubit couplers are experimentally feasible for uniting low-interaction idling with fast entangling operations between transmon qubits, provided coupler relaxation is mitigated.

title: Lifting: Quantum State Discrimination Framework for Mid-Circuit Measurements
summary: Quantum computing promises new capabilities beyond classical computation. Mid-circuit measurements (MCMs) enable error correction and outcome-dependent control, but their reliability is limited by noise on superconducting hardware. These operations depend on accurate quantum state discrimination (QSD), which assigns measured signals to state labels. Neural network-based (NN-based) QSD improves this assignment, yet its error remains bounded below by the Bayes risk of the available readout distributions. A complementary challenge is state deterioration as successive measurements accumulate and circuit execution advances, making static calibration less representative of the workload. We present Lifting, a QSD framework that addresses both challenges through repetition encoding, neural decoding, and in situ calibration. Encoding supplies joint in-phase and quadrature (I-Q) readout signals from the target and auxiliary qubits, while contextual calibration trains the decoder for the conditions encountered during execution. Our theoretical analysis shows that retaining additional channels from a fixed joint distribution cannot increase Bayes risk and establishes sufficient conditions for contraction of an overlap-based upper bound. Experiments across three IBM processors evaluate the framework on repeated stabilizer measurement, parity-check, and teleportation workloads.

AI.tldr: Lifting is a quantum state discrimination framework combining repetition encoding, neural decoding, and in situ calibration to improve mid-circuit measurement reliability on noisy superconducting hardware.
AI.motivation: Mid-circuit measurements enable error correction and outcome-dependent control in quantum computing, but their reliability on superconducting hardware is limited by noise. Accurate quantum state discrimination (QSD) is required to assign measured signals to state labels, and while neural network-based QSD improves this assignment, its error remains bounded below by the Bayes risk of the available readout distributions. Additionally, state deterioration as successive measurements accumulate makes static calibration less representative of the actual workload conditions.
AI.method: Lifting integrates three components: repetition encoding, neural decoding, and in situ calibration. Encoding supplies joint in-phase and quadrature (I-Q) readout signals from both target and auxiliary qubits, while contextual calibration trains the decoder for the conditions encountered during actual execution.
AI.result: Theoretical analysis shows that retaining additional channels from a fixed joint distribution cannot increase Bayes risk and establishes sufficient conditions for contraction of an overlap-based upper bound. Experiments across three IBM processors evaluate the framework on repeated stabilizer measurement, parity-check, and teleportation workloads.
AI.conclusion: Lifting addresses both improved state discrimination and state deterioration through its combination of repetition encoding, neural decoding, and in situ calibration, with theoretical guarantees on Bayes risk and demonstrated evaluation on multiple IBM quantum processors.

title: Steering the Fidelity in State Preparation on Noisy Bosonic Systems with Risk-Seeking Optimization
comment: 12 pages, 1 table, accepted at International Workshop on AI for Quantum and Quantum for AI (AIQxQIA 2026), co-located with AIxIA 2026, Perugia, Italy
summary: In order to execute quantum algorithms on bosonic quantum computers, it is necessary to encode their inputs into a desired target quantum state, with a process called state preparation. In real settings, state preparation methods operate in stochastic scenarios, where the prepared state is represented as a mixed state, that is a probabilistic ensemble of pure states. Therefore, existing state preparation methods optimize a variational ansatz by averaging over all possible sequences of photon loss events contained in the prepared ensemble, yielding an output state which approximates the desired target with a certain average fidelity. Such an approach, however, does not take into account directly the distribution of fidelities across states in the ensemble. In this work, we aim to maximize the fidelity of only a subset of pure states sampled from the prepared ensemble, at the cost of reducing the average fidelity overall. This trade-off is relevant when the goal is to obtain high-fidelity states with a certain probability, rather than maximizing the average fidelity of the prepared ensemble. We borrow and adapt objective functions from risk-sensitive optimization, a framework that optimizes specific characteristics of a distribution rather than only its expectation, and that has been successfully applied in Reinforcement Learning. In the considered experimental settings, our results show that the infidelities of some pure states in the prepared ensemble can be reduced by up to four orders of magnitude when using risk-seeking objectives, compared to those achieved using the standard optimization of the average fidelity. Furthermore, we show that it is possible to control the trade-off between the probability of obtaining high-fidelity states and the lowest infidelity threshold reached, providing the flexibility to select the operating point that best suits a certain application.

AI.tldr: This work applies risk-sensitive objective functions to bosonic state preparation, trading average fidelity for much higher fidelity in a subset of pure states within the mixed-state ensemble, reducing infidelities of some states by up to four orders of magnitude.
AI.motivation: State preparation on bosonic quantum computers occurs in stochastic settings where the prepared state is a mixed ensemble of pure states. Existing methods optimize only the average fidelity over all photon-loss event sequences, ignoring the distribution of fidelities across ensemble members. When the goal is to obtain a high-fidelity state with some probability, average fidelity is an inadequate objective.
AI.method: The authors borrow and adapt objective functions from risk-sensitive optimization, a framework that optimizes specific characteristics of a distribution rather than its expectation alone. They maximize the fidelity of only a subset of pure states sampled from the prepared ensemble, deliberately accepting reduced average fidelity. Risk-seeking objectives are employed to reshape the fidelity distribution.
AI.result: In the considered experimental settings, infidelities of some pure states in the prepared ensemble are reduced by up to four orders of magnitude using risk-seeking objectives compared to standard average-fidelity optimization. The trade-off between the probability of obtaining high-fidelity states and the lowest infidelity threshold reached can be explicitly controlled.
AI.conclusion: Risk-sensitive objectives offer a flexible alternative to average-fidelity optimization for bosonic state preparation, allowing selection of an operating point that balances the probability of high-fidelity outcomes against achievable fidelity, tailored to a given application.

title: On the Increase of Boltzmann Entropy in Closed Macroscopic Quantum Systems
summary: We consider a closed macroscopic quantum system in a pure state $ψ$ evolving unitarily with Hamiltonian $H$ in a finite-dimensional Hilbert space $\mathscr{H}$. Following von Neumann, we assume a decomposition of $\mathscr{H}$ into mutually orthogonal subspaces $\mathscr{H}_ν$, where each $ν$ represents a macro state, and $\mathscr{H}_ν$ contains the pure states compatible with $ν$. We define the quantum Boltzmann entropy for a macro state $ν$ as $S_\mathrm{qB}(ν) = k_{\mathrm{B}} \log \dim \mathscr{H}_ν$, where $k_\mathrm{B}$ is the Boltzmann constant. Goldstein et al. [http://arxiv.org/abs/1903.11870] have suggested, as a version of the second law of thermodynamics, that $S_\mathrm{qB}$ predominantly increases with time for realistic macroscopic systems. Here, we discuss precise versions of this statement and confirm them for several simple models of $H$ and $\mathscr{H}_ν$.

AI.tldr: The paper formalizes and verifies the quantum Boltzmann entropy increase (second law) for simple models of Hamiltonian and macro-state decompositions.
AI.motivation: Goldstein et al. proposed that the quantum Boltzmann entropy $S_\mathrm{qB}$ predominantly increases with time for realistic macroscopic systems as a version of the second law. This claim needs precise formalization and verification for tractable models.
AI.method:
The system is a closed macroscopic quantum system in a pure state $\psi$ evolving unitarily under Hamiltonian $H$ on finite-dimensional Hilbert space $\mathscr{H}$. $\mathscr{H}$ is decomposed into orthogonal subspaces $\mathscr{H}_
u$ representing macro states, and quantum Boltzmann entropy is defined as $S_\mathrm{qB}(
u)=k_\mathrm{B}\log\dim\mathscr{H}_
u$. The authors discuss precise versions of the entropy-increase statement and test them for several simple models of $H$ and $\mathscr{H}_
u$.
AI.result: The precise versions of the entropy-increase statement are confirmed for several simple models of the Hamiltonian and macro-state decomposition.
AI.conclusion: The quantum Boltzmann entropy's predominant increase with time holds in the tested simple models, supporting the proposed quantum version of the second law.

title: Can the system dynamics remain structurally non-Markovian while its experimentally accessible memory signatures disappear?
comment: The manuscript spans the first 22 pages and includes 18 figures, followed by the appendices in the remaining
summary: We investigate how unresolved quasistatic disorder in system bath coupling affects non-Markovian dynamics in spin environments. The coupling is fixed within each experimental shot but varies between shots, so repeated shot tomography reconstructs a disorder averaged dynamical map. For a single spin bath with pure dephasing Ising interaction, disorder can drive a transition to CP-divisible dynamics for fixed bath preparations, with a critical strength set by bath polarization along the interaction axis. However, when the bath state fluctuates physically between shots, the averaged dynamics remain CP indivisible at any finite disorder strength. We extend these results analytically to inhomogeneously coupled pure dephasing baths of any number \(N\) of non-interacting spins. At any finite disorder strength, one unpolarized bath spin suffices to retain CP-indivisible dynamics, whereas a fully polarized bath yields Markovian (CP-divisible) dynamics. Dynamics with physically fluctuating bath states likewise remain non-Markovian (CP indivisible) at finite disorder for arbitrary \(N\) in the pure dephasing case. For anisotropic Heisenberg interactions, any nonzero transverse exchange eliminates the disorder driven transition to CP divisibility in a single spin bath. Exact diagonalization of anisotropic models with inhomogeneous couplings up to \(N=12\) reveals persistent trace distance revivals for fixed bath preparations, sampled Haar random preparations, and physically fluctuating bath states, showing that this effect of transverse exchange extends beyond a single bath spin. Increasing disorder still suppresses experimentally accessible revivals and can make memory effects unresolvable at finite measurement resolution even as the dynamics remain CP indivisible. Thus, transverse exchange and physical bath state fluctuations preserve dynamical indivisibility against unresolved coupling disorder.

AI.tldr: Unresolved quasistatic disorder in system-bath coupling is studied for non-Markovian spin dynamics; disorder can induce CP-divisibility for fixed pure-dephasing baths, but physical bath-state fluctuations and transverse exchange preserve CP-indivisibility.
AI.motivation: The paper addresses how shot-to-shot fluctuating (unresolved quasistatic) disorder in system-bath coupling influences the non-Markovianity of spin environments, a regime relevant to repeated-shot tomography where only a disorder-averaged dynamical map is accessible.
AI.method: Analytical treatment of pure dephasing Ising baths with inhomogeneous couplings for arbitrary N non-interacting spins, plus exact diagonalization of anisotropic Heisenberg models with inhomogeneous couplings up to N=12, comparing fixed bath preparations, Haar-random preparations, and physically fluctuating bath states.
AI.result: For a single pure-dephasing spin bath, disorder can drive a transition to CP-divisible dynamics at a critical strength set by bath polarization. With physically fluctuating bath states, averaged dynamics remain CP-indivisible at any finite disorder. For any N, one unpolarized spin suffices to retain CP-indivisibility, while a fully polarized bath yields Markovian dynamics. Any nonzero transverse exchange eliminates the disorder-driven transition to CP-divisibility; exact diagonalization up to N=12 shows persistent trace-distance revivals across all preparation types. Increasing disorder suppresses accessible revivals, potentially making memory effects unresolvable at finite measurement resolution despite underlying CP-indivisibility.
AI.conclusion: Transverse exchange and physical bath-state fluctuations preserve dynamical indivisibility against unresolved coupling disorder, while disorder primarily suppresses experimentally accessible non-Markovian signatures rather than the underlying CP-indivisibility.

title: $T$-efficient unitary synthesis via block-sparse Hamiltonian simulation
summary: We construct Clifford+$T$ circuits implementing arbitrary $n$-qubit unitaries with worst-case $T$-count $\widetilde{O}(N^{8/7})$ at constant operator-norm error, where $N=2^n$, improving the previous exponent $5/4$. The construction uses $\widetilde{O}(N^{6/7})$ clean ancillas. The main idea is to reduce the data addressed by each query to the block-encoding circuit for a sparse piece while controlling the additional simulation work needed to combine the pieces. We simulate a Hermitian logarithm of the target by flattening its traceless part with a two-layer random similarity transformation, randomly partitioning the transformed generator into block-sparse Hermitian pieces, and combining their evolutions using qDRIFT. For a target operator-norm error $ε\in(0,1/2)$, let $L=\log_2(N/ε)$, the qubit count plus the requested bits of accuracy. By successively correcting the approximation error, we obtain a circuit using $\widetilde{O}(N^{8/7}L^{3/7}+NL)$ $T$ gates and $\widetilde{O}(N)$ clean ancillas whenever $L\le N$. We also prove that, at constant precision, the exponent $8/7$ is optimal within a sequential block-SELECT model.

AI.tldr: This paper constructs Clifford+T circuits for arbitrary n-qubit unitaries with worst-case T-count Õ(N^{8/7}) at constant operator-norm error (N=2^n), improving the prior exponent 5/4, using Õ(N^{6/7}) clean ancillas, and proves 8/7 is optimal in a sequential block-SELECT model at constant precision.
AI.motivation: Prior Clifford+T constructions for arbitrary n-qubit unitaries had worst-case T-count scaling with exponent 5/4. Reducing this exponent lowers the resource cost of universal quantum simulation and circuit synthesis, motivating a better construction and an understanding of its optimality.
AI.method: The construction simulates a Hermitian logarithm of the target unitary: it flattens the traceless part with a two-layer random similarity transformation, randomly partitions the transformed generator into block-sparse Hermitian pieces, and combines their evolutions via qDRIFT. The key idea is to reduce the data addressed by each query to the block-encoding circuit for a sparse piece while controlling extra simulation work needed to combine pieces. Successive error correction refines the approximation using a parameter L = log2(N/ε) (qubits plus accuracy bits).
AI.result: Worst-case T-count Õ(N^{8/7}) at constant operator-norm error, improving the previous exponent 5/4, with Õ(N^{6/7}) clean ancillas. For target operator-norm error ε∈(0,1/2), the circuit uses Õ(N^{8/7}L^{3/7}+NL) T gates and Õ(N) clean ancillas whenever L≤N. The paper also proves that, at constant precision, the exponent 8/7 is optimal within a sequential block-SELECT model.
AI.conclusion: The work improves the T-count exponent for arbitrary n-qubit unitary synthesis to 8/7 and shows this exponent is optimal in a sequential block-SELECT model at constant precision, providing both an improved construction and a matching lower bound within that model.

title: Explicitly correlated ground states with a feedback-free variational hybrid algorithm
summary: Explicitly correlated methods, which represent dominant short-range correlations by a diagonal Jastrow-type correlator, are designed to accurately describe systems of strongly correlated electrons, such as the fully periodic 2D Fermi--Hubbard model. However, as the reference state is compact in momentum space whereas the correlator acts naturally in real space, there is a fundamental mismatch of bases that classical algorithms resolve only by restricting the reference or the correlator. Here we propose a hybrid algorithm in which a quantum processor prepares a low-entanglement momentum-space matrix product state (MPS), precomputed classically by the transcorrelated method at the cost of a nonvariational energy, rotates it to real space, and measures in bases fixed by the Hamiltonian. Because the measurement bases are independent of the correlator, the correlator can be variationally optimized entirely in classical post-processing with no quantum-classical feedback loop. We demonstrate our algorithm on 32 qubits of Quantinuum's H2-2 with a bond-dimension-4 MPS for the half-filled $4 \times 4$ lattice and achieve a relative ground-state energy error of $16 \pm 4\%$ after postselection, reduced to $3.5 \pm 0.5\%$ by calibration using low-order moments from the MPS. Compared with other feedback-free hybrid algorithms, even under generous assumptions, our method requires fewer samples than quantum-selected configuration interaction and fewer two-qubit gates than quantum Krylov methods.

AI.tldr: A hybrid quantum-classical algorithm combines a quantum-prepared momentum-space MPS with a variationally optimized Jastrow correlator in classical post-processing, achieving 3.5% ground-state energy error on a 4x4 Fermi-Hubbard lattice with 32 qubits.
AI.motivation: Explicitly correlated methods accurately describe strongly correlated electrons but face a fundamental basis mismatch: the reference state is compact in momentum space while the Jastrow correlator acts in real space. Classical algorithms resolve this only by restricting either the reference or the correlator, limiting accuracy for systems like the 2D Fermi-Hubbard model.
AI.method: A hybrid algorithm where a quantum processor prepares a low-entanglement momentum-space MPS (precomputed classically via the transcorrelated method at the cost of a nonvariational energy), rotates it to real space, and measures in Hamiltonian-fixed bases. Since measurement bases are independent of the correlator, the correlator is variationally optimized entirely in classical post-processing without any quantum-classical feedback loop.
AI.result: Demonstrated on 32 qubits of Quantinuum's H2-2 with a bond-dimension-4 MPS for the half-filled 4x4 lattice, achieving a relative ground-state energy error of 16 +/- 4% after postselection, reduced to 3.5 +/- 0.5% via calibration using low-order moments from the MPS. Compared to other feedback-free hybrid algorithms, it needs fewer samples than quantum-selected configuration interaction and fewer two-qubit gates than quantum Krylov methods under generous assumptions.
AI.conclusion: The proposed feedback-free hybrid algorithm efficiently unites quantum state preparation with classically optimized correlations, offering resource advantages over existing feedback-free hybrid approaches and accurately describing strongly correlated electron systems.

title: PULSUS: Direct Frequency-Domain Multidimensional Spectroscopy Beyond the Impulsive Rotating-Wave Approximation
summary:
We introduce PULSUS, a direct frequency-domain framework for multidimensional spectroscopy of open quantum systems beyond the impulsive rotating-wave approximation. Coherence-frequency intervals are represented through Liouvillian resolvents, while finite Gaussian pulses are incorporated through operator-valued functions of the field-free Liouvillian. This enables direct evaluation on Cartesian grids or arbitrary spectral coordinates while retaining molecular evolution during the pulse envelopes and, when required, the complete light--matter interaction.
  The implementation is validated against analytical and independent time-domain benchmarks and supports targeted spectral sampling that reduces the number of evaluated coordinates when the response is spectrally localized. A controlled hierarchy of finite-pulse, rotating-wave, short-pulse, and impulsive models separates the errors introduced by each approximation. For a coupled electronic dimer, the total impulsive-RWA error is nonmonotonic in pulse duration: an intermediate regime provides the highest accuracy, whereas ultrashort pulses expose coupling-enabled beyond-RWA pathways and longer pulses develop substantial finite-pulse corrections. These results show that the impulsive and rotating-wave approximations cannot be assumed to improve simultaneously and should be tested when quantitatively interpreting multidimensional spectra. PULSUS provides a direct frequency-domain framework for carrying out that comparison.

AI.tldr: PULSUS is a direct frequency-domain framework for multidimensional spectroscopy of open quantum systems that goes beyond the impulsive rotating-wave approximation, using Liouvillian resolvents and finite Gaussian pulses, and shows that impulsive and rotating-wave errors do not vanish simultaneously.
AI.motivation: Standard multidimensional spectroscopy relies on the impulsive and rotating-wave approximations (RWA), which are often assumed to be valid together. The paper questions this assumption, aiming to quantify and separate the errors introduced by finite-pulse, rotating-wave, short-pulse, and impulsive approximations in open quantum systems.
AI.method: PULSUS represents coherence-frequency intervals via Liouvillian resolvents and incorporates finite Gaussian pulses through operator-valued functions of the field-free Liouvillian. This allows direct evaluation on Cartesian grids or arbitrary spectral coordinates, retaining molecular evolution during pulse envelopes and the full light-matter interaction when needed. A controlled hierarchy of models (finite-pulse, RWA, short-pulse, impulsive) is used to isolate approximation errors.
AI.result: The implementation is validated against analytical and independent time-domain benchmarks and supports targeted spectral sampling that reduces evaluated coordinates for spectrally localized responses. For a coupled electronic dimer, the total impulsive-RWA error is nonmonotonic in pulse duration: an intermediate regime gives the highest accuracy, ultrashort pulses expose coupling-enabled beyond-RWA pathways, and longer pulses develop substantial finite-pulse corrections.
AI.conclusion: The impulsive and rotating-wave approximations cannot be assumed to improve simultaneously and must be tested when quantitatively interpreting multidimensional spectra. PULSUS offers a direct frequency-domain framework for performing this comparison.

title: Finite-energy two-way assisted capacities: Exact formulas for multimode loss and fading
summary: We study quantum communication, entanglement distribution, and secret-key generation through multimode bosonic loss and fading channels, assisted by local quantum operations and two-way classical communication. Using sector teleportation, we determine the exact two-way quantum and secret-key capacities of multimode pure-loss channels under a mean photon-number constraint, allowing arbitrary adaptive quantum protocols. We extend these results to continuous frequency-dependent loss under a power constraint and identify the optimal allocation of photons among optical modes. For constant loss over an unlimited bandwidth, we obtain a closed-form capacity proportional to the square root of power. For randomly varying loss, we determine exact finite-energy capacities when the channel realization is publicly revealed, distinguishing knowledge before and after transmission. When fading remains unobserved, we derive capacity bounds and explicit formulas for an on/off channel. We also establish strong-converse bounds, with exact thresholds for the deterministic loss models considered here, observed fading, and unobserved fading with finitely many possible transmissivities. Under mean energy constraints, these thresholds generally exceed the corresponding finite-energy capacities. These results guide energy allocation and provide benchmarks for energy-constrained optical quantum communication with multimode signals and variable loss.

AI.tldr: The paper determines exact two-way quantum and secret-key capacities of multimode bosonic loss and fading channels using sector teleportation, covering continuous frequency-dependent loss, constant loss over unlimited bandwidth, and observed/unobserved fading, along with strong-converse bounds.
AI.motivation: Multimode bosonic loss and fading channels are central to practical optical quantum communication, yet exact capacities under realistic energy and power constraints, arbitrary adaptive protocols, and fading uncertainty remain incompletely characterized. The work aims to provide exact capacities and benchmarks for energy-constrained optical quantum communication.
AI.method: The authors employ sector teleportation to compute exact two-way quantum and secret-key capacities of multimode pure-loss channels under a mean photon-number constraint, allowing arbitrary adaptive quantum protocols. They extend the analysis to continuous frequency-dependent loss under a power constraint, optimize photon allocation across optical modes, treat constant loss over unlimited bandwidth, and analyze randomly varying loss with channel realization revealed before or after transmission. For unobserved fading they derive bounds and explicit formulas for an on/off channel, and establish strong-converse bounds with exact thresholds.
AI.result: Exact two-way quantum and secret-key capacities are obtained for multimode pure-loss channels. For continuous frequency-dependent loss, the optimal photon allocation across modes is identified. For constant loss over unlimited bandwidth, a closed-form capacity proportional to the square root of power is derived. For randomly varying loss with public realization, exact finite-energy capacities are determined, distinguishing knowledge before versus after transmission. For unobserved fading, capacity bounds and explicit on/off channel formulas are given. Strong-converse thresholds are established and generally exceed finite-energy capacities under mean energy constraints.
AI.conclusion: The results provide exact capacities, optimal energy allocation strategies, and strong-converse benchmarks for energy-constrained multimode optical quantum communication and secret-key generation over loss and fading channels, guiding practical energy allocation.

title: Quantum-enhanced mechanical sensing with machine-learning estimation
summary: Massive mechanical oscillators couple directly to forces, accelerations and gravity, making them attractive probes of new physics and of quantum mechanics at macroscopic scales. Pushing sensitivities beyond the standard quantum limit for signals of unknown phase requires non-Gaussian quantum states, whose metrological advantage has so far been confined to lighter systems such as trapped ions. Here we operate a microgram-scale acoustic mode of a high-overtone bulk acoustic wave resonator as a phase-insensitive quantum-enhanced sensor. A transmon qubit prepares the mode in Fock states of up to seven phonons by optimal control, and resolves its phonon-number distribution after interaction with a weak resonant signal. Bayesian analysis yields a Fisher information five times the vacuum value, a 7.0 dB gain in signal-amplitude sensitivity over any classical probe state, irrespective of its energy, currently limited by state preparation infidelities. We then train a neural network on the measured sensor response to perform Bayesian estimation without any analytical model of the system, showing the same sensitivity gain with half the systematic bias. Our results establish acoustic resonators prepared in non-Gaussian states as quantum-enhanced probes for high-frequency gravitational waves, dark matter and wave-function collapse.

AI.tldr: A microgram-scale acoustic mode of a bulk acoustic wave resonator is prepared in phonon Fock states via a transmon qubit, achieving a Fisher information five times the vacuum value and a 7.0 dB phase-insensitive sensitivity gain, with a neural network matching this gain at half the systematic bias.
AI.motivation: Massive mechanical oscillators couple directly to forces, accelerations and gravity, making them attractive probes of new physics and macroscopic quantum mechanics. Surpassing the standard quantum limit for signals of unknown phase requires non-Gaussian quantum states, but their metrological advantage has so far been limited to lighter systems such as trapped ions.
AI.method: A transmon qubit prepares a microgram-scale acoustic mode of a high-overtone bulk acoustic wave resonator in Fock states of up to seven phonons using optimal control. The phonon-number distribution is resolved after interaction with a weak resonant signal, and Bayesian analysis extracts the Fisher information. A neural network is trained on the measured sensor response to perform Bayesian estimation without an analytical model of the system.
AI.result: Bayesian analysis yields a Fisher information five times the vacuum value, corresponding to a 7.0 dB gain in signal-amplitude sensitivity over any classical probe state regardless of its energy, currently limited by state-preparation infidelities. The neural-network estimator achieves the same sensitivity gain with half the systematic bias.
AI.conclusion: Acoustic resonators prepared in non-Gaussian states are established as quantum-enhanced probes for high-frequency gravitational waves, dark matter, and wave-function collapse.

title: Deterministic and programmable generation of mechanical multipartite entangled states
summary: Multimode mechanical resonators offer a large set of densely packed, long-lived bosonic modes within a single compact device, making them attractive for quantum simulation, quantum information processing, and quantum-enhanced sensing. Many such applications rely on multipartite entanglement, yet deterministic mechanical entanglement has so far been largely limited to pairs of modes. Here we demonstrate the deterministic and programmable preparation of multipartite entangled states among the phonon modes of a high-overtone bulk acoustic wave resonator coupled to a superconducting transmon qubit. By sequentially applying optimal-control-engineered isometries between the qubit and successive modes, we generate matrix product states of bond dimension two, including $W$, Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ), and cluster states. We fully characterize these states via quantum state tomography and certify genuine multipartite entanglement among up to four modes. We further demonstrate correlated-noise sensing by exploiting the complementary decoherence responses of the stored $W$ and GHZ states, isolating inter-mode phase correlations from local decoherence and placing quantitative bounds on collective dephasing. Our results establish a scalable approach to preparing multipartite entangled states in mechanical systems, with promising applications in multiparameter sensing and tests of quantum mechanics with massive objects.

AI.tldr: Deterministic, programmable preparation of multipartite entangled phonon states (W, GHZ, cluster) in a high-overtone bulk acoustic wave resonator coupled to a transmon qubit, using optimal-control isometries to generate matrix product states of bond dimension two, certified up to four modes, and applied to correlated-noise sensing.
AI.motivation: Multimode mechanical resonators provide densely packed, long-lived bosonic modes for quantum simulation, information processing, and sensing, but most applications require multipartite entanglement, which had been largely limited to pairs of modes. A scalable route to deterministic multipartite mechanical entanglement is needed.
AI.method: A high-overtone bulk acoustic wave resonator is coupled to a superconducting transmon qubit. Sequential optimal-control-engineered isometries between the qubit and successive phonon modes are applied to deterministically generate matrix product states of bond dimension two (W, GHZ, and cluster states). States are characterized via quantum state tomography and genuine multipartite entanglement certification, and correlated-noise sensing exploits complementary decoherence of W and GHZ states.
AI.result: Deterministic and programmable preparation of multipartite entangled phonon states, including W, GHZ, and cluster states, with full tomographic characterization and certified genuine multipartite entanglement among up to four modes. Correlated-noise sensing isolates inter-mode phase correlations from local decoherence and places quantitative bounds on collective dephasing.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes a scalable approach to preparing multipartite entangled states in mechanical systems, with promising applications in multiparameter sensing and tests of quantum mechanics with massive objects.

title: Relative-Entropy Geometry and Convergence in Nonconvex Wiretap Optimization
summary: We develop and analyze an entropic descent method for a nonconvex optimization problem on probability simplices arising in classical and quantum secure communication. The optimization variables describe a randomized encoder, allowing its input distribution and stochastic preprocessing to be optimized jointly. An exact relative-entropy identity yields a channel-independent majorization bound and an explicit mirror-descent iteration with a fixed unit step size. We establish quantitative descent, convergence of objective values, and stationarity of accumulation points on their support faces for arbitrary finite classical channels, without assuming degradedness or less noisiness. For strictly positive transition matrices, a square-root parametrization and a Kurdyka--Łojasiewicz argument establish finite length of the transformed trajectory and convergence of the entire sequence, including limits on the simplex boundary. For less-noisy channels, a restricted convex formulation admits global convergence with an explicit \(O(1/t)\) objective-error bound. We extend the relative-entropy construction to noncommuting quantum outputs and derive monotone alternating updates for covariant encoders, including correlated preprocessing over a fixed block. Numerical experiments compare the method with analytic benchmarks and constrained optimization, reveal multiple attracting values, and demonstrate strict improvements from stochastic preprocessing.

AI.tldr: The paper develops an entropic (mirror) descent method for nonconvex optimization over probability simplices arising in classical and quantum secure communication, jointly optimizing input distribution and stochastic preprocessing of a randomized encoder, with convergence guarantees and numerical validation.
AI.motivation: Optimization problems on probability simplices arise in classical and quantum secure communication, where the variables describe a randomized encoder whose input distribution and stochastic preprocessing must be optimized jointly. Existing methods typically require restrictive assumptions such as degradedness or less noisiness, and lack convergence guarantees for such nonconvex simplex-constrained problems.
AI.method: An exact relative-entropy identity yields a channel-independent majorization bound and an explicit mirror-descent iteration with a fixed unit step size. For strictly positive transition matrices, a square-root parametrization combined with a Kurdyka-Łojasiewicz argument is used. For less-noisy channels, a restricted convex formulation is adopted. The relative-entropy construction is extended to noncommuting quantum outputs, yielding monotone alternating updates for covariant encoders with correlated preprocessing over a fixed block.
AI.result: The authors establish quantitative descent, convergence of objective values, and stationarity of accumulation points on their support faces for arbitrary finite classical channels, without assuming degradedness or less noisiness. For strictly positive transition matrices, finite trajectory length and full sequence convergence (including boundary limits) are proved. For less-noisy channels, global convergence with an explicit O(1/t) objective-error bound is obtained. Numerical experiments reveal multiple attracting values and strict improvements from stochastic preprocessing.
AI.conclusion: The proposed entropic descent method provides a unified framework for optimizing randomized encoders on probability simplices in classical and quantum secure communication, with strong convergence guarantees under mild conditions, and demonstrates practical benefits of stochastic preprocessing.

title: $\mathsf{EFI}\Leftrightarrow\mathsf{1PRS}$
summary: A series of recent works has established EFI pairs as the "minimal" assumption for quantum cryptography. Recently, Cavalar et al. [CCC+26] showed that EFI pairs are equivalent to non-uniform expanding single-copy pseudorandom state generators (1PRS), and obtained a non-uniform meta-complexity characterization of EFI pairs. We remove the non-uniformity in their construction and prove that EFI pairs are equivalent to expanding 1PRS. As a corollary, we obtain the first uniform meta-complexity characterization of EFI pairs. Together with the equivalence of statistically verifiable one-way state generators and commitments proved by Batra and Jain [BJ24], this gives a quantum analogue of the classical equivalence between one-way functions, commitments, and pseudorandom generators.

AI.tldr: This paper removes the non-uniformity in Cavalar et al.'s [CCC+26] construction, proving EFI pairs are equivalent to expanding 1PRS and yielding the first uniform meta-complexity characterization of EFI pairs.
AI.motivation: EFI pairs have been established as the minimal assumption for quantum cryptography, and Cavalar et al. [CCC+26] showed EFI pairs are equivalent to non-uniform expanding single-copy pseudorandom state generators (1PRS), obtaining a non-uniform meta-complexity characterization. However, the non-uniformity in their construction is a limitation; removing it is desirable to strengthen the equivalence and obtain a uniform characterization.
AI.method: The authors remove the non-uniformity in the Cavalar et al. [CCC+26] construction, establishing a uniform equivalence between EFI pairs and expanding 1PRS.
AI.result: EFI pairs are proven equivalent to expanding 1PRS. As a corollary, the first uniform meta-complexity characterization of EFI pairs is obtained. Combined with the equivalence of statistically verifiable one-way state generators and commitments by Batra and Jain [BJ24], this yields a quantum analogue of the classical equivalence among one-way functions, commitments, and pseudorandom generators.
AI.conclusion: The non-uniformity is removed, upgrading the EFI-pair/1PRS equivalence to the uniform setting and providing a uniform meta-complexity characterization, thereby completing a quantum analogue of the classical OWF–commitment–PRG equivalence.

title: On the coincidence of discrete and continuous definitions of Entanglement of Formation
comment: 14 pages, preliminary vesion, any comments are welcome
summary:
It is proved that every Borel ensemble of pure states on a separable bipartite Hilbert space with finite average entanglement admits a countable ensemble with the same barycenter and arbitrarily small additional average entanglement. Consequently, the discrete and continuous versions of the Entanglement of Formation coincide on the whole space of states of infinite-dimensional bipartite quantum system (with infinite values allowed).
